Why it is open: 24 sessions give about 3-4 trials per event type. Thresholds of 80-90% and 95% confidence intervals cannot be supported. Calibration data is excluded from Go evidence.

B. Use a pooled or Bayesian rule across types. Workable with 24 sessions. Per-type thresholds weaken. go_detection_thresholds; KPI dashboard.

impaired_confidence_and_suspension Impaired-confidence status if a divergence is unresolved at 72 hours or a Tier 2 clock expires; automatic suspension of the affected site or event class at 7 days unresolved divergence or Tier 3 expiry; lifting needs double-key proposed threshold User requires these procedures. 72 h and 7 days follow the risk file; suspension is rule-based and pre-signed by both co-chairs, which reconciles 'automatic' with 'no unilateral suspension'.
discrepancy_clock_tiers Tier 1 = 24 hours; Tier 2 = 72 hours; Tier 3 = 14 days; one extension of up to 50% per case by the joint adjudication unit with written reasons proposed threshold Risk file; extension rule matches Decision 12 option 2 (e.g. Tier 1 up to 36 h, Tier 3 up to 21 days). Unresolved-discrepancy age KPI uses these limits.
ledger_sync_and_detection_bounds Local event recorded immediately; counterpart sync target <1 hour (TBD); divergence detected within 2 hours; sync divergence >4 hours escalated; target resolution of technical sync divergence within 4 hours. Ledger: two independently verifiable national copies, signed entries, offline backups, operational and stress-tested on non-covered equipment by Month 4 (2027-02-08) proposed threshold Assumption and risk files; the 1-hour figure is provisional and validated in the Month 4 (2027-02-08) stress test and calibration. The Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) resilience test in the risk file is rejected: the system cannot exist before the instrument and funds. The word 'blockchain' is not used.
ledger_identity_forensics Joint forensic panel (3-5 specialists per country, equal national membership, no casting vote) issues identity findings within 48 hours; failing consensus, co-chairs decide within 24 hours; shift-handover cross-signing by mirrored inspectors; no separate neutral escrow copy in the baseline decision Combines Decision 7 options 1 and 3. 48 + 24 = 72 hours, matching the 72-hour impaired-confidence point. Escrow copy rejected: it adds a high-value target and a hosting-trust issue. The 'binding' panel authority is rejected where it would let one side be overruled.
evidence_corroboration_rule Fixed pre-agreed rule: identity confirmed when at least 2 independent layers agree, including physical inspection plus identifier match and, where available, validated attestation; if attestation is unavailable, physical inspection plus 2 independent records; no single source decisive; provenance recorded proposed threshold Risk file offers this only as an example; adopted as the proposed fixed rule (Decision 2 option 1) to be validated in calibration; changes only by recorded protocol change.
inspection_zones Fixed narrow, physically marked zones limited to staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas; operator-run redaction audited by inspectors; three-tier infraction protocol (Tier 3 = immediate access suspension, co-chair review within 24 hours) decision Decision 3 option 1. Dynamic zones rejected for delay inside the escalation clocks. Tier 3 'no co-chair review' is rejected; removal is precautionary and reviewed under double-key.
vendor_refusal_ladder Ladder: vendor request (day 0), operator escalation (day 1), examiner notified (day 2), exam (day 3-5), report (day 10); then clean-room or validated attestation; unverifiable at day 10, one extension of up to 50% (to day 15) proposed threshold Review file Day-10 clock; 10 x 1.5 = 15. Its 3-4 week clean-room estimate does not fit; clean rooms must be pre-staged, otherwise equipment is classed unverifiable.
vendor_fallback_pool Pre-bind top 8-12 vendors per site; pool of 3-5 independent examiner labs per country and 2 clean-room facilities per geography, agreements signed by Month 4 (2027-02-08) estimate Review file counts. Dates moved from Month 0.5-1 to Month 4 (2027-02-08), with operator/vendor binding after domestic authority exists.
calibration_exercise Pre-clock calibration/dry run on non-covered equipment (100-150 reserved units per site, 50-100 events per site), Months 4-5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08), outside the 90 days; calibration data sets and validates thresholds but is excluded from the Go/Modify/Stop evidence base decision Merges Decision 5 option 2 and dry-run ideas. Shifted from Months 1-2 (2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08) because sites (Month 2 = 2026-12-08), schedule (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) and authority (Month 3.5 = 2027-01-23) must exist first; runs with inspectors as they are approved (16-week vetting ends about Month 4.2 = 2027-02-14; full roster Month 5 = 2027-03-08). Reuse of calibration data rejected: data that set the thresholds would make the verdict look tuned; cost is fewer verdict events. Counts are review-file estimates.
threshold_lock All Go/Modify/Stop thresholds double-key signed and locked by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), before the first formal blind exercise; later change only by recorded protocol change decision Calibration ends Month 5 (2027-03-08), lock Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), clock starts Month 6 (2027-04-08) (ordering feasible). The assumptions' Month 3 (2027-01-08) lock precedes calibration, so rejected.
go_detection_thresholds Go requires blind-challenge detection of at least 90% unreported arrival, 85% substitution, 80% record falsification (provisional, TBD); false positives <5% proposed threshold Assumptions file; unsupported figures validated in calibration; the other event types (delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal, reluctant operator) get targets set before the Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) lock.
go_other_thresholds Go also requires parity within 20%; unresolved discrepancies <10% of events; unverifiable equipment <5% per site; zero unresolved ledger divergence >7 days; zero material asymmetric-access incidents; zero material IP/CI incidents proposed threshold Assumptions file, all provisional. Parity review is triggered within 5 days when the gap exceeds 20%.
modify_and_stop_rules Modify: correctable weakness remains (detection 70% up to target; unverifiable 5-10%). Stop: access asymmetric and unresolved; unverifiable >10% at a site; a government shields an operator; evidence divergence unresolved; funding withheld; detection <70% proposed threshold Reconciles Go <5% with the file's >10% site-fail line; the 70% floor is the lower edge of the file's Modify band. Bands are contiguous: <5% Go, 5-10% Modify, >10% Stop.

Cost: 434 x 0.5 = 217M; x 0.625 = 271M; x 0.5625 = 244M; 750/244 = 3.1 years. The 1,200-1,500 FTE claim is rejected: it contradicts the file's own 640-840. Rate and headcount provisional.

Vetting begins at Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) (not Month -2, already past); candidate pool about 260 per country (217 x 1.2 = 260).

Cap resolves conflict with '5-10 exercises per site'. Multiple blind events may be seeded per session; event counts for statistical validity are TBD and validated in calibration.
maintenance_emergency_rules Emergency = repair restoring a failed system within 4 hours, with continuous recording and a report within 24 hours; >3 emergencies per site per month triggers independent review; >50% ruled non-emergency triggers escalation proposed threshold Risk file figures, provisional.

Release verification sampled at 20-30% monthly, provisional.
kpi_dashboard_provisional Dashboard KPIs: blind detection by event type, FN/FP, identity confidence (at least 90% of intake events confirmed, TBD), latency, divergence/reconciliation time, parity, discrepancy age, unverifiable equipment, vendor refusals, IP/cyber incidents, production disruption, funding timeliness, audit exceptions proposed threshold User-listed KPIs. Unsupported values are provisional/TBD and validated in the Months 4-5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) calibration.
scope_and_success_statement Success covers only monitored changes at participating declared sites; no total-capacity estimate, workload or model-weight inspection, hidden-facility claim, foreign-hosted coverage or comprehensive AI-governance regime user constraint User constraints; the final decision must state this limit.

Focus and Context

The Consortium is a bilateral US–China 90-day Phase One verification mechanism testing the detection of undeclared changes to frontier computing equipment at 4 matched declared datacenters (2 US, 2 China). Uncontrolled frontier AI computing threatens both nations; the Consortium bridges mutual suspicion with a double-key governed, reciprocal verification design featuring mirrored inspection teams, a replicated tamper-evident ledger with split-custody cryptographic signing, and pre-committed decision thresholds. Success measures whether bilateral verification of critical technology is possible without surrendering intellectual property or strategic autonomy. Phase One runs Months 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) after mandatory entry-condition certification (Months 0–6 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-04-08), issuing a Go, Modify, or Stop decision at Month 10 (2027-08-08).

Purpose and Goals

Establish a joint US–China verification mechanism to detect undeclared arrivals, installations, removals, transfers, and maintenance changes to declared frontier computing equipment at matched datacenters. Success criteria: (1) blind-challenge detection ≥90% unreported arrivals, ≥85% substitutions, ≥80% record falsification (proposed thresholds); (2) reciprocal-access parity within 20%; (3) <5% equipment unverifiable per site; (4) zero unresolved ledger divergence >7 days; (5) credible double-key Go/Modify/Stop decision. Scope excludes total-capacity estimates, workload inspection, hidden-facility claims, and comprehensive AI governance. Success is bounded to monitored changes at participating declared sites only.

Key Deliverables and Outcomes

Phase One delivers: (1) operational replicated tamper-evident ledger with <1-hour sync target and 2-hour divergence detection; (2) mirrored national inspection teams (217 per country, 36 per site) executing 24/7 shift coverage; (3) joint forensic-identity panel issuing equipment-identity findings within 48 hours; (4) blind-challenge detection exercises across all 7 event types, at most 2 sessions per site per month (up to 6 per site, 24 across 4 sites in 90 days), scored by independent testing unit; the 50-100 events per site belong to the Months 4-5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) calibration on non-covered equipment, excluded from Go evidence, and detection-threshold statistical power is provisional; (5) calibration-validated Go/Modify/Stop thresholds double-key locked by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23); (6) final bilateral decision with documented justification by Month 10 (2027-08-08). Phase Two (contingent on Go) expands to additional sites using validated procedures and established infrastructure.

Timeline and Budget

USD 5.0B total (50/50 split, hard cap per user constraint). Envelope allocation: ledger/attestation USD 1.25B; site prep + operator comp. USD 1.0B; inspectors/training USD 0.75B; secure facilities USD 0.75B; testing/red teams USD 0.5B; legal USD 0.25B; contingency USD 0.5B. Entry-condition gates: instrument Month 2 (2026-12-08), sites Month 2 (2026-12-08), appropriations Month 3 (2027-01-08), authority Month 3.5 (2027-01-23), vendor agreements Month 4 (2027-02-08), inspector approval Month 5 (2027-03-08), certification Month 6 (2027-04-08). Phase One: Months 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08, exactly 90 days). Decision: Month 10 (2027-08-08). Contingency worst-case exposure ~USD 515M (gate delay USD 300M + site replacement USD 200M + examiner overrun USD 11M + incidents USD 4M), exceeding reserve by ~USD 15M.

Risks and Mitigations

Critical risks: (1) Domestic authority enactment delay defers Phase One indefinitely, consuming USD 150–300M holding cost (3-month slip); mitigation: bilateral steering committee with weekly reviews, and a Month 9 (2027-07-08) double-key extend-or-stop backstop (no conditional start). (2) Vendor refusal cascades leave material equipment unverifiable; mitigation: early generic (non-site-specific) outreach with letters of intent from Tier-1 vendors by Month 1 (2026-11-08) and examiner/clean-room pool soundings by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) as early-warning indicators only (draft, not locked); per-site vendor lists after the Month 2 (2026-12-08) site ratification; binding agreements and examiner/clean-room MOUs signed by Month 4 (2027-02-08). (3) Ledger divergence forensic authority not pre-authorized; automatic suspension triggers on technical faults; mitigation: start forensic panel vetting at Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) with provisional appointment pending clearance, draft evidence hierarchy and shift-signing procedures by Month 1 (2026-11-08) (not locked), stress-test by Month 4 (2027-02-08).

Audience Tailoring

The primary audience is bilateral national-security leadership, appropriations authorities, and domestic legislators in both countries. Secondary audiences are participating operators, equipment vendors, and treaty-implementation teams. The tone is formal, procedural, and impartial; emphasis is on reciprocity, auditability, and double-key governance rather than trust. The plan assumes expertise in arms-control verification, treaty law, and bilateral diplomacy; technical details on cryptography, ledger design, and supply-chain evidence are deferred to specialist annexes. Budget and schedule constraints are paramount; the USD 5.0B cap and 18-month appropriation window are hard constraints, not targets.

Action Orientation

Immediately (Month 0 = 2026-10-08): establish bilateral entry-conditions steering committee, decompose domestic authority enactment per country, nominate forensic-panel candidates, prepare inspector counterintelligence vetting (starts Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23). By Month 0.5 (2026-10-23): begin generic (non-site-specific) vendor soundings and RFQs, start forensic panel and inspector vetting submissions. By Month 1 (2026-11-08): draft forensic-panel charter and evidence hierarchy (not locked), collect letters of intent as early-warning indicators only, and begin generic examiner and clean-room soundings. After Month 2 (2026-12-08) site ratification: identify top 8–12 vendors per site; binding agreements and examiner/clean-room MOUs by Month 4 = 2027-02-08; any optional pre-clock dry run on non-covered equipment runs after Month 2 (2026-12-08) (or on a generic non-site basis) and does not start the 90 days. By Month 5.5 (2027-03-23): complete calibration exercise, validate and double-key lock all decision thresholds. By Month 6 (2027-04-08): certify all 7 entry conditions, issue go-ahead for Phase One clock start. Owner: bilateral co-chairs and named steering-committee leads per country.

Overall Takeaway

The Consortium succeeds or fails on execution of three critical entry-condition workstreams in parallel: (1) domestic authority legislative enactment (uncontrolled external dependency, high schedule risk); (2) vendor pre-binding and examiner pre-qualification (bilateral negotiation, high cost-overrun risk); (3) ledger forensic authority operationalization (bilateral trust and technical complexity, high procedure-gap risk). If all three stay on the entry-gate milestones (binding agreements by Month 4 = 2027-02-08), Phase One clock can start on schedule at Month 6 (2027-04-08) with calibrated thresholds and pre-authorized escalation procedures, enabling a credible Go/Modify/Stop verdict. If any slips >4 weeks (about USD 50–100M holding cost, estimate; a 3-month slip costs USD 150–300M), cascading delays compress calibration and force unvalidated threshold lock-in, raising Modify-outcome probability from a baseline of 15–25% (estimate) to 30–40% (estimate). Geopolitical resilience and bilateral political commitment are decisive; the mechanism works only if both sides sustain trust through procedural friction.

Feedback

To strengthen this executive summary: (1) Specify which legislative acts each country must pass (US: Congressional ratification + domestic access authority statute; China: State Council directive) with realistic timelines per government to support the Month 3.5 (2027-01-23) authority-enactment deadline, removing ambiguity around critical-path identification. (2) Document preliminary vendor-willingness assessment or RFQ results for at least 3–5 Tier-1 vendors per country to validate the cost assumptions (budget USD 20–30k per exam, late USD 50–100k per exam, 80% cooperation probability) and reduce contingency-exposure tail risk. (3) Add a quantitative sensitivity analysis: if gate slips 4 weeks, what is the Modify-outcome probability and does recalibration of thresholds prevent it? (4) Clarify the fallback operator or alternate site procurement timeline (4–8 weeks, USD 50–200M estimate) with actual Site-2 nominee candidate profiles so replacement viability can be pre-assessed. (5) Include a bilateral political-commitment letter from both leaders (or cabinet-equivalent) by Month 0 (2026-10-08) confirming high-level backing and the 18-month appropriation hold, reducing reputational and financial collapse risk from geopolitical deterioration.

Part 2: Supporting analysis

Persuasive elevator pitch.

Bilateral AI Frontier-Technology Verification Consortium

Project Overview

Uncontrolled frontier AI computing represents a strategic threat neither the US nor China can ignore. The Consortium bridges the gap between suspicion and verification: a 90-day test of a revolutionary bilateral mechanism to detect undeclared changes to computing equipment at declared datacenters. Built on double-key governance, mirrored inspection teams, and cryptographic ledgers that neither side controls alone, it proves that transparent verification of critical technology is possible without surrendering intellectual property or national security. A Go decision at Month 10 (2027-08-08) enables phased expansion to additional sites and sets the precedent for reciprocal high-stakes verification between great powers.

Target Audience

US and Chinese national security leadership, appropriations authorities, datacenter operators in both countries, and equipment vendors. Secondary audiences include bilateral treaty implementers, arms-control verification experts, and domestic legislatures that must authorize funding and access authority. The pitch assumes skepticism about reciprocity and sensitivity to intellectual property exposure, with emphasis on the mechanism's safeguards and the strict gating that keeps the test clean.

Risks and Mitigation Strategies

  • Entry delays (vetting, domestic authority) can slip the clock by 3 months and cost USD 150–300M; weekly co-chair reviews, strict gate milestones and a Month 9 (2027-07-08) backstop force decision
  • Ledger divergence or sync failure triggers automatic escalation and suspension protocols; a joint forensic panel (3–5 per side, 48-hour findings) resolves contested identities
  • Vendor refusal leaves equipment unverifiable; a pre-bound pool of 3–5 examiner labs per country and clean-room facilities per region (agreements by Month 4 = 2027-02-08) provide fallbacks on a day-10 ladder
  • Intellectual property exposure causes consent withdrawal; narrow marked zones, audited operator redaction and three-tier infraction enforcement limit risk

A contingency fund of USD 500M (double-key release, fast lane up to USD 50M) covers each identified fallback individually; the coincident worst case (about USD 515M) exceeds it by about USD 15M (estimate).

Metrics for Success

Detection performance:

  • Blind-challenge detection of at least 90% unreported arrivals, 85% substitutions, 80% record falsifications (provisional, validated in pre-clock calibration)
  • False positives <5%
  • Reciprocal-access parity within 20% (proposed threshold); an unresolved asymmetry leads to a Stop decision

Operational and integrity targets:

  • Unresolved discrepancies <10% of events
  • Unverifiable equipment <5% per site
  • Zero unresolved ledger divergence >7 days
  • Zero material asymmetric-access or IP/counterintelligence incidents

Schedule and governance:

  • Entry certification achieved by Month 6 (2027-04-08)
  • Phase One completes on schedule
  • Final decision issued by Month 10 (2027-08-08) with documented, double-key justification that both governments accept as principled rather than tuned

Stakeholder Benefits

  • US and China: Credible bilateral verification mechanism with no known precedent, insulating critical-technology policy from mutual suspicion
  • Operators: Participation protects them against unilateral sanctions and provides legitimate channel for compliance
  • Vendors: Pre-binding agreements and fallback examiner pools remove surprise and uncertainty
  • Legislatures and treasuries: Auditable, principled decision process with double-key governance ensures no single side manipulates the outcome
  • Inspectors: Carefully vetted, rotating teams with conduct oversight and separation of duties reduce espionage and coercion risk

Reciprocal-access parity within 20% (proposed threshold) is required; material asymmetric access that stays unresolved leads to suspension of the affected site or event class and a Stop decision.

Ethical Considerations

The Consortium respects sovereignty and reciprocity: each government vets its own inspectors, administers its own spending, and holds a veto on every decision. No unilateral truth-seeking. Bounded zones and operator-run, audited redaction protect intellectual property and workload confidentiality; evidence is filtered before it leaves the site. Inspector conduct is governed by joint rules and monitored by both sides; no single-country surveillance. Equipment identity is confirmed only when independent evidence layers agree; no source is decisive. The 90-day gate ensures setup is complete and honest before evidence-gathering begins. The design assumes absent trust and builds reciprocity through mechanism, not hope.

Collaboration Opportunities

Not applicable. This is a sovereign public-sector national-security verification program; sponsorship, partnerships and market demand do not apply. Oversight stays with the two governments, their legislatures and auditors under double-key governance.

Long-Term Vision

A single 90-day test is a proof-of-concept; success enables a phased expansion to additional sites and equipment classes, deepening bilateral transparency on frontier computing without requiring unified global AI governance. Over 24–36 months, the mechanism can mature into a standing body managing multiple sites, vendor relationships and continuous evolution of the covered-equipment schedule. This is not comprehensive AI governance; it is focused, bounded, bilateral, and auditable verification of the equipment changes most likely to signal an asymmetric leap. It buys time for policy to catch up with technology and demonstrates that great-power verification of frontier technology is possible. Long-term impact: a new generation of verification practice between actors with conflicting interests but aligned recognition that uncontrolled change is worse for both.

Mission Justification and Appropriations Governance

Call to action: Not applicable (no revenue, investors, customers or ROI). The actions below are mission and appropriations requirements.

  • Authorize bilateral instrument signature by Month 2 (2026-12-08), commit appropriations (USD 2.5B per country) by Month 3 (2027-01-08), and nominate sites for joint pairing within 4 weeks
  • Designate co-chairs and establish a weekly entry-condition review cadence starting Month 0 (2026-10-08)
  • Parallel domestic action: Each government initiates domestic access-authority legislation, inspector vetting, and operator engagement
  • Gate compliance: The 90-day clock starts only when all 7 entry conditions are certified; this gating protects both sides against setup failure
  • Backstop decision: Failure to reach certification by Month 9 (2027-07-08) triggers a double-key decision to extend or stop

Goal Statement: Establish The Consortium, a jointly governed US–China mechanism, and run a 90-day Phase One test (Month 6 = 2027-04-08 to Month 9 = 2027-07-08) verifying arrivals, installations, removals, transfers, maintenance changes and decommissioning of declared frontier-relevant computing equipment at 4 matched declared sites, ending in a Go/Modify/Stop decision at Month 10 (2027-08-08). Success covers only monitored changes at participating declared sites.

SMART Criteria

  • Specific: Verify declared-equipment changes at 4 participating declared datacenters (2 US, 2 China) using layered evidence and a replicated tamper-evident ledger, then issue a double-key Go, Modify or Stop decision. Excluded: total capacity estimates, workload or model-weight inspection, hidden-facility claims, foreign-hosted infrastructure, comprehensive AI governance.
  • Measurable: Blind-challenge detection of at least 90% unreported arrivals, 85% substitutions, 80% record falsification (provisional, TBD); false positives <5%; parity within 20%; unverifiable equipment <5% per site; unresolved discrepancies <10% of events; zero unresolved ledger divergence >7 days (all proposed thresholds, validated in calibration).
  • Achievable: Both leaders provide political backing and authority to compel participation. USD 5.0 billion (user constraint) is split 50/50 and fully allocated to envelopes. Scope is deliberately narrow. Trust, legal symmetry and willingness to expose technology are not assumed, so the design relies on bounded zones, mirrored teams and double-key governance.
  • Relevant: Both governments view uncontrolled frontier AI as a threat to national security and political control. A credible verification mechanism provides mission justification and public value through auditable, reciprocal change verification. Revenue, investors, customers, ROI and market demand: Not applicable.
  • Time-bound: Start ASAP at Month 0 (2026-10-08). Entry conditions certified by Month 6 (2027-04-08), outside the 90 days; Phase One runs Months 6-9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08); final decision at Month 10 (2027-08-08). If certification is not reached by Month 9 (2027-07-08), co-chairs decide by double-key to extend or stop.

Resources Required

  • Replicated tamper-evident ledger, attestation, evidence and secure communications systems (USD 1.25B envelope)

  • About 434 FTE full-time mirrored inspection, technical, legal, cybersecurity, counterintelligence, translation, audit, logistics and adjudication staff (estimate)

Related Goals

  • Refine the confidential, versioned covered-equipment schedule as hardware evolves

  • Pre-bind top 8-12 vendors per site; 3-5 examiner labs per country and 2 clean-room facilities per geography by Month 4 (2027-02-08); day-10 ladder
  • Narrow marked zones, audited operator redaction, three-tier infraction protocol, inspector rotation and continuous access-log audit
  • Calibrate on non-covered equipment, lock thresholds by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), cap exercises at 2 sessions per site per month in staging, spare, maintenance or expansion areas; contingency released by double-key, fast lane up to USD 50M

Primary Decisions

The vital few decisions that have the most impact.

The five Critical levers address the plan's core tensions. Reciprocity Gate Stringency covers validity versus delay. Evidence Layer Weighting covers detection versus gaming. Inspection Zone Boundary Design covers coverage versus IP exposure. Challenge Exercise Independence covers credibility versus disruption. Threshold Calibration covers principled versus tuned verdicts. The High levers cover execution, including ledger integrity, vendor refusal, escalation, staffing and vetting. No major dimension is missing, though funding-timeliness governance is only implicit.

Decision 1: Reciprocity Gate Stringency

Lever ID: 223d1d0c-a010-4db9-a7a0-d8ccbfe91ea7

The Core Decision: Defines the entry certification that separates setup work from the 90-day Phase One test. Its scope covers the signed instrument, appropriations, domestic access authority, approved sites and inspectors, operator and vendor participation, and the provisional schedule. Success is measured by the time from Month 0 (2026-10-08) to certified start, the number of authority gaps found before the clock, and zero setup failures later logged as verification failures.

Why It Matters: This sets how completely the bilateral instrument, appropriations, domestic access authority, site selection, inspector approvals, operator and vendor participation, and covered-equipment schedule must be in place before the 90-day clock starts. A strict gate protects the validity of the test but can delay the start indefinitely. A loose gate starts the clock sooner but lets setup failures be recorded as verification failures.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Require every entry condition to be fully satisfied and independently certified by both sides before the Phase One clock starts, with no partial-start exceptions.
  2. Allow a conditional start in which the clock begins at each site once the conditions for that site are met, while the final decision requires all matched sites to complete the full period.
  3. Run a pre-clock dry-run gate where both sides exchange access credentials and test the legal authority on non-covered equipment, so that authority gaps appear before the formal clock and the entry certification.

Trade-Off / Risk: A strict gate keeps the 90-day result clean, but it hands whichever side is slower on domestic authority an effective veto over timing. Conditional starts reduce that leverage but weaken the comparability of the evidence.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Provisional Covered-Equipment Schedule Governance, because a certified gate requires an adopted schedule before the clock, and strengthens Go-Modify-Stop Threshold Calibration by keeping the evidence base clean enough to support a defensible decision.

Conflict: Trades off against Matched Site Selection Logic and Inspector Vetting and Conduct Oversight: a strict gate makes slow site pairing or inspector approval a timing veto, and one side's domestic delay can postpone the whole test.

Justification: Critical, Critical because it separates setup failure from verification failure and sets the start of the 90-day clock. It links to schedule governance, site selection, vetting and attestation ceremonies, and controls the validity-versus-delay trade-off. Without it, the Go/Modify/Stop evidence base is unreliable.

Decision 2: Evidence Layer Weighting

Lever ID: e7828387-7f21-405e-99a5-6c0a7388782d

The Core Decision: Specifies how attestation, physical inspection, customs and shipment records, identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure changes and witnessed movement combine into an equipment-identity confidence rating. It is the main driver of false-negative and false-positive rates and of how contested a finding becomes. Success is measured by detection rates in blind exercises, reproducible ratings across the mirrored teams, and provenance recorded for every layer.

Why It Matters: This decides how cryptographic attestation, physical inspection, customs and shipment records, identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure changes, and witnessed movement are combined into an equipment-identity confidence rating. Because no single source is decisive, the weighting rules drive both false-negative and false-positive rates. Rules that are too rigid can be learned and gamed by an adversary, while rules that are too flexible invite disputes.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Use a fixed, pre-agreed corroboration rule in which identity is confirmed only when a stated minimum number of independent evidence layers agree, with every layer's provenance recorded.
  2. Use a graded confidence score derived from layer-specific reliability ratings that are recalibrated after each exercise round by the independent testing group, with both co-chairs approving every change.
  3. Randomize which evidence layers are required for each event, with the selection drawn from a sealed double-key schedule, so that no operator can predict which checks to defeat.

Trade-Off / Risk: Fixed rules are easy to audit but easy to defeat once learned. Graded scoring adapts, but it adds numerical judgment that both governments may contest, and recalibrating thresholds mid-test can be seen as moving the goalposts.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Works with Attestation Trust Root Provenance, since weighting is only as sound as the independently validated trust roots feeding it, and with Challenge Exercise Independence, which supplies the blind results used to justify or recalibrate weights.

Conflict: Conflicts with Go-Modify-Stop Threshold Calibration and Inspection Zone Boundary Design: recalibrating weights mid-test can appear to move the goalposts, and narrow zones deprive some layers of evidence, which limits any weighting scheme.

Justification: Critical, Critical because it is the analytical core. It sets equipment-identity confidence and drives false-negative and false-positive rates. It connects to attestation, vendor fallbacks, zones, exit evidence, escalation and thresholds, and it controls the rigidity-versus-gaming trade-off.

Decision 3: Inspection Zone Boundary Design

Lever ID: 43d82cbd-f2f1-4301-a824-728309d4358d

The Core Decision: Defines the physical and informational perimeter of inspection: which staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas inspectors may enter, and how evidence is filtered before leaving the site. It balances detection coverage against protection of workloads, weights, topology and source code. Success is measured by zero material IP or counterintelligence incidents, no consent withdrawal, and low blind-spot exposure in challenge exercises.

Why It Matters: This sets where inspectors may go, what they may see, and how evidence is filtered before it leaves the site. Narrow zones protect workloads, model weights, topology, and source code but leave blind spots where substitution or unreported arrivals can occur. Wider zones raise detection but increase intellectual-property and counterintelligence exposure, which could cause one government to withdraw consent.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Fix narrow, physically marked zones limited to staging, spare inventory, and maintenance bays, with all evidence passing through an operator-run redaction step that inspectors can audit.
  2. Use dynamic zones that expand only for a specific event under double-key approval and shrink when it closes, with escorted access and time-limited credentials.
  3. Place sealed capture instruments in the zones that record only identifiers, seals, and movement metadata, so that inspectors review filtered data and enter only when a discrepancy is open.

Trade-Off / Risk: Narrower zones lower the spying risk that makes governments hesitate, but the unseen margin is where a motivated operator would hide a substitution. Dynamic zones add procedural friction that can delay access and create their own disputes.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Maintenance and Third-Party Access Scheduling, because defined zones and escort rules make vendor visits predictable and auditable, and supports Inspector Vetting and Conduct Oversight by limiting what any inspector can observe.

Conflict: Trades off against Evidence Layer Weighting and Discrepancy Escalation Clock and Tiering: tighter zones reduce evidence available for identity confidence, while dynamic expansion needs double-key approvals that consume time inside escalation deadlines.

Justification: Critical, Critical because it controls the central trade-off between detection coverage and IP and counterintelligence exposure, which decides whether governments keep consenting. It constrains evidence availability, escalation timing, exit witnessing and maintenance access, and it determines where blind spots exist.

Decision 4: Challenge Exercise Independence

Lever ID: 746e5a9f-762c-4613-b60a-be2ef724f82f

The Core Decision: Determines who designs, schedules and scores the live challenge exercises, and how blind inspectors and operators remain to timing and content. It governs the credibility of the detection evidence behind the final decision. Key measures: blind-challenge detection by event type, false negatives and positives, comparability of scenarios between countries, and absence of production disruption during exercises in staging and spare areas.

Why It Matters: This sets who designs and runs the unreported arrival, substitution, record-falsification, delayed-access, disputed-identity, vendor-refusal, and reluctant-operator exercises, and how blind they are to inspectors. More independence improves the credibility of the detection results that drive the Go/Modify/Stop decision. It also raises coordination cost and the risk that an exercise disturbs live operations.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Have an independent testing unit designed by both governments run all exercises in a sealed, double-key schedule, with only a small group at each site aware of the timing.
  2. Let each country's red team design challenges against the other country's inspectors, then have an audit unit review the scenarios for fairness and comparability before and after the exercise.
  3. Blend scheduled exercises with unannounced real events, scoring detection on real changes recorded in the ledger as well as the staged ones, to measure performance under ordinary conditions.

Trade-Off / Risk: Cross-national red teams create adversarial realism but also an opening for each side to design tests that favor its own inspectors. Mixing in real events increases validity but risks interfering with active computational work.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Supplies the detection evidence that Go-Modify-Stop Threshold Calibration needs to be meaningful, and tests Discrepancy Escalation Clock and Tiering and Vendor Refusal Response Path under realistic, unannounced conditions.

Conflict: Competes with Mirrored Shift Roster Architecture and Maintenance and Third-Party Access Scheduling: stronger blindness and real-event mixing raise coordination burden and the risk of disturbing live operations in staging and maintenance areas.

Justification: Critical, Critical because blind exercises produce the detection evidence that justifies the Go/Modify/Stop decision and recalibrates weights. It feeds thresholds, escalation and vendor paths, and balances credibility against live-operations disruption and coordination burden.

Decision 5: Go-Modify-Stop Threshold Calibration

Lever ID: 453c25dc-ed80-4416-8ce0-d6182c098250

The Core Decision: Determines how numeric and categorical thresholds for detection, false results, parity and unverifiable equipment are justified, validated and locked before the final Go, Modify or Stop decision. It also fixes which failures are non-negotiable Stop conditions. Success means a verdict that both governments accept as principled rather than tuned, with provisional figures validated against calibration or exercise evidence and recorded under double-key authority.

Why It Matters: Determines how KPI thresholds for detection, false results, parity and unverifiable equipment are set and validated before the final decision. Thresholds fixed in advance by the co-chairs make the verdict resistant to post-hoc bargaining, but they rest on provisional figures that exercises may show to be mis-set. Thresholds derived from exercise results are better grounded but invite accusations of tuning the outcome.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Fix every decision threshold and its justification before the first exercise, double-key sign them, and permit changes only through a documented protocol change that is itself recorded.
  2. Set provisional thresholds, run a short pre-test calibration exercise outside the formal clock, and lock the validated values before the blind challenges that feed the decision.
  3. Define the decision as a rule over trends and categories rather than single numbers, with independent auditors scoring each KPI band and a rubric stating which failure types are non-negotiable Stop conditions.

Trade-Off / Risk: Locking thresholds early protects against motivated reinterpretation, but because most figures start as provisional, a mis-set value can force a Modify outcome that reflects the yardstick rather than the mechanism's real performance.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Challenge Exercise Independence, because independently run blind challenges give locked thresholds credible test data, and Discrepancy Escalation Clock and Tiering, whose unresolved-age limits become explicit decision criteria.

Conflict: Early locking constrains Challenge Exercise Independence and Reciprocity Gate Stringency, since mis-set values cannot be adjusted after exercises reveal real performance, while calibration-based options risk accusations of tuning the outcome.

Justification: Critical, Critical because it turns KPI evidence into a verdict both governments accept as principled rather than tuned. It governs the lock-early versus calibrate-later trade-off and ties together exercises, escalation clocks, the gate and unverifiable-equipment outcomes.

Secondary Decisions

These decisions are less significant, but still worth considering.

Decision 6: Matched Site Selection Logic

Lever ID: 6afa6cea-9703-48d2-90d2-e450c9a1a380

The Core Decision: Sets the method for choosing the small matched set of declared datacenters and the degree of resemblance required between US and Chinese sites. It governs whether the Go decision rests on representative conditions or convenient ones. Success is measured by documented parity in event frequency, vendor mix and staging layout (thresholds TBD), neither side steering selection, and inclusion of sites hard enough to test detection.

Why It Matters: This determines how the small set of declared datacenters is chosen and how closely the US and Chinese sites must resemble each other in equipment turnover, vendor mix, and layout. Tighter matching strengthens reciprocal-access parity and the fairness of the Go decision. It narrows the candidate pool and may favor sites that are unrepresentative of real operations.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Select sites by structured pairing on observable characteristics such as event frequency, staging layout, and vendor dependence, with each side vetoing sites it considers to be unrepresentative.
  2. Let each government nominate a longer list, then use a sealed double-key draw from the jointly vetted shortlist, so neither side can steer the other toward easy or hard sites.
  3. Include one deliberately hard site on each side, chosen for complex maintenance and third-party access, so the test exercises the protocol under the conditions where it is most likely to fail.

Trade-Off / Risk: Pairing improves parity on paper, but sites that look matched on paper can differ in operator cooperation and vendor leverage. Random draws offset gaming but may select sites too trivial to prove detection credibility.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Enables Challenge Exercise Independence, since comparable or deliberately hard sites make blind-challenge results meaningful, and supports Vendor Refusal Response Path by exposing real vendor dependence early in the test.

Conflict: Constrains Reciprocity Gate Stringency, because a narrow candidate pool and mutual vetoes delay site agreement before the clock starts. It also conflicts with Inspection Zone Boundary Design where hard sites carry wider exposure.

Justification: High, High because site matching drives reciprocal-access parity and whether challenge results are meaningful. It enables exercise independence and vendor exposure, but constrains the gate and zone design. Its influence is large but mostly upstream and one-time, rather than a continuing hub.

Decision 7: Ledger Divergence Handling

Lever ID: b0c99e97-ad27-4a5a-88e4-f36b872595c1

The Core Decision: Governs how the two national ledger copies record events locally, synchronize within a bounded delay, and are reconciled when they disagree. It turns divergence into a defined status: technical fault, impaired confidence, or automatic suspension. Success is measured by synchronization latency, ledger divergence counts, reconciliation time, and the absence of unresolved divergence, which is a Stop condition.

Why It Matters: This determines how the two national ledger copies record events locally, synchronize within a bounded delay, and resolve differences when they disagree. Immediate local recording preserves evidence but permits temporary divergence. The resolution method decides whether divergence is a technical fault, a trigger for impaired-confidence status, or grounds for automatic suspension.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Treat any unresolved divergence beyond a stated time bound as an automatic impaired-confidence trigger, with reconciliation led by a jointly staffed forensic team working from both copies.
  2. Maintain a third neutral escrow record held under double-key control, used only to arbitrate which copy diverged, with its access rules fixed in the bilateral instrument.
  3. Reconcile through event-by-event cross-signing by mirrored inspectors at shift handover, so most divergences are caught within hours rather than at periodic synchronization.

Trade-Off / Risk: A neutral escrow record helps settle disputes, but it creates a new high-value target and a trust question about who hosts it. Handover cross-signing is cheap and fast but depends on inspectors acting at the same shift boundaries.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Strengthens Discrepancy Escalation Clock and Tiering, since divergence time bounds can feed the same escalation tiers, and Mirrored Shift Roster Architecture, because shift handover cross-signing uses the paired national teams already on duty.

Conflict: Constrains Mirrored Shift Roster Architecture and Go-Modify-Stop Threshold Calibration: handover cross-signing depends on aligned shifts, and strict divergence triggers may produce Stop outcomes from technical faults rather than real concealment.

Justification: High, High because unresolved divergence is an explicit Stop condition, and the lever links ledger integrity to escalation tiers, rosters and thresholds. It defines the status path from technical fault to automatic suspension. It is narrower than the evidence and zone hubs.

Decision 8: Vendor Refusal Response Path

Lever ID: 1475e028-59f1-437f-b52e-a71b5b2afb8a

The Core Decision: Defines the sequence of fallback evidence routes when a critical manufacturer, maintenance provider or logistics firm refuses cooperation, and the documentation needed before equipment is labelled unverifiable. Scope covers who decides each step, how trade-secret exposure is bounded, and how refusals are timed within the 90-day test. Key metrics: vendor-refusal outcomes, unverifiable-equipment count, and time from refusal to disposition.

Why It Matters: This defines what happens when a critical manufacturer, maintenance provider, or logistics firm declines to cooperate. The fallback options (vendor-supervised testing, filtered evidence, accredited independent examiners, clean-room procedures, validated attestation) vary in evidentiary strength and in exposure of trade secrets. The chosen order determines how often equipment ends up classified as unverifiable, which can fail a site.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Apply a fixed escalation ladder that starts with vendor-supervised testing and moves to accredited independent examiners and clean-room examination, with each step documented before unverifiable status is assigned.
  2. Require operators to contract vendor cooperation as a condition of covered-equipment installation, so refusal becomes a pre-installation barrier rather than a post-arrival crisis.
  3. Pre-qualify a pool of independent examiners and validated attestation methods for each equipment class before the clock starts, so refusals can be bypassed without negotiating with the vendor.

Trade-Off / Risk: Contract-based binding shifts risk to operators and slows deployments, which may breach the no-disruption commitment. Independent examiners reduce vendor leverage but need enough vendor-specific knowledge to be credible, which refusing vendors may deny them.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Works with Evidence Layer Weighting, which sets how much substitute evidence from examiners or clean rooms counts, and with Attestation Trust Root Provenance, since validated attestation is a fallback route when a vendor withholds access.

Conflict: Strains Maintenance and Third-Party Access Scheduling, because contract-binding or escalation steps delay maintenance windows, and Go-Modify-Stop Threshold Calibration, since a stricter ladder raises unverifiable counts that can fail a site.

Justification: High, High because it determines how often equipment becomes unverifiable, which can fail a site. It governs a fundamental tension between evidence sufficiency and trade-secret exposure, and it interacts with attestation, weighting, maintenance and escalation clocks.

Decision 9: Mirrored Shift Roster Architecture

Lever ID: da397295-b325-4d20-af2c-35654594f345

The Core Decision: Sets the full-time headcount and rostering model per site: shift coverage, mirrored national pairing, leave cover, separation of duties and surge reserve. It is the main driver of the personnel envelope and of vetting workload before the clock starts. Key measures: coverage gaps by shift, event-recording latency, roster fill rate, inspector turnover, and surge activation time.

Why It Matters: Determines how many full-time inspectors, technicians and adjudicators are needed per participating site, based on shift coverage, leave cover and separation of duties. A leaner roster conserves the USD 750 million personnel envelope but leaves thin cover during leave or surge. A deeper roster improves continuity and detection at night and weekends, but enlarges the counterintelligence vetting load and the entry-condition timeline for approving inspectors.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Staff each site with a fixed round-the-clock mirrored roster sized to peak expected equipment traffic, accepting higher fixed payroll in exchange for uninterrupted coverage of staging and maintenance areas.
  2. Staff each site with a core day-shift mirrored roster and a rapid-call duty team that activates on declared arrivals or maintenance windows, trading continuous presence for lower cost and a bounded detection gap.
  3. Rotate inspectors across paired sites on a scheduled and randomized basis so that neither operator nor vendor can predict who is present, using a shared bench that doubles as the surge reserve.

Trade-Off / Risk: A randomized rotation pool defeats operator familiarity and cuts idle headcount, but it multiplies travel, clearances and information-barrier handoffs, and it could break the shift continuity that separation-of-duties rules depend on.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Enables Inspector Vetting and Conduct Oversight by fixing how many people need clearance, and supports Inspection Zone Boundary Design by determining who can staff bounded zones continuously across shifts.

Conflict: Trades off against Inspector Vetting and Conduct Oversight, since deeper or rotating rosters enlarge the counterintelligence vetting load and entry timeline, and against Challenge Exercise Independence, which needs small, discreet groups.

Justification: High, High because it is the main driver of the personnel envelope, coverage gaps and vetting workload. It connects to vetting, zones, divergence cross-signing, exit witnessing and exercise discretion. It mostly sizes capability rather than shaping the core verdict logic.

Decision 10: Attestation Trust Root Provenance

Lever ID: 1e85fd29-a525-4d04-ac84-b263511f158e

The Core Decision: Decides who creates, holds, validates and can revoke the cryptographic roots behind device-identity attestation, and therefore how far attestation can be trusted as one evidence layer. It frames resistance to unilateral forgery, key-ceremony security and exposure of vendor secrets. Key measures: equipment-identity confidence, attestation validation failure rate, key-custody audit exceptions, and ceremony delay.

Why It Matters: Sets who generates, holds and validates the cryptographic keys and device-identity roots behind attestation evidence. A jointly generated root limits unilateral forgery, but it needs hardware and ceremonies that each side may distrust. Choices here shape equipment-identity confidence and determine how much weight attestation can carry among the layered evidence sources, none of which is decisive.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Run a joint key ceremony in a shared secure facility with split custody, so neither government alone can mint or revoke attestation credentials for covered equipment.
  2. Maintain two independent national attestation roots that cross-validate each other's claims, accepting duplicate infrastructure cost in return for the removal of any shared trusted component.
  3. Delegate attestation validation to accredited third-country laboratories that hold no key material and re-derive device identity from physical measurement, treating cryptographic claims only as corroboration.

Trade-Off / Risk: Split custody avoids unilateral forgery, but a joint ceremony facility becomes a high-value espionage target and a single point of delay, while third-country labs introduce a political dependency neither government fully controls.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Strengthens Evidence Layer Weighting by giving attestation a defensible weight, and supports Ledger Divergence Handling by providing a trusted identity basis for reconciling conflicting national ledger entries.

Conflict: Conflicts with Vendor Refusal Response Path when vendors withhold attestation hooks, and with Reciprocity Gate Stringency, as joint ceremonies and facilities may lengthen entry conditions and create a shared espionage target.

Justification: High, High because it decides how much weight cryptographic attestation can carry and whether unilateral forgery is possible. It supports evidence weighting and ledger reconciliation, but it is one layer among several, with no single source decisive.

Decision 11: Provisional Covered-Equipment Schedule Governance

Lever ID: 70f3602e-c67e-401a-9efc-9e60c8862cdb

The Core Decision: Governs how the confidential, versioned, manufacturer-neutral schedule defining covered equipment is drafted, amended and protected during Phase One. It balances stable test baselines against hardware evolution and threshold gaming. Key measures: amendment count and cycle time, disputes over coverage, share of real changes falling outside the schedule, and double-key approval timeliness.

Why It Matters: Controls how the confidential, versioned technical schedule of covered equipment is drafted, amended and kept manufacturer-neutral. Frequent amendment keeps coverage aligned to evolving hardware but creates repeated double-key negotiation points and potential disputes over what counts. A stable schedule is predictable, but it may become obsolete or leave a threshold-gaming gap during the test.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Freeze the schedule for the full Phase One test and defer all revisions to the Go/Modify/Stop decision, ensuring a stable baseline for measuring detection performance.
  2. Allow scheduled amendment windows with double-key approval and a short notice period, letting specialists add equipment categories while keeping all changes recorded in the ledger.
  3. Define coverage by function and risk-relevance criteria evaluated by a standing technical panel, and have each side submit sealed candidate lists that are reconciled only at the panel stage.

Trade-Off / Risk: A frozen schedule gives clean test data, but any mid-test hardware shift would leave real changes outside coverage, so the exercise results could overstate how well the mechanism works against current equipment.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Provides the scope basis for Matched Site Selection Logic and Inspection Zone Boundary Design, and gives Challenge Exercise Independence a clear, comparable set of equipment classes against which detection is scored.

Conflict: Tension with Challenge Exercise Independence and Go-Modify-Stop Threshold Calibration: frequent amendments disturb clean test baselines, while a frozen schedule risks results that overstate detection against current hardware.

Justification: Medium, Medium because it sets the scope baseline for site selection, zones and exercise scoring and creates tension between a stable baseline and hardware evolution. It is largely a scoping input to higher-level levers rather than a hub of the core trade-offs.

Decision 12: Discrepancy Escalation Clock and Tiering

Lever ID: de71d074-72ff-46d0-bec4-aae42aa77c9a

The Core Decision: Defines severity tiers, clock start events, and expiry consequences for every open discrepancy, from minor record mismatches to disputed equipment identity. Its scope includes who may pause a clock, what counts as resolution, and how aged items feed the unresolved-discrepancy-age KPI. Success means timely closure without turning administrative lag into a spurious Stop trigger within the 90-day window.

Why It Matters: Sets time limits and severity tiers for resolving discrepancies, which determines unresolved-discrepancy age and when automatic suspension fires. Short clocks force prompt resolution and deter stalling, but increase false suspensions during a short test. Long clocks give room for fact-finding but allow unresolved items to accumulate and cloud the final decision.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Apply short fixed deadlines by severity tier, with automatic suspension of the affected site or event class when a clock expires, prioritizing deterrence over fact-finding thoroughness.
  2. Use extendable clocks that a joint adjudication unit may lengthen once per case with written reasons, balancing fact-finding against the risk of indefinite delay.
  3. Run an independent technical referee panel that can issue a non-binding evidential opinion before the clock expires, giving co-chairs a shared factual basis without removing their double-key authority.

Trade-Off / Risk: Automatic suspension on expiry removes the option to stall, but in a 90-day test it can turn routine paperwork lag into a Stop trigger, distorting the dashboard and the final decision.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Works with Go-Modify-Stop Threshold Calibration, since fixed tier deadlines supply the unresolved-age thresholds the verdict relies on, and with Evidence Layer Weighting, which gives adjudicators a defensible basis for closing items before a clock expires.

Conflict: Tight clocks trade off against Vendor Refusal Response Path, where clean-room or accredited-examiner routes take longer than deadlines allow, and against Maintenance and Third-Party Access Scheduling, whose post-event reviews can age out.

Justification: High, High because it defines when automatic suspension fires and supplies the unresolved-age thresholds behind the verdict. It conflicts with vendor routes and maintenance reviews, and short clocks risk turning administrative lag into spurious Stop triggers.

Decision 13: Exit Disposition Assurance Depth

Lever ID: 8809b39b-c070-479f-bf53-dae39ec692d6

The Core Decision: Sets the evidentiary standard for assigning each departure one of the five dispositions: witnessed destruction, verified permanent disablement, transfer to another participating site, documented release beyond the monitored system, or unresolved. It determines inspector presence at recycling, destruction and transit points, and how honestly the ledger records the limit of knowledge. Key metrics are the share of departures per disposition and re-entry detection in exercises.

Why It Matters: Controls how much evidence is needed before a departure is labelled witnessed destruction, permanent disablement, transfer or release. Deeper witnessing reduces the chance that equipment re-enters use unseen, but it requires inspectors at recycling, destruction and transit points that may sit outside the inspection zone. Shallower witnessing keeps the boundary clean but increases the share of departures recorded as released beyond the monitored system or unresolved.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Witness every destruction or disablement end-to-end with inspectors present at the process, including at third-party facilities, and record chain of custody until the equipment is demonstrably unusable.
  2. Witness the departure at the site boundary and the receiving party's acknowledgement, then record the disposition as released beyond the monitored system without claiming further knowledge.
  3. Apply full witnessing to a randomly selected subset of departures chosen after the fact, and record the remainder at boundary-level assurance, using the sample to estimate reliability of declared dispositions.

Trade-Off / Risk: Full end-to-end witnessing is the most defensible against re-entry claims, but it stretches inspectors into third-party sites and blurs the agreed boundary the plan insists must never be implied beyond.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Reinforces Evidence Layer Weighting by supplying chain-of-custody and destruction evidence for departures, and supports Ledger Divergence Handling because a clearly bounded disposition record leaves fewer ambiguous exit entries to reconcile between national copies.

Conflict: Deeper witnessing pulls against Inspection Zone Boundary Design, since inspectors at third-party facilities extend beyond bounded zones, and strains Mirrored Shift Roster Architecture by requiring mirrored staff for off-site, travel-heavy events.

Justification: Medium, Medium because it sets the evidence standard for departures and keeps the knowledge boundary honest. It is an important protocol, but it mostly affects one event class and trades off with zone design and rosters without governing the system's core conflicts.

Decision 14: Inspector Vetting and Conduct Oversight

Lever ID: 54ab2b1c-93af-4168-a9fc-e9dbe66f2dd4

The Core Decision: Governs how inspectors are screened, approved, rotated and monitored so they cannot be used for intelligence collection or coerced by their own services. It also covers conduct rules, access-log audit, discipline and replacement. Because inspector approval is a mandatory entry condition, it sets the pace of start-up. Success is measured by zero substantiated collection incidents, timely approvals and reciprocal acceptance of each side's roster.

Why It Matters: Defines how approved inspectors are screened, rotated and monitored so that they cannot be used for intelligence collection or be coerced by their own service. Strict vetting and rotation reduce espionage and capture risk, but they lengthen the entry-condition timeline for approving inspectors and reduce accumulated site familiarity. Looser oversight shortens onboarding but invites mutual suspicion that can collapse reciprocity.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Subject inspectors to joint bilateral review of their conduct, with rotation across sites and a standing mirrored counterintelligence unit that audits each inspector's access logs and notes.
  2. Allow each government to vet and discipline its own inspectors under shared published conduct rules, with the counterpart empowered only to veto an individual and request replacement.
  3. Pair every inspector with a counterpart observer from the host country for all activities, accepting reduced independence in exchange for continuous transparency about what the inspector sees and records.

Trade-Off / Risk: Joint conduct review builds mutual confidence, but giving each side visibility into the other's personnel files and access logs is itself a sensitive disclosure that either government may resist.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Strengthens Mirrored Shift Roster Architecture by supplying a trusted, rotatable pool for mirrored teams, and supports Reciprocity Gate Stringency because credible conduct controls make each government more willing to grant counterpart access.

Conflict: Strict vetting and rotation constrain Mirrored Shift Roster Architecture through slower approvals and lost site familiarity, and joint personnel-file review conflicts with Reciprocity Gate Stringency where either government resists disclosure.

Justification: High, High because inspector approval is a mandatory entry condition that sets start-up pace and mutual trust. It addresses the espionage-versus-speed tension and links to rosters, the gate and zones, but it is more of an enabling control than a core strategy choice.

Decision 15: Maintenance and Third-Party Access Scheduling

Lever ID: 6f1dc358-8cd8-4a5c-84a1-ba37cd139bf2

The Core Decision: Sets how maintenance, repair and vendor visits are notified, escorted, sealed and logged in spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas so hardware changes stay visible without halting computation. Beyond the scheduling mechanics, it defines what qualifies as an emergency and the abuse controls on it. Key metrics are the share of changes with inspector coverage, emergency-use frequency and production disruption.

Why It Matters: Governs how maintenance, repair and vendor visits are announced, escorted and logged so that they are visible without interrupting active computational work. Advance-notice scheduling gives inspectors time to prepare and keeps disruption low, but it blocks urgent repairs and creates an incentive to misclassify emergencies. Open-ended emergency access protects uptime but opens a route for unlogged hardware changes.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Require advance notice for all maintenance and third-party access, with inspectors present at the start and end of each window and sealed work areas during the intervening period.
  2. Create a rapid-response emergency lane where operators may proceed immediately but must file a continuous recording and a post-event inspector review, with repeated emergency use triggering escalation.
  3. Consolidate all hardware-affecting maintenance into pre-agreed recurring windows with inspector teams on standby, and defer non-urgent work outside those windows.

Trade-Off / Risk: Pre-agreed windows reduce disruption and ease inspector planning, but a rigid schedule invites operators to bypass it through claimed emergencies, so the emergency lane's abuse controls decide whether the design holds.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Vendor Refusal Response Path by giving a predictable window in which vendor-supervised testing or escorted access can be arranged, and feeds Evidence Layer Weighting with maintenance records and witnessed movement as independent evidence layers.

Conflict: Fixed windows and standby teams strain Mirrored Shift Roster Architecture by raising peak staffing demand, and an emergency lane conflicts with Discrepancy Escalation Clock and Tiering, as repeated emergencies create discrepancies needing fast resolution.

Justification: Medium, Medium because it manages the uptime-versus-visibility trade-off for hardware changes and feeds maintenance evidence into weighting. It matters operationally, especially through the emergency lane, but it mainly supports other levers such as zones, vendor paths and rosters.

Choosing our strategic path.

The Strategic Context

Understanding the core ambitions and constraints that guide our decision.

Ambition and Scale: Sovereign, bilateral US–China program with USD 5 billion (user constraint) split 50/50. Scope is deliberately narrow: verify declared-equipment changes at a small matched set of datacenters. Staffing is large, with full-time mirrored units. It is high-stakes in geopolitical terms but bounded in technical scope, with explicit exclusions: no total-capacity estimates, no workload or weight inspection, no hidden-facility claims.

Risk and Novelty: Novel and politically high-risk, with no known precedent for bilateral verification of frontier computing equipment (not verified). Trust is assumed absent. The main risks are IP and counterintelligence exposure, consent withdrawal, asymmetric access, vendor refusal, and ledger divergence. The plan is a 90-day test whose outcome (Go/Modify/Stop) depends on credible and defensible evidence, so it needs a conservative, auditable design rather than an exploratory one.

Complexity and Constraints: High operational complexity: shift coverage, mirrored teams, separation of duties, a replicated tamper-evident ledger, Intake and Exit Protocols, and third-party access. Hard constraints: mandatory entry conditions that sit outside the 90-day clock; double-key authority with no casting vote; exercises limited to staging, spare, maintenance or expansion areas with no interruption of active computation; bounded zones and filtered evidence; KPI thresholds that must be justified, with unsupported figures marked provisional and validated.

Domain and Tone: Government national-security and fiscal-accountability tone. It is formal, procedural, and neutral on trust. It is not commercial. Emphasis is on auditability, reciprocity, protection of sensitive technology, and principled decision rules.

Holistic Profile: A cautious, rules-first, audit-heavy sovereign verification pilot. It is built to produce a clean, defensible, mutually acceptable Go/Modify/Stop result. That calls for strict entry gating, bounded inspection zones, independent blind exercises kept away from live production, and pre-committed decision criteria. Adaptive or exploratory mechanisms are secondary to predictability and non-reinterpretability.

The Path Forward

This scenario aligns best with the project's characteristics and goals.

The Fixed-Rules Bastion

Strategic Logic: Predictability, auditability and minimal exposure of sensitive technology come first. Every entry condition is certified before the clock starts. Corroboration rules, zone boundaries and decision thresholds are fixed and double-key signed in advance. A single independent testing unit runs the exercises on a sealed schedule. This minimizes room for reinterpretation, goalpost disputes and production disruption. In exchange, it accepts slower entry, more exposure to learned evasion, and a higher chance that a mis-set provisional figure drives a Modify outcome.

Fit Score: 8/10

Why This Path Was Chosen: Fully certified entry conditions match the plan's explicit gate-before-clock logic. Fixed narrow zones, operator-run auditable redaction, fixed corroboration rules and double-key-signed thresholds fit the low-trust, IP-protective, audit-centred posture. The main weakness is that fixed provisional thresholds may be mis-set; the plan's own Modify outcome and the protocol-change route partly absorb this.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Reciprocity Gate Stringency: Require every entry condition to be fully satisfied and independently certified by both sides before the Phase One clock starts, with no partial-start exceptions.
  • Evidence Layer Weighting: Use a fixed, pre-agreed corroboration rule in which identity is confirmed only when a stated minimum number of independent evidence layers agree, with every layer's provenance recorded.
  • Inspection Zone Boundary Design: Fix narrow, physically marked zones limited to staging, spare inventory, and maintenance bays, with all evidence passing through an operator-run redaction step that inspectors can audit.
  • Challenge Exercise Independence: Have an independent testing unit designed by both governments run all exercises in a sealed, double-key schedule, with only a small group at each site aware of the timing.
  • Go-Modify-Stop Threshold Calibration: Fix every decision threshold and its justification before the first exercise, double-key sign them, and permit changes only through a documented protocol change that is itself recorded.

The Decisive Factors:

  • Gate: the plan treats signed instruments, appropriations, domestic authority, sites, inspectors, vendor participation and the equipment schedule as mandatory entry conditions outside the 90 days. Full certification before the clock is the direct expression of this. It also keeps setup failures from being logged as verification failures.
  • Low trust and IP protection: narrow, marked zones with auditable operator-run redaction fit the bounded-zone, filtered-evidence requirement. They limit counterintelligence exposure and the risk of consent withdrawal.
  • No goalpost disputes: fixed corroboration rules and double-key-signed thresholds support a Go/Modify/Stop verdict that neither government can reinterpret. Provisional figures remain marked and are changed only through recorded protocol changes.
  • Pioneer's Gambit is less suitable: conditional starts, real-event scoring and randomized evidence rules conflict with the entry conditions and the no-disruption constraint, and they invite disputes.
  • Pragmatic Foundation is less suitable: per-round recalibration and dynamic zones add negotiation friction and delay inside the escalation clocks, at the cost of the stability the decision needs.

Alternative Paths

The Pioneer's Gambit

Strategic Logic: Detection is tested under realistic, unpredictable conditions. Per-site conditional starts remove either government's timing veto. Randomized evidence checks, sealed capture instruments and blended real-event scoring make the mechanism hard to game, and show whether it works in ordinary operations rather than only in staged ones. The cost is higher procedural complexity, more risk of friction with active computational work, and greater exposure to disputes over judgment-based scoring. Both sides must accept that risk to learn faster.

Fit Score: 3/10

Assessment of this Path: Conditional per-site starts contradict the plan's mandatory entry conditions. Blending unannounced real events into scoring conflicts with the requirement not to interrupt active computation. Randomized evidence rules and trend-based judgment add dispute risk that an adversarial, low-trust setting cannot absorb.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Reciprocity Gate Stringency: Allow a conditional start in which the clock begins at each site once the conditions for that site are met, while the final decision requires all matched sites to complete the full period.
  • Evidence Layer Weighting: Randomize which evidence layers are required for each event, with the selection drawn from a sealed double-key schedule, so that no operator can predict which checks to defeat.
  • Inspection Zone Boundary Design: Place sealed capture instruments in the zones that record only identifiers, seals, and movement metadata, so that inspectors review filtered data and enter only when a discrepancy is open.
  • Challenge Exercise Independence: Blend scheduled exercises with unannounced real events, scoring detection on real changes recorded in the ledger as well as the staged ones, to measure performance under ordinary conditions.
  • Go-Modify-Stop Threshold Calibration: Define the decision as a rule over trends and categories rather than single numbers, with independent auditors scoring each KPI band and a rubric stating which failure types are non-negotiable Stop conditions.

The Pragmatic Foundation

Strategic Logic: A pre-clock dry run exposes authority and credential gaps on non-covered equipment before the formal clock starts. This keeps the 90-day test clean without handing a veto to the slower side. Graded evidence scoring, dynamic event-specific zones and an independent sealed exercise schedule add adaptability. Calibrating thresholds outside the formal clock and locking them before the blind challenges keeps the yardstick fixed for the decision. Every adaptive element stays under double-key control.

Fit Score: 6/10

Assessment of this Path: The dry run on non-covered equipment and the pre-test calibration of provisional thresholds suit the plan's 'provisional, then validate' requirement. However, recalibrating evidence weights after each round invites goalpost disputes. Dynamic zones add double-key delays that can interfere with the delayed-access tests and expand exposure.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Reciprocity Gate Stringency: Run a pre-clock dry-run gate where both sides exchange access credentials and test the legal authority on non-covered equipment, so that authority gaps appear before the formal clock and the entry certification.
  • Evidence Layer Weighting: Use a graded confidence score derived from layer-specific reliability ratings that are recalibrated after each exercise round by the independent testing group, with both co-chairs approving every change.
  • Inspection Zone Boundary Design: Use dynamic zones that expand only for a specific event under double-key approval and shrink when it closes, with escorted access and time-limited credentials.
  • Challenge Exercise Independence: Have an independent testing unit designed by both governments run all exercises in a sealed, double-key schedule, with only a small group at each site aware of the timing.
  • Go-Modify-Stop Threshold Calibration: Set provisional thresholds, run a short pre-test calibration exercise outside the formal clock, and lock the validated values before the blind challenges that feed the decision.

Purpose

Purpose: business

Purpose Detailed: Large-scale, sovereign public-sector national-security and governmental initiative, not a for-profit venture. It covers strategic planning and program/project management for a bilateral verification institution: a replicated tamper-evident ledger, an Intake Protocol and Exit Protocol, mirrored full-time inspectorates, double-key co-governed decision-making, live challenge exercises, KPI-based evaluation, and a final Go/Modify/Stop decision. Scope is limited to monitored changes at participating declared sites. The program is funded by appropriations (USD 2.5 billion from each country) and involves cross-border governance, infrastructure, and fiscal accountability. Under the classification rules, governmental, societal-scale and infrastructure initiatives count as "business" even though the plan has no commercial or profit motive.

Topic: The Consortium: a jointly governed US–China verification mechanism for declared frontier-relevant computing equipment changes (arrivals, installations, removals, transfers, maintenance changes, decommissioning) at a small matched set of declared datacenters, with a 90-day Phase One operational test and a USD 5 billion budget split 50/50

Domain

Primary domain: Arms Control Verification

Secondary domains: Hardware Supply Chain Security, Treaty Law, Counterintelligence and Information Security

Rationale: Arms Control Verification is the outcome discipline with the highest importance × specificity (25). Its mission is bilateral verification of declared equipment changes under mutual distrust. Bilateral Program Management is also an outcome but scores lower (20) and is a delivery vehicle. Treaty Law, Counterintelligence and Information Security, and the method candidates are subordinate.

Disciplines this project involves:

Plan Type

This plan requires one or more physical locations. It cannot be executed digitally.

Explanation: The plan is physical. It sets up a bilateral inspection and verification mechanism for computing equipment at declared datacenters in the United States and China, and almost every part of it needs a real-world presence.
