Quarterly auditor-attestation report preparation (internal working meetings 2–3 weeks before publication). Quarterly results briefing to BESC (1–2 hours). Ad-hoc meetings to investigate audit exceptions or material findings flagged by BESC within 24 hours.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Ledger integrity audit: cryptographic signing validation, sync-divergence counts, offline backup testing, forensic findings on disputed identities
  • Evidence-handling audit: chain-of-custody verification, intake/exit protocols, vendor-refusal escalations, documentation completeness and accuracy
  • Entry-condition compliance: tracking of bilateral instrument, appropriations, domestic authority, site selection, inspector vetting, operator/vendor binding, equipment schedule; flags for any condition >4 weeks behind plan
  • Spending variance analysis: actual vs. planned expenditure per envelope, cost-center reconciliation, large-tranche authorization (>USD 25M)
  • Personnel vetting status: clearance validation, rapid-replacement pool pre-vetting, single-person critical-function check
  • Exercise audit: scenario fairness and realism, blind maintenance, scoring objectivity, statistical analysis of detection rates and false rates
  • KPI dashboard monthly: detection rates by event type, false positive/negative counts, identity confidence, sync divergence resolution time, parity metrics, discrepancy age, unverifiable counts, vendor outcomes, production disruption, funding timeliness, audit exceptions
  • Quarterly attestation findings: summary of key audit results, material findings, recommended corrective actions, validation of Phase One credibility

Escalation Path: Audit exceptions or material findings (e.g., ledger divergence >7 days unresolved, spending variance >5%, vetting gaps, exercise-integrity concerns) are escalated to BESC within 24 hours with recommended corrective actions. If BESC disputes an auditor finding, the auditor may be asked to provide supporting documentation; if disagreement persists, a peer-review audit by a third-party firm (cost from contingency) is initiated. KPI thresholds are locked at Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) by BESC; after that, KPI deviations from locked thresholds are tracked and reported monthly as evidence for the final Go/Modify/Stop decision.

Governance Implementation Plan

1. Project sponsor (senior US and Chinese political leadership) jointly confirms commitment and authority to establish The Consortium; establishes co-chair mandate and decision-making authority framework in principle.

Responsible Body/Role: US and Chinese Political Leadership (Presidential/Prime-ministerial level or equivalent)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0 (2026-10-08)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Joint political commitment statement or directive
  • Co-chair mandate and authority scope (outlined, not yet signed)
  • Authorization to proceed with bilateral instrument drafting

Dependencies:

  • Project initiation decision by both governments

2. Bilateral instrument drafting team (legal counsel from both countries, nominated by political leadership) drafts the foundational bilateral agreement specifying double-key governance, decision thresholds, escalation procedures, deadlock resolution, reciprocity requirements, inspector immunity, technology-transfer rules and participant obligations.

Responsible Body/Role: Joint Bilateral Legal Drafting Team (US and Chinese legal counsel, co-led)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0 (2026-10-08) to Month 1.5 (2026-11-23 to 2026-11-23)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Draft bilateral instrument v0.1 (internal working version)
  • Governance structure and decision-rights framework section
  • Double-key authority terms and deadlock-resolution protocols
  • Inspector vetting, immunity and conduct-code provisions
  • Entry-condition specification and certification procedures
  • Dispute-escalation and referee-panel selection mechanism

Dependencies:

  • Political leadership commitment in principle
  • Nomination of US and Chinese lead legal counsel

3. Legal drafting team circulates draft bilateral instrument for review and comment by nominated members of the Bilateral Executive Steering Committee (both co-chairs designate), Joint Forensic Panel leads, and Independent Auditor designate.

Responsible Body/Role: Joint Bilateral Legal Drafting Team

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) to Month 2 (2026-12-08 to 2026-12-08)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Feedback summary from all reviewers
  • Consolidated list of requested clarifications or amendments
  • Redline draft v0.2 with tracked changes

Dependencies:

  • Draft v0.1 completed and circulated to designated reviewers
  • Reviewers identified and briefing materials prepared

4. Senior US political leadership (National Security Advisor or equivalent Cabinet-level sponsor) nominates the US National Co-Chair (Cabinet-level or equivalent senior executive) and the US Deputy National Co-Chair (Head of US National Operations Unit or designated proxy).

Responsible Body/Role: US Political Leadership (via National Security Council or Presidential directive)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0.5 (2026-10-23)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Written nomination and confirmation of US National Co-Chair
  • Written nomination and confirmation of US Deputy National Co-Chair

Dependencies:

5. Senior Chinese political leadership (State Council or Communist Party equivalent) nominates the Chinese National Co-Chair (State Council or equivalent level) and the Chinese Deputy National Co-Chair (Head of Chinese National Operations Unit or designated proxy).

Responsible Body/Role: Chinese Political Leadership (via State Council or equivalent)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0.5 (2026-10-23)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Written nomination and confirmation of Chinese National Co-Chair
  • Written nomination and confirmation of Chinese Deputy National Co-Chair

6. Nominated US and Chinese National Co-Chairs hold an inaugural bilateral meeting (in person or secure video) to ratify the bilateral instrument governance language, confirm their mutual understanding of double-key authority, and establish weekly steering-committee meeting schedule and decision-recording protocols.

Responsible Body/Role: US and Chinese National Co-Chairs (jointly)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 1 (2026-11-08)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Meeting minutes documenting governance agreement, weekly schedule confirmation and decision-recording SOP
  • Bilateral instrument governance sections finalized and co-signed in principle

7. US National Co-Chair and Deputy nominate and select members of the US-side internal governance bodies: Joint Forensic Panel US specialist team (3–5 FTE hardware identity/forensics experts), US National Operations Unit leadership (Director, Deputy Director, Chief of Inspections, Chief of Ledger Operations, vetting officer, operator engagement head, evidence handler), and US inspector cadre leadership roles.

Responsible Body/Role: US National Co-Chair (with advice from US Deputy Co-Chair and US-side technical leads)

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) to Month 1 (2026-11-08 to 2026-11-08)

Chinese National Co-Chair and Deputy nominate and select members of the Chinese-side internal governance bodies: Joint Forensic Panel Chinese specialist team (3–5 FTE hardware identity/forensics experts), Chinese National Operations Unit leadership (Director, Deputy Director, Chief of Inspections, Chief of Ledger Operations, vetting officer, operator engagement head, evidence handler), and Chinese inspector cadre leadership roles.

Decision Escalation Matrix

Budget Request Exceeding Envelope Authority Escalation Level: Bilateral Executive Steering Committee (BESC) Approval Process: Double-key co-chair consensus. Budget tranches >USD 25M per side require written joint approval. Contingency releases up to USD 50M per side (USD 25M each) approved within 5 business days via fast-lane double-key signature. Larger contingency draws require extended BESC deliberation with spending justification documented in the ledger. Rationale: National Operations Units (US and Chinese) have authority over operational spending within their USD 2.5B envelopes. Any tranche authorization >USD 25M or contingency request >USD 50M total (USD 25M per country) exceeds standard approval authority and requires double-key co-chair consensus to ensure mutual accountability and prevent unilateral budget overspend. Negative Consequences: Unauthorized spending or tranche delays cascade to facility deployment, inspector vetting, vendor-fallback activation or exercise coordination. A delayed USD 25M+ tranche approval can defer Phase One start by 2-4 weeks, consuming the calibration window and increasing risk of mis-set thresholds. Uncontrolled contingency draws could exhaust the USD 500M reserve, leaving no surge capacity and forcing a Modify or Stop decision if additional failures occur.

Ledger Divergence Unresolved Beyond Threshold Escalation Level: Joint Forensic and Evidence Adjudication Panel; if unresolved beyond 7 days, automatic escalation to Bilateral Executive Steering Committee for double-key decision on site suspension or impaired-confidence status Approval Process: Joint Forensic Panel issues binding or co-chair-delegated findings within 48 hours of escalation. If consensus fails or divergence persists >4 hours, escalate immediately to both National Operations Units' Chiefs of Ledger Operations for forensic troubleshooting within 2 hours. If divergence >7 days unresolved, automatic impaired-confidence status triggers; lifting requires double-key co-chair authorization. Automatic site suspension follows at 14 days unresolved unless co-chairs jointly extend in writing. Rationale: The replicated ledger is the foundational evidence record. Unresolved divergence between national copies (target <1 hour sync, detection within 2 hours) indicates either a technical failure or contested identity claims that undermine verification integrity. A divergence persisting >7 days blocks discrepancy resolution and triggers mandatory escalation to prevent indefinite disputes from stalling Phase One. Negative Consequences: Unresolved ledger divergence >7 days forces automatic impaired-confidence status or site suspension, effectively ending Phase One operations at that site. A material unresolved divergence (contested equipment identity with no forensic consensus) can render a site's evidence base unreliable and trigger a Modify or Stop outcome. Repeated divergence events suggest either technical fragility or adversarial ledger manipulation, either of which undermines the entire bilateral mechanism's credibility.

Critical Vendor Refusal Cascading to Unverifiable Equipment Count >Threshold Escalation Level: Bilateral Executive Steering Committee (BESC), with Joint Forensic Panel input on unverifiable classification Approval Process: Vendor refusal activates the 10-day escalation ladder: direct request (day 0) → operator (day 1) → independent examiner notification (day 2) → examination (day 3-5) → report (day 10). At day 10, if no evidence is available, equipment is marked unverifiable. If unverifiable equipment exceeds 5% of deployed at a site (proposed threshold), the site risks Go-threshold failure. BESC double-key reviews the vendor-refusal outcome and either approves alternative fallback (clean-room, validated attestation) or certifies unverifiable status for final-decision impact. Rationale: Vendor refusal on critical equipment (e.g., a major manufacturer withholding attestation or maintenance records) can block identity verification for 5-20% of deployed items per site (estimate). If fallback routes (independent examiners, clean-room facilities, validated attestations) are not pre-positioned or fail, material equipment becomes unverifiable. Equipment unverifiable >5% at a site violates the Go threshold and requires co-chair decision on whether the site passes Phase One. Negative Consequences: A major vendor refusal (e.g., 10-15% of equipment affected) can cascade to unverifiable counts exceeding the 5% Go threshold, forcing a site to fail Phase One. Unresolved vendor refusals consume the 10-day escalation clock and may collide with discrepancy deadlines, triggering multiple escalations. If multiple vendors refuse at the same site, the site may become entirely unverifiable, triggering a Modify or Stop outcome. Cost impact: late-engaged independent examiners cost USD 50-100k per exam vs. USD 20-30k planned, consuming contingency funds.

Inspector Conduct Violation—Tier 3 (Material Espionage Risk or Serious Unauthorized Access) Escalation Level: Bilateral Inspector Conduct and Reciprocity Oversight Panel (for investigation within 12 hours); if Tier 3 removal is recommended, immediate escalation to Bilateral Executive Steering Committee for double-key authorization of inspector removal Approval Process: Tier 3 incident (undisclosed photography of workload location, network topology, unauthorized collection) triggers joint panel investigation within 12 hours. Panel issues removal recommendation within 24 hours if consensus is reached. Removal of an inspector requires written findings from both national panel members and joint Conduct Panel chair approval; the offending government's Deputy Co-Chair is notified with justification within 24 hours. BESC may be asked to confirm the removal if the offending government contests the finding. Rationale: Inspector espionage or coerced collection risk is high in a low-trust bilateral environment. A Tier 3 incident (material breach of conduct code or serious unauthorized access) signals potential intelligence collection by or against the inspector, which could collapse reciprocal trust if not escalated and resolved immediately. Immediate removal prevents further exposure and demonstrates that both governments enforce conduct rules equally. Negative Consequences: Failure to escalate and remove a Tier 3 offender can trigger the other government to suspect espionage and reciprocally expel counterpart inspectors, collapsing reciprocal access and failing Phase One. A substantiated Tier 3 incident discovered post-Phase One (e.g., unauthorized device access or photography) undermines the credibility of that inspector's observations and potentially invalidates evidence from their shift. If 1-2 Tier 3 incidents occur per country during Phase One, both governments may withdraw consent and terminate the mechanism.

Discrepancy Escalation Clock Expiry Without Resolution (Tier 2 or Tier 3 Deadlock) Escalation Level: Bilateral Executive Steering Committee (co-chairs), with Independent Auditor input; if both co-chairs disagree on resolution, neutral referee panel escalation Approval Process: Tier 2 (72-hour) clock managed by Joint Adjudication Unit: allows one 36-hour extension with written reasons. If Tier 2 is not resolved by hour 108 (72 hours + extension), escalate to BESC within 2 hours with the Adjudication Unit's technical findings. BESC has 12 hours to issue a co-chair decision on disposition (resolved, escalated to Tier 3, or marked impaired-confidence). If co-chairs disagree, neutral referee panel (3-5 senior officials) provides a non-binding opinion within 5 days. Tier 3 (14-day) automatic suspension fires at day 14 unless BESC jointly authorizes a further extension (recorded in ledger). Rationale: Discrepancy clocks (Tier 1 = 24h, Tier 2 = 72h, Tier 3 = 14d) prevent indefinite delays and test whether the mechanism can resolve disputes within operationally acceptable timeframes. A Tier 2 clock expiry without resolution indicates either a legitimate fact-finding dispute (requiring co-chair or referee arbitration) or gaming/obstruction (requiring escalation to suspension). Automatic Tier 3 suspension at day 14 prevents unresolved items from accumulating and clouding the final decision. Negative Consequences: If Tier 2 clocks expire at multiple sites within a short period, automatic escalation to BESC overwhelms governance bandwidth and delays other decisions. A Tier 3 automatic suspension, even if the mechanism is working correctly, forces the final decision to account for suspension events and may falsely lower confidence in Phase One. Repeated Tier 2/3 expirations (>3 unresolved items per site) suggest either insufficient fact-finding resources or adversarial obstruction by one side, either of which can trigger a Modify or Stop outcome.

Reciprocal Access Parity Breach—Asymmetric Access or Evidence Denial Escalation Level: Bilateral Inspector Conduct and Reciprocity Oversight Panel (for parity analysis); if asymmetry >20% and unresolved after 10 days, escalation to Bilateral Executive Steering Committee with potential neutral referee arbitration Approval Process: Monthly Conduct Panel audit compares inspector deployment, zone-access hours, event-witnessing parity and escalation authority across both countries. If parity diverges >20% (proposed threshold), Conduct Panel flags asymmetry to BESC within 5 days with remediation options (e.g., expanding one side's access, reducing the other's, rebalancing escalation authority). BESC has 10 days to resolve the asymmetry by mutual agreement or authorize a neutral referee panel to recommend parity restoration. If unresolved >10 days, the offending country must restore parity or face equivalent counter-restriction by the other side (automatic parity-restoration mechanism). Rationale: The bilateral mechanism is founded on reciprocal access and mutual trust. If one country grants its inspectors narrower zone access, longer maintenance windows, or faster escalations than its counterpart receives, the other side has grounds to suspect unequal verification and may object to the Go decision. Asymmetry >20% is material (proposed threshold) and requires immediate escalation to prevent confidence collapse. Negative Consequences: Asymmetric access discovered late in Phase One (e.g., at Month 8 = 2027-06-08, near final decision) can trigger the disadvantaged country to reject the Go verdict as invalid, delaying the final decision by 2-4 weeks. One country's unilateral access restriction citing national security (which cannot be disputed by referees) can activate the other side's equivalent counter-restriction, cascading into mutual narrowing of access that undermines detection effectiveness. If asymmetry persists >14 days unresolved, both countries may withdraw consent and terminate Phase One.

Monitoring Progress

1. Tracking Entry-Condition Certification Progress and Reciprocity Gate Status

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Entry-Condition Steering Committee Weekly Tracking Dashboard (spreadsheet with milestone status, blockers, escalation flags)
  • Bilateral Instrument and Legal Authority Checklist (signed documents, domestic legislation status tracker)
  • Inspector Vetting Status Tracker (counterintelligence clearance progress by candidate, agency delays flagged)
  • Site Selection and Operator Binding-Agreement Log (contracts signed, ratification status)

Frequency: Weekly steering-committee review (Months 0–6 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-04-08); escalation to political leadership if any condition lags >4 weeks behind plan

Responsible Role: Bilateral Executive Steering Committee (both co-chairs jointly), with designated entry-condition owners (US and Chinese) for each of the 7 mandatory conditions

Adaptation Process: If a single condition (e.g., inspector vetting, domestic legislation) extends >4 weeks beyond plan, co-chairs immediately escalate to political leadership with a decision memo: either expedite the lagging condition, or authorize a conditional/partial-start fallback (e.g., pre-clock dry run on non-covered equipment). If delay persists to Month 9 (2027-07-08), co-chairs invoke the gate backstop and double-key decide to extend Phase One start or stop. Any entry-condition failure is escalated to BESC and reflected in monthly KPI reporting.

Adaptation Trigger: Any single entry condition >4 weeks behind plan (Month 2 = 2026-12-08 baseline for site selection, Month 3 = 2027-01-08 for appropriations/authority, Month 4 = 2027-02-08 for operator/vendor binding, Month 5 = 2027-03-08 for inspector approval); or any condition not certified by Month 6 (2027-04-08) triggers the Month 9 (2027-07-08) backstop review for extend-or-stop decision

2. Monitoring Critical Success Factor: Ledger Divergence and Forensic Identity Resolution

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Bilateral Ledger Synchronization Dashboard (real-time or hourly update of sync latency, divergence counts, reconciliation status per site)
  • Joint Forensic Panel Findings Log (contested identities escalated, evidence layers analyzed, findings issued, status of resolution)
  • Discrepancy Clock Tracking (Tier 1/2/3 escalation status, clock expirations, extensions granted, automatic suspensions triggered)
  • Ledger Divergence Event Report (monthly summary: divergence count, detection time, resolution time, unresolved cases)

Frequency: Real-time divergence detection and escalation within 2 hours of divergence discovery; forensic panel activation on-demand (estimated 1–2 per week per site); monthly divergence and forensic summary report by Independent Auditor

Responsible Role: US and Chinese National Operations Units (Chiefs of Ledger Operations, jointly for forensic escalation); Joint Forensic and Evidence Adjudication Panel (for identity findings); Independent Auditor (for monthly reporting on ledger integrity)

Adaptation Process: Divergence >4 hours unresolved escalates to both Ledger Chiefs within 30 minutes for technical root-cause analysis and recovery. If divergence persists >7 days unresolved, automatic impaired-confidence status fires and the site enters escalation protocol; lifting requires double-key co-chair authorization and must be documented in the ledger. Any unresolved ledger divergence is flagged in monthly KPI reporting and counted as an audit exception. If forensic panel consensus fails on a contested identity, the matter escalates to co-chairs for decision within 24 hours; if co-chairs cannot agree, a neutral referee panel provides a non-binding opinion within 5 days.

Adaptation Trigger: Ledger divergence >4 hours unresolved (triggers technical escalation to Ledger Chiefs); divergence >7 days unresolved (automatic impaired-confidence status and escalation to BESC); contested equipment identity unresolved by forensic panel within 48 hours (escalation to co-chairs); Tier 2 or Tier 3 discrepancy clock expiry without forensic resolution

3. Monitoring Critical Success Factor: Vendor Refusal Escalation and Equipment Unverifiability

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Vendor Cooperation Status Tracker (pre-binding agreement status, signed vs. pending, refusal alerts)
  • Vendor Refusal Escalation Ladder Log (each refusal tracked day-by-day: request, operator escalation, examiner notification, exam scheduling, report, unverifiable classification)
  • Unverifiable Equipment Count Dashboard (equipment count by site, reason for unverifiable status, percentage of deployed)
  • Independent Examiner and Clean-Room Facility Utilization Report (pool availability, actual engagement, cost tracking against budget)

Frequency: Weekly vendor-cooperation status review (Months 1–4 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-02-08 during pre-binding phase); daily escalation ladder tracking once a refusal is reported; monthly unverifiable-equipment count report

Responsible Role: US and Chinese National Operations Units (Head of Operator Engagement, jointly for vendor coordination); Joint Forensic Panel (for unverifiable classification review); US and Chinese Technical Leads (for independent-examiner engagement)

Adaptation Process: Vendor refusal activates the 10-day escalation ladder automatically: if no fallback evidence is available by day 10, equipment is marked unverifiable. If unverifiable count approaches or exceeds 5% of deployed at a site, a bilateral review convenes to assess whether alternative evidence routes (clean-room, validated attestation) can recover the equipment or whether the site will fail the Go threshold. If a major vendor (affecting 5–15% of equipment) refuses cooperation, both co-chairs are notified within 24 hours and decide whether to escalate to operator/government level or invoke the vendor-refusal Stop condition (equipment unverifiable >10% per site). Monthly unverifiable counts are tracked in the KPI dashboard and feed the final Go/Modify/Stop decision.

Adaptation Trigger: Vendor refusal reported (activates 10-day escalation ladder); vendor refusal affecting 5% or more of site equipment (escalates to BESC for remediation decision); unverifiable equipment reaching 5% of deployed per site (triggers bilateral review of Go-threshold risk); unverifiable >10% at a site (Stop condition candidate)

4. Monitoring Critical Success Factor: Blind-Challenge Detection Performance and Exercise Integrity

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Independent Testing Unit Sealed Exercise Schedule and Execution Log (exercises run, timing, scenarios, real-time incident tracking)
  • Detection Scorecard by Event Type (monthly: unreported arrivals, substitutions, record falsification, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal, reluctant operator; true positives, false negatives, false positives per type)
  • Monthly Detection Rate Summary and Threshold Deviation Report (observed rates vs. locked thresholds for Go decision, deviation flags)
  • Exercise Audit and Fairness Report (post-exercise independent auditor sign-off on blind integrity, scoring objectivity, scenario realism)

Frequency: Per-exercise real-time incident logging and immediate post-exercise scoring (within 72 hours); monthly detection-rate compilation and threshold-deviation analysis; quarterly fairness and integrity audit by Independent Auditor

Responsible Role: Independent Testing Unit (Scoring Lead, Site Coordinators, Red-Team Facilitators; reports to BESC); Independent Auditor (quarterly fairness review); Bilateral Executive Steering Committee (monthly threshold-deviation review)

Adaptation Process: Monthly detection-rate data is compiled and compared against locked thresholds (90% unreported arrival, 85% substitution, 80% falsification, <5% false positives, proposed). If observed detection for any event type falls >10% below locked threshold by Month 7 (2027-05-08), BESC is notified and reviews whether corrective training, protocol clarification or evidence-layer adjustment is needed. If detection remains <70% for a category at Month 8 (2027-06-08), that feeds into the final Go/Modify/Stop decision as evidence of a weakness. If any exercise is discovered to be compromised (advance notice to inspectors, unplanned facility disruption), the Independent Auditor flags it as void and recommends re-execution or exclusion from the evidence base. Monthly detection reports are published in the KPI dashboard.

Adaptation Trigger: Observed detection rate for any event type falls >10% below locked threshold by Month 7 (2027-05-08); any exercise detection <70% at any site; post-exercise audit discovers exercise contamination or fairness violation (void the exercise, recommend re-run or exclusion from evidence base); disparity in detection rates between US and Chinese inspectors suggests asymmetric training or capability (triggers bilateral review and potential rebalancing of inspector roles)

5. Monitoring Critical Success Factor: Inspector Conduct and Reciprocal-Access Parity

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Monthly Access-Log Audit Report (inspector zone-boundary compliance, device-access patterns, location-tracking validation, anomaly flags)
  • Tier 1/2/3 Conduct Incident Log (infraction severity, investigation status, resolution/removal recommendation, status tracking)
  • Reciprocal-Access Parity Dashboard (inspector deployment per country per site, zone-access hours, witnessed events, escalation authority—all metrics compared for >20% asymmetry)
  • Inspector Rotation and Rapid-Replacement Pool Status (rotation schedule compliance, surge-pool readiness, clearance expiry tracking)

Frequency: Monthly access-log audits and conduct-incident review (conducted by Bilateral Conduct Panel); monthly reciprocal-access parity metrics (compared by Conduct Panel); ad-hoc Tier 2/3 incident investigation (within 12–24 hours of report)

Responsible Role: Bilateral Inspector Conduct and Reciprocity Oversight Panel (co-chairs per country, counterintelligence staff); US and Chinese National Operations Units (liaison and rapid-replacement coordination)

Adaptation Process: Monthly access-log audits flag any zone-boundary infractions, device-access anomalies or location-tracking gaps. Tier 1 infractions (minor, first offense) are handled as written warnings within the panel; Tier 2 (repeated or deliberate violation) escalates to formal notice and Conduct Panel review within 24 hours; Tier 3 (material espionage risk, serious unauthorized access) triggers immediate removal investigation and removal recommendation to co-chairs within 12 hours. Reciprocal-access parity metrics are compared monthly; if asymmetry >20% (proposed threshold) is detected, Conduct Panel flags it to BESC within 5 days with remediation options (expand one side's access, rebalance escalation authority). If asymmetry persists >10 days, an automatic counter-restriction activates (the advantaged side voluntarily narrows its access to match the disadvantaged side). Any substantiated Tier 3 incident or material parity breach is escalated to BESC and tracked as a potential Go-decision risk factor.

Adaptation Trigger: Tier 2 or Tier 3 conduct incident reported (escalation within 12–24 hours for investigation); reciprocal-access asymmetry >20% detected (5-day BESC notification and remediation planning); Tier 3 removal recommendation (immediate co-chair authorization required); repeated Tier 2 incidents by same inspector (automatic escalation to Tier 3 investigation)

6. Monitoring Budget Timeliness and Contingency Drawdown

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Monthly Spending Variance Report (actual vs. planned spending per envelope; flags variance >5%; cost-center reconciliation)
  • Contingency Fund Release Log (all contingency tranches >USD 25M tracked; fast-lane releases <USD 50M documented)
  • Tranche Timing Tracker (each USD 625M (US) and USD 625M (China) quarterly tranche release and obligation timeline; 45-day appropriation-release window monitored)
  • Deficit or Overrun Alert Dashboard (cumulative spending vs. remaining budget by envelope and month; red-flag if overrun threatened)

Frequency: Monthly spending-variance audit (by Independent Auditor); monthly tranche-release timing review (by Bilateral Executive Steering Committee); quarterly comprehensive budget-reconciliation audit

Responsible Role: US and Chinese National Operations Units (financial officers, spending authorization); Independent Auditor (variance flagging and monthly reporting); Bilateral Executive Steering Committee (contingency authorization)

Adaptation Process: Each month, actual spending is reconciled against planned spending per envelope. If variance >5% (proposed threshold) is detected in Months 0–3 (2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08), the Independent Auditor flags the variance to BESC within 5 days; the relevant National Operations Unit must provide explanation and corrective action plan within 10 days. If variance persists or repeats, it signals budget-execution risk and may trigger early contingency release or spending restraint in other envelopes. If tranche release is delayed beyond 45 days (plus a 30-day cure window = 75 days total), the delay counts as funding withheld (a Stop condition). If contingency drawdown approaches USD 400M of the USD 500M total (80% utilization), BESC is alerted and must review whether surge capacity is being depleted faster than planned; if contingency is fully drawn before Month 8 (2027-06-08), BESC must authorize either austerity measures or notify both governments of funding shortfall risk.

Adaptation Trigger: Spending variance >5% in Months 0–3 (2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08) (5-day escalation to BESC); tranche late beyond 75 days (45-day release window + 30-day cure) (counts as funding withheld, Stop condition); contingency utilization >80% (alerts BESC for surge-capacity review); any single cost overrun >USD 100M (escalates to BESC for authorization)

7. Monitoring Go/Modify/Stop Decision Threshold Readiness and KPI Dashboard Convergence

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Locked Thresholds Validation Document (all Go/Modify/Stop decision thresholds, double-key signed, baseline and validated by calibration exercise, recorded in ledger)
  • Monthly KPI Dashboard (detection rates, false rates, identity confidence, sync divergence, reciprocal-access parity, discrepancy age, unverifiable counts, vendor refusals, funding timeliness, audit exceptions; all metrics compared to locked thresholds with deviation flags)
  • Final-Decision Evidence Summary Report (compiled at Month 9 = 2027-07-08, summarizing all 90-day data against Go/Modify/Stop rubric)

Frequency: Thresholds locked by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), before first formal blind exercise; monthly KPI dashboard published by Independent Auditor (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08); final decision package assembled at Month 9 (2027-07-08)

Responsible Role: Bilateral Executive Steering Committee (threshold lock and Go/Modify/Stop decision); Independent Testing Unit (detection-rate data); Independent Auditor (KPI compilation and final-decision package)

Adaptation Process: Locked thresholds are published pre-Phase One (by Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23) with full justification documented in the bilateral ledger. During Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), monthly KPI data is compiled and compared to thresholds; any material deviation (detection <70%, false positives >10%, unverifiable >10%, unresolved divergence >7 days, reciprocal-access asymmetry >20%) is flagged in real-time reporting and escalated to BESC. At Month 9 (2027-07-08), a comprehensive evidence summary is prepared, comparing all 90-day metrics to the locked thresholds. If performance exceeds Go thresholds, BESC authorizes a Go decision (Phase Two or continuation). If performance is correctable (Modify criteria: detection 70–85%, unverifiable 5–10%), BESC issues Modify with remediation timeline. If performance triggers Stop criteria (asymmetric access, unverifiable >10%, divergence unresolved, funding withheld, detection <70%), BESC issues Stop and closure procedures.

Adaptation Trigger: Thresholds not locked by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) (escalates to BESC for emergency lock; formal clock start may be delayed); any monthly KPI showing detection <70%, false positives >10%, or unverifiable >10% (real-time escalation to BESC and trigger for corrective action or early warning); final-decision readiness at Month 9 (2027-07-08) showing any Stop criteria met (automatic escalation to co-chairs for Go/Modify/Stop final decision at Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23)

Governance Extra

Governance Validation Checks

  1. Completeness: All core governance components are generated: 5 primary internal bodies (BESC, Joint Forensic Panel, USNOU, CNOU, ITU), 2 oversight bodies (Conduct Panel, Independent Auditor), 28-step implementation plan, 5-item escalation matrix with approval processes and triggers, and 6-area monitoring plan with adaptation procedures. Bilateral instrument, entry-condition tracking, KPI dashboard, and Go/Modify/Stop decision framework are present. The architecture directly addresses double-key governance, deadlock resolution, forensic identity adjudication, ledger divergence handling and vendor-refusal fallbacks specified in the strategic decisions.
  2. Internal Consistency: The governance bodies align logically with the decision-escalation matrix and implementation timeline. BESC (equal co-chairs, no casting vote) makes all strategic decisions; Joint Forensic Panel (equal national teams, consensus or co-chair escalation) resolves contested identities within 48 hours; bilateral Conduct Panel (one co-chair per country) manages inspector conduct with three-tier escalation (Tier 3 removal requires BESC); ITU (independent) runs blind exercises on sealed schedule; Independent Auditor (external, jointly selected) publishes monthly KPI dashboard and quarterly attestation. National Operations Units (USNOU and CNOU) are mirror entities with identical roles but no authority over each other, reporting to co-chairs and BESC. Timeline is internally consistent: entry-condition certification by Month 6 (2027-04-08), Phase One Months 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), decision Month 10 (2027-08-08). Escalation paths are documented (Tier 1→2→3 for conduct; Tier 2→Tier 3→automatic suspension for discrepancies; 7-day deadlock→referee panel→automatic suspension for contested identity). No contradictions detected between stages.
  3. Critical Gaps—Forensic Authority and Contested Identity Deadlock: The Joint Forensic Panel is empowered to issue 'binding or co-chair-delegated findings' on equipment identity within 48 hours, but the decision-escalation matrix does not specify under what conditions findings are binding vs. delegated to co-chairs. If both national panel members dispute the evidence (one says identity confirmed, the other says unverifiable), does the panel issue a 'split finding' or immediately escalate to co-chairs? The escalation matrix states disputed findings escalate within 48 hours with a 'technical opinion' to co-chairs for final decision, but does not specify the co-chair decision window before automatic escalation to the neutral referee panel (the deadlock rule says 7 days for decision-critical items, but forensic escalations are time-sensitive within discrepancy clocks). If a Tier 2 discrepancy clock expires while awaiting a contested forensic finding, which takes precedence: the forensic escalation timeline (48 hours to co-chairs) or the discrepancy clock (72 hours + 36-hour extension = 108 hours)? The governance does not explicitly bind these two critical timelines or define what happens if a forensic finding cannot be issued before a discrepancy clock expires. Recommendation: Define forensic consensus rules (e.g., panel consensus required for binding finding; split finding with >36 hours to co-chair decision triggers automatic one-time extension of discrepancy clock by 24 hours) and document the interaction between forensic and discrepancy-clock timelines in the bilateral instrument.
  4. Critical Gaps—Operator Non-Compliance Escalation and Site Suspension Authority: The implementation plan specifies binding operator agreements by Month 4 (2027-02-08) and operator engagement as a mandatory entry condition, but the escalation matrix and implementation plan do not define what happens if an operator breaches the agreement during Phase One (e.g., refuses inspector access to a maintenance window, withholds evidence, disrupts an exercise, or shields a vendor refusal). The governance bodies are authorized to escalate vendor refusals, discrepancy clocks, and inspector conduct violations, but there is no escalation path for operator non-compliance that doesn't match those categories. If an operator claims force majeure (production emergency, facility failure) to deny access, who decides whether the access denial is justified or a violation? Does the BESC have authority to suspend a site if the operator breaches the binding agreement, or does that require a formal renegotiation of the bilateral instrument? The governance implicitly assumes operator cooperation; the absence of an escalation path for operator refusal or non-compliance is a gap. Recommendation: Add an Operator Breach Escalation procedure: (1) USNOU or CNOU escalates alleged operator non-compliance to BESC within 24 hours with evidence; (2) BESC reviews and, if justified, issues a co-chair notice to the operator with cure deadline (3–7 days depending on severity); (3) if not cured, site enters impaired-confidence status or suspension; (4) an uncooperative operator is grounds for site replacement (activate fallback site from shortlist within 4–8 weeks) or Phase One termination.
  5. Critical Gaps—Ledger Key Material Custody and Compromise Response: The implementation plan specifies a joint key ceremony (or two independent national roots) by Month 4 (2027-02-08), but does not define who physically holds the cryptographic keys between ceremonies, access controls, audit procedures, or the incident-response protocol if key material is suspected compromised. If one government's copy of a shared key is suspected exposed to unauthorized access, does that trigger an automatic key rotation (taking 1–2 weeks) and re-signing of all ledger entries? The governance assumes cryptographic integrity but does not specify how divergence due to key compromise is distinguished from technical faults or adversarial manipulation. The stress test for the ledger (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) includes cryptographic signing validation, but does not specify whether the test includes simulated key-compromise recovery. Recommendation: Document the key-custody protocol (who holds keys, access logs, multi-factor controls, audit frequency—recommend monthly cryptographic-material audit); define a key-compromise incident response procedure (immediate key rotation, re-signing, forensic investigation, notification to co-chairs within 4 hours); include key-compromise recovery drill in the Month 4 (2027-02-08) ledger stress test.
  6. Critical Gaps—Threshold Calibration and Provisional-to-Validated Conversion: The implementation plan locks thresholds at Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) after calibration exercise (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08); the calibration report is supposed to 'validate or adjust' thresholds if observed performance differs >20% from provisional. However, the decision-escalation matrix does not specify the approval process for threshold amendment: Is a >20% adjustment a 'recorded protocol change' requiring full bilateral instrument amendment and double-key signature, or can BESC approve it with a simple recorded memo? The implementation plan says 'documented protocol change signed by both co-chairs before formal clock starts,' implying a lightweight amendment process, but the bilateral instrument (user constraints) specifies that 'protocol changes' require double-key authorization. If the calibration exercise reveals that provisional thresholds are unrealistic (e.g., observed false-negative rate is 15% instead of 5% target), a threshold adjustment from <5% to 15% is a material change that redefines what constitutes Go success. Does that amendment require renegotiation of the bilateral instrument itself, or is it treated as an operational parameter adjustment by co-chairs? The governance does not clarify this distinction. Recommendation: Define 'protocol change' vs. 'operational adjustment' in the bilateral instrument: Protocol changes (double-key, recorded amendment) include decision thresholds, escalation clocks, infraction tiers, and corroboration rule; operational adjustments (co-chair memo) include exercise scheduling, inspection-roster details, and facility-deployment timelines. Threshold amendments post-calibration but pre-Phase One are treated as protocol changes and must be double-key signed and recorded in the ledger before formal clock starts.

Tough Questions

  1. By Month 2 (2026-12-08), what is the documented status of domestic access-authority legislation in each country? Specifically: (US) What is the legislative vehicle and Congressional committee timeline for authorization? (China) What State Council directive number, agency assignment and enforcement mechanism have been designated? If either is delayed >4 weeks beyond the Month 2–3 baseline (2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08), what is the contingency—a pre-clock dry run, or does Phase One clock start defer to Month 9 (2027-07-08) backstop decision?
  2. At the Month 5 (2027-03-08) inspector-vetting completion milestone, provide the actual fill rate (cleared inspectors ÷ 144 baseline per country). If fill rate is <80% at either country, name which critical posts remain unfilled, provide the specific reason for each vetting delay (security-agency backlog, candidate disqualification, clearance hold), and specify the date by which remaining clearances will be obtained or how surge-pool activation will compensate. A shortfall at clock start (Month 6 = 2027-04-08) is an entry-condition failure; do not proceed without documented recovery plan.
  3. Before Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) threshold lock, provide evidence that the calibration exercise detected at least one substitution, one record falsification, and one vendor-refusal scenario with >70% inspector detection rate. If calibration detected any event type with <70% detection (proposed threshold for Stop consideration), explain why the detection gap is acceptable under Go criteria or justify the threshold adjustment. Do not lock thresholds on provisional figures without calibration validation.
  4. At Month 6 (2027-04-08), when Phase One clock formally starts, produce a signed entry-condition certification memo from both co-chairs attesting that all 7 mandatory conditions are complete: bilateral instrument, appropriations, domestic authority, sites, inspectors, operators/vendors, and equipment schedule. If any condition is incomplete or partially satisfied (e.g., 'equipment schedule in draft,' 'inspectors subject to final clearance clearance'), the clock does not start; escalate to Month 9 (2027-07-08) backstop for double-key extend-or-stop decision. No partial starts are permitted.
  5. During Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), track and report monthly the count of ledger divergences, divergence detection time, divergence resolution time, and number of divergences unresolved at 7 days. If any divergence exceeds 7 days unresolved, document the reason (technical fault, contested identity, co-chair disagreement) and whether automatic impaired-confidence status or suspension was triggered. A pattern of >2 divergences per site per month or >1 unresolved divergence per site suggests ledger unreliability; provide immediate mitigation or recommend site suspension.
  6. At the final Go/Modify/Stop decision (Month 9.5 = 2027-07-23), provide the blind-challenge detection scorecard by event type (unreported arrivals, substitutions, record falsifications, delayed-access tests, disputed identities, vendor refusals, reluctant-operator scenarios), with true-positive count, false-negative count, false-positive count, and detection time distribution for each. State whether observed detection rates meet or exceed the locked thresholds (90% arrival, 85% substitution, 80% falsification, <5% false positives). If any event type falls short of its threshold, justify whether the mechanism still merits a Go decision or whether the deficiency warrants Modify or Stop.

Summary

The Consortium governance framework establishes a bilateral US–China verification mechanism for frontier computing equipment changes at 4 matched datacenters over a 90-day Phase One test (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). The framework emphasizes procedural rigor, double-key authority with mutual veto and no casting vote, bounded inspection zones with operator-run redaction, mirrored full-time national teams, a replicated tamper-evident ledger with <1-hour synchronization, fixed corroboration rules requiring ≥2 independent evidence layers for equipment identity, and sealed independent-examiner challenge exercises scoring detection against locked thresholds. Entry-condition gating defers the 90-day clock until all 7 mandatory conditions (bilateral instrument, appropriations, domestic authority, sites, inspectors, operators/vendors, equipment schedule) are certified by Month 6 (2027-04-08). Go/Modify/Stop decision is issued at Month 10 (2027-08-08) based on blind-challenge detection (90% unreported arrival, 85% substitution, 80% falsification), false-positive rates (<5%), reciprocal-access parity (±20%), unverifiable equipment (<5%), and zero material asymmetry or IP exposure. The design prioritizes auditability, reciprocity and measured risk acceptance over speed, reflecting low-trust bilateral context and exclusive focus on declared-equipment change verification at monitored sites.

Suggestion 1 - New START Treaty Inspection and Verification Regime (US–Russia)

Bilateral treaty (in force 2011, expired February 2026 per public record; status after expiry not verified) with reciprocal on-site inspections, data exchanges, unique identifiers on strategic delivery vehicles, and a Bilateral Consultative Commission (BCC) for disputes. Inspectors verified declared items at declared facilities under mutual distrust. Inspections were suspended in 2020 (COVID) and later disputed by Russia.

Success Metrics

Number of inspections completed per year against treaty quota (see US State Department reports) Unique-identifier coverage of declared items Suspension of inspections in 2020 and Russia's 2023 suspension show reciprocity can fail; use as a Stop-condition analogue

Risks and Challenges Faced

Asymmetric access and reciprocity disputes: addressed through quota parity and the BCC; ultimately not fully resolved. Inspector escort and sensitive-site protection: managed through agreed inspection procedures and pre-notified timelines. Political deterioration: the treaty lacked a mechanism to insulate verification from politics; the Consortium needs double-key and a gate backstop.

Where to Find More Information

US State Department Bureau of Arms Control, Deterrence and Stability: state.gov (New START pages) Arms Control Association: armscontrol.org (New START fact sheets) Congressional Research Service reports on New START

Actionable Steps

Contact the State Department Bureau of Arms Control, Deterrence and Stability via its public press and congressional liaison channels. Approach the Arms Control Association research staff via armscontrol.org for former-inspector referrals. Seek former On-Site Inspection Agency or Defense Threat Reduction Agency inspection-unit alumni via DTRA public affairs.

Rationale for Suggestion

Closest bilateral analogue: reciprocal inspections of declared items by mutually distrustful great powers, with unique identifiers and a dispute body. Geographically and politically distant from US–China, but the structure of parity, quotas and dispute resolution maps directly onto the reciprocity gate and double-key governance.

Suggestion 2 - OPCW Chemical Weapons Convention Industry Verification and Challenge Inspections

The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (The Hague, operating since 1997) inspects declared industrial facilities worldwide, including in both the US and China. It uses managed access to protect confidential business information, with inspected parties able to shield sensitive equipment. Challenge inspections are provided for but rarely invoked.

Success Metrics

Annual inspection counts and declared-facility coverage in OPCW annual reports Clean-audit results of the OPCW budget and financial statements Confidentiality-breach incidents (OPCW reports few public cases; exact figures not verified)

Risks and Challenges Faced

Protecting confidential commercial information: handled through managed access, inspector confidentiality undertakings and an internal confidentiality regime. Inspector conduct and espionage concerns: addressed by the staff confidentiality code, sworn secrecy and investigation procedures. State disputes over findings: handled through the Executive Council and a consultation process.

Where to Find More Information

OPCW website: opcw.org (verification, managed access and confidentiality policy) OPCW Annual Reports and Programme and Budget documents Chemical Weapons Convention text, Verification Annex

Actionable Steps

Contact the OPCW Verification Division and the Office of Confidentiality and Security via the opcw.org contact page. Request a briefing from OPCW Inspectorate on managed-access practice. Consult US and Chinese National Authorities for the CWC, which each country maintains, for national implementation experience.

Rationale for Suggestion

Both the US and China already host OPCW inspections of private and state-owned industry, so this is the most culturally and jurisdictionally proximate example of inspectors working inside both countries. It directly informs bounded zones, filtered evidence and operator-run protection of IP.

Suggestion 3 - IAEA Safeguards and Euratom Joint Inspection Arrangements

IAEA safeguards verify declared nuclear material and equipment through containment and surveillance (seals, cameras), material accountancy and inspections. In the EU, IAEA and Euratom ran partnership approaches with shared and cross-checked verification, including independent measurements and analytical laboratories.

Success Metrics

Annual Safeguards Implementation Report conclusions per state Seal and surveillance coverage rates and anomaly resolution (aggregate figures in IAEA reports) Independent-lab sample cross-check consistency (qualitative; figures not verified)

Risks and Challenges Faced

Layered evidence without a single decisive source: addressed by combining accountancy, seals, surveillance and sampling. Duplicated inspection burden between two verifiers: reduced via joint use of equipment and data-sharing arrangements. Open anomalies lingering: handled by state-level evaluation and follow-up requests.

Where to Find More Information

IAEA Safeguards: iaea.org/topics/safeguards IAEA Safeguards Implementation Reports (annual) Euratom Safeguards: energy.ec.europa.eu

Actionable Steps

Contact the IAEA Department of Safeguards through iaea.org press and information office. Approach the European Commission DG ENER Euratom Safeguards directorate for joint-verification experience. Engage the Institute of Nuclear Materials Management (INMM) for retired safeguards inspectors.

Rationale for Suggestion

Provides the model for layered evidence (seals, surveillance, accountancy), cross-checking by two verifiers, and a bounded knowledge claim, matching the Consortium's rule that no single source is decisive. Distant domain, but mature and well documented.

Suggestion 4 - SECONDARY: US DMEA Trusted Foundry / Trusted Supplier Accreditation Program

Secondary suggestion. A US Department of Defense program accrediting microelectronics suppliers for supply-chain integrity, using audits and chain-of-custody controls. Fewer details are given; confirm scope and current status with the program office.

Success Metrics

Number of accredited suppliers (public figure not verified) Audit pass rates (not published; ask the program office)

Risks and Challenges Faced

Vendor cooperation with audits: handled through accreditation as a condition of defence business. Protecting trade secrets during audits: managed through confidentiality agreements and cleared auditors.

Where to Find More Information

Defense Microelectronics Activity: dmea.osd.mil DoD Trusted Systems and Networks policy documents

Actionable Steps

Contact the Defense Microelectronics Activity public affairs or accreditation office listed at dmea.osd.mil.

Rationale for Suggestion

Informs vendor binding, chain-of-custody and accredited-examiner pools for the vendor-refusal ladder. Secondary because it is unilateral, not bilateral, and covers only the US.

Summary

No precedent exists for bilateral US–China verification of computing equipment (not verified), so the references below are analogues from arms control, chemical weapons inspection and supply-chain assurance. The strongest are the New START inspection regime, OPCW industry inspections under the Chemical Weapons Convention, and the IAEA safeguards regime with Euratom. A secondary suggestion is the US Trusted Foundry / DMEA accreditation program. They inform mirrored inspection, bounded access with IP protection, challenge inspections, and entry-condition sequencing. Geographic or cultural proximity is limited: only the US–Russia case is bilateral, and no US–China verification case exists. All figures and contacts should be confirmed directly with the named organizations. Fiscal and revenue framing is Not applicable; value is measured as mission justification and public accountability.

1. Domestic Authority Enactment Timeline and Legislative Critical Path

Domestic authority enactment is the critical-path bottleneck for entry-condition gate certification (Month 6 = 2027-04-08). A single government's legislative delay of 4+ weeks can defer the 90-day Phase One clock indefinitely, accumulating USD 150–300M holding cost and consuming contingency. Without explicit decomposition and a pre-agreed conditional-start fallback, whichever government is slower gains a unilateral timing veto, violating reciprocity principles. This data determines whether Phase One is viable by Month 6 (2027-04-08) or must be deferred, compressed, or restructured.

Data to Collect

  • Specific legislative or executive acts required per country (e.g., US Congressional ratification, China State Council directive)
  • Approval bodies, committee schedules, and realistic enactment windows per country
  • Interdependencies and single-item critical path (which country's authority is slowest)
  • Named domestic-authority leads and escalation contacts per government
  • Fallback options if one country's authority slips >4 weeks (conditional-start mechanism, deferral authority)

Simulation Steps

  • Use a bilateral entry-conditions timeline spreadsheet (Excel or Smartsheet) to map each required act through its approval process; identify critical path and float
  • Model three scenarios: on-time completion (baseline), 4-week slip in Country A, 4-week slip in Country B; calculate cost impact (USD 50–100M/month holding cost per canonical facts)
  • Cross-check realistic timelines against comparable bilateral programs (New START ratification, OPCW instrument, IAEA safeguards agreements); access Congressional Record, parliamentary archives, State Department records
  • Simulate the conditional-start fallback: model Phase One clock start at each site independently, with joint certification required for final decision; verify bilateral instrument language supports this model

Expert Validation Steps

  • Consult US State Department Bureau of Arms Control, Deterrence and Stability on Congressional ratification procedures and typical timelines for bilateral verification instruments
  • Consult US Treasury and OMB on appropriations cycle timelines and statutory authorities for verification participation
  • Consult Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs and relevant State Council office on domestic delegation procedures and typical approval timelines
  • Obtain signed commitment from both governments' domestic-authority leads confirming the decomposed milestones and escalation contacts by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23)

Responsible Parties

  • US State Department co-chair (primary US authority lead)
  • Chinese government co-chair (primary China authority lead)
  • Bilateral legal implementation unit (document mapping)
  • Both countries' legislative/executive liaison offices

Assumptions

  • High: Both governments can identify and expedite required domestic legislation (Congressional bill, China State Council directive) without undue delay; expedited timelines are achievable within 14–18 weeks (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23 to Month 3 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-01-08).
  • High: Neither government will use domestic-authority procedures as a deliberate delaying tactic to renegotiate bilateral terms or withdraw from the program; both maintain political commitment through entry-condition work.
  • Medium: A conditional-start fallback (Phase One beginning site-by-site rather than all simultaneously) is acceptable to both governments; the fallback is pre-agreed before Month 1 (2026-11-08) and codified in the bilateral instrument.
  • Medium: Holding costs of USD 50–100M/month (per canonical facts) are accurate and acceptable to both treasuries as a contingency charge if gate delays occur; no additional appropriation is sought.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 0.5 (2026-10-23 17:00), both governments provide a written decomposition of required domestic acts, named leads, and committee schedules, with zero unresolved items. By Month 2 (2026-12-08), all required legislation is drafted and submitted for approval; if any item is >4 weeks behind baseline, a conditional-start fallback is invoked in writing. By Month 3.5 (2027-01-23), domestic authority is enacted in at least one country and tracked at 80%+ completion in both; a written escalation plan exists for any item that will miss Month 4 (2027-02-08) deadline.

Notes

  • Domestic authority enactment is outside the project's direct control and is the primary vector for external delay; weekly steering-committee reviews are essential.
  • Conditional-start fallback must be negotiated and codified before Months 0–1 (2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) deadline; attempting fallback negotiation after Month 1 (2026-11-08) creates crisis dynamics.
  • Holding-cost modeling assumes USD 50–100M/month and 3-month worst-case slip; if actual costs are higher or slip is longer, contingency exposure increases and site replacement or examiner overruns become unfundable.
  • Parliamentary recess, committee delays, and interagency review in either country are foreseeable; a domestic-authority lead should be senior enough to escalate to cabinet level if blocked.

2. Vendor Pre-Binding and Independent-Examiner Pre-Qualification

Vendor refusal is a high-probability scenario (20–30% per risk analysis); without pre-bound vendors and pre-qualified examiner fallbacks, material equipment will be classified unverifiable by the day-10 ladder, exceeding the 5% Go threshold and failing sites. Pre-qualification by Month 1 (2026-11-08) ensures fallback availability when refusals occur; delays to Month 4 (2027-02-08) or later leave Phase One exposed to cascading unverifiable-equipment accumulation and contingency overruns (USD 3.6–11.2M estimated). This data is critical to site-level Go/Modify/Stop viability and contingency management.

Data to Collect

  • Identity, tier ranking, and dependency profile for the top 8–12 critical vendors per participating site (manufacturers, attestation-key custodians, maintenance providers, logistics firms)
  • Vendor willingness to sign pre-Phase-One cooperation agreements (attestation disclosure, maintenance-record preservation, penalty clauses USD 500k–2M per material refusal)
  • Signed vendor cooperation agreements with counterpart acknowledgment (target 80% of Tier 1 vendors by Month 1 = 2026-11-08)
  • Identification and pre-qualification of independent examiner labs (3–5 per country, 6–10 total) and clean-room facilities (2 per geography, 4–8 total) with confirmed availability, cost per exam (target USD 20–50k), and parallel-exam capacity (minimum 5 per week per facility)
  • Written day-10 vendor-refusal escalation ladder locked in bilateral instrument before Phase One clock starts

Simulation Steps

  • Use a vendor-dependency mapping tool (supplier matrix, equipment bills of materials) to identify the top 8–12 vendors per site; rank by attestation criticality, supply-chain custody, and maintenance exclusivity
  • Model three vendor-refusal scenarios per site: (a) 0% refusal, (b) 20% refusal (2–3 Tier 1 vendors per site), (c) 40% refusal; calculate the unverifiable-equipment count and impact on the 5% Go threshold per canonical facts
  • Identify candidate independent examiner labs and clean-room facilities in the US and China; obtain preliminary cost estimates and capacity data via RFQ (request for quote) from at least 2 labs per country
  • Simulate the day-10 vendor-refusal ladder: for each scenario, calculate whether fallback examiners can be engaged, scheduled, and report within day 10; identify schedule bottlenecks or cost overruns

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage US-based semiconductor equipment manufacturers (Intel, Nvidia, AMD, FPGA vendors) and Chinese equipment suppliers (Huawei, ZTE, Alibaba cloud equipment divisions) via government trade and technology liaison channels to assess willingness to participate in pre-Phase-One cooperation agreements
  • Consult equipment-testing and authentication laboratories accredited by NIST (US) and China Certification and Accreditation Administration (CNCA) to identify potential independent examiners and clean-room facilities capable of equipment-identity verification without vendor cooperation
  • Obtain bilateral legal review of vendor cooperation-agreement language (penalty clauses, trade-secret protection, confidentiality) from both countries' legal teams; ensure enforceability under domestic law
  • Conduct a pre-Phase-One vendor engagement briefing with both countries' procurement and technology teams to secure political backing for binding agreements and penalty enforcement

Responsible Parties

  • Bilateral vendor-management unit (lead negotiator, identification of Tier 1 vendors)
  • US and Chinese procurement teams (contract language, domestic vendor engagement)
  • Independent-laboratory industry associations (INMM, ASQ, Chinese equipment-testing associations) for referrals
  • Both countries' legal teams (enforcement of penalty clauses, trade-secret compartmentalization)

Assumptions

  • High: At least 80% of Tier 1 vendors per site will agree to sign pre-Phase-One cooperation agreements; no major vendor withholds participation outright before Month 1 (2026-11-08).
  • High: Independent examiner labs and clean-room facilities exist in sufficient numbers (3–5 per country) and can be contracted with <4 week lead time by Month 1 (2026-11-08) to be operational by Phase One start (Month 6 = 2027-04-08).
  • Medium: Vendor penalty clauses (USD 500k–2M per material refusal) are economically meaningful and enforced; neither government will signal that penalties are unenforceable or waivable, undermining deterrence.
  • Medium: Independent examiners are capable of equipment-identity verification (cryptographic attestation, physical inspection, measurement) without vendor cooperation; cost and schedule targets (USD 20–50k per exam, 5 parallel exams/week) are realistic.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 0.5 (2026-10-23 17:00), both governments provide written identification of top 8–12 vendors per site and initial vendor-engagement strategy. By Month 1 (2026-11-08 17:00), at least 80% of Tier 1 vendors have signed pre-Phase-One cooperation agreements; 3–5 independent examiner labs and 2 clean-room facilities per geography are contracted with confirmed cost and capacity. Day-10 vendor-refusal ladder is locked in the bilateral instrument. By Month 4 (2027-02-08), all pre-qualified examiners have completed a full mock equipment-identity examination to validate methodology and timeline.

Notes

  • Vendor negotiations must start immediately (Month 0 = 2026-10-08) to allow 8–12 weeks for agreement signing; delays to Month 2 (2026-12-08) compress the engagement timeline.
  • Contingency reserve of USD 2–4M per site (USD 8–16M total) should be earmarked at Month 3 (2027-01-08) for late-engaged examiner costs if pre-qualification is incomplete.
  • Examiner cost uncertainty (USD 20–50k per exam) creates contingency exposure; locking cost targets by Month 1 (2026-11-08) is essential to avoid budget variance.
  • Vendor refusal at a hard site (high third-party traffic, complex maintenance) could trigger cascading unverifiable-equipment counts >10%, failing the site outright; hard sites must have vendor pre-binding as Entry Condition precedent.

3. Ledger Divergence Forensic Authority and Shift-Boundary Cross-Signing Operationalization

Unresolved ledger divergence >7 days is an explicit Stop condition (canonical facts). Without a pre-authorized forensic panel, pre-agreed evidence hierarchy, and operationalized shift-boundary cross-signing, divergences will escalate unchecked and automatic suspension will fire, appearing to fail a functioning mechanism when the root cause is procedural gridlock. This data determines whether the ledger system can reliably detect and resolve contested identity disputes within required timelines, preventing spurious Stop triggers.

Data to Collect

  • Joint forensic-identity panel composition and vetting status (3–5 specialists per country, 6–10 total, counterintelligence approval from both governments)
  • Pre-agreed evidence-weighting corroboration hierarchy codified in bilateral instrument (e.g., attestation > physical inspection + chain of custody > maintenance records > third-party logs)
  • Shift-boundary cross-signing procedures operationalized at 08:00, 16:00, 24:00 UTC daily; ledger entries signed by mirrored inspectors certifying no undisclosed divergences
  • Automatic divergence-detection system configuration (latency <2 hours) and escalation routing (alert to forensic panel within 15 minutes)
  • Forensic panel decision-making procedures: findings within 48 hours, deadlock escalation to co-chairs within 24 hours, enforcement mechanism

Simulation Steps

  • Build a mock bilateral ledger system on non-covered equipment at one pilot site (Month 1 = 2026-11-08); configure two independent national ledger copies with simulated 1-hour sync latency and deliberate divergences injected (e.g., timestamp skew of 5–30 minutes, equipment-identifier mismatch)
  • Run a mock shift-handover cross-signing ceremony with two inspectors (one per country) signing a ledger entry; measure time to detect and escalate divergence; verify <2-hour detection and <48-hour forensic investigation are achievable
  • Simulate the forensic-panel decision-making process: present a contested equipment-identity dispute to the panel (3–5 per country); measure consensus time and decision quality using the pre-agreed corroboration hierarchy
  • Model three divergence scenarios: (a) technical sync fault (recoverable within 4 hours), (b) contested identity (requiring 48-hour forensic investigation), (c) unresolvable deadlock (requiring co-chair escalation); calculate timeline and escalation path for each

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage cryptographic systems engineers and distributed-ledger architects to validate that the proposed <2-hour divergence-detection window and <48-hour forensic-finding timeline are technically feasible given network latency, clock-sync tolerances, and investigation procedures
  • Consult bilateral legal experts to ensure that the forensic panel's authority to issue 'binding' findings on contested identity is enforceable under both countries' national law and the bilateral instrument
  • Obtain both governments' agreement on the pre-agreed evidence-weighting corroboration hierarchy by Month 1 (2026-11-08) and ensure it is codified in writing in the bilateral instrument with no ambiguity
  • Conduct a full-system stress test of the ledger and forensic-panel procedures on non-covered equipment by Month 4 (2027-02-08), simulating network outages, system crashes, and key unavailability; verify recovery and forensic response within SLA

Responsible Parties

  • Joint forensic-identity panel (3–5 per country, appointed and vetted by Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23)
  • Bilateral ledger-operations and cryptographic-custody teams (system design, divergence detection, escalation routing)
  • Bilateral legal implementation unit (forensic-panel charter, bilateral instrument language)
  • Independent testing unit (mock divergence scenarios and stress-test execution)

Assumptions

  • High: A joint forensic-identity panel of 3–5 specialists per country can be recruited, vetted, and pre-authorized by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) without security or political objections from either government.
  • High: A pre-agreed evidence-weighting corroboration hierarchy can be locked in the bilateral instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08); neither government contests the hierarchy or attempts to revise it mid-Phase-One.
  • Medium: Ledger systems are capable of detecting divergence within 2 hours and mirrored inspectors can perform shift-handover cross-signing within 10–30 minutes; no technical barriers prevent operationalization by Phase One clock start (Month 6 = 2027-04-08).
  • Medium: Forensic-panel findings are binding on both governments; neither government can unilaterally reject a finding or appeal to national courts to override it. The bilateral mechanism's authority supersedes domestic legal challenge.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 0.5 (2026-10-23 17:00), forensic-panel members are identified and vetting initiated. By Month 1 (2026-11-08 17:00), panel is appointed and pre-authorized; forensic-panel charter and evidence-weighting hierarchy are signed by both co-chairs and codified in bilateral instrument. By Month 4 (2027-02-08), ledger stress test confirms <2-hour divergence detection, mock divergence scenarios are resolved within 48 hours, and shift-handover cross-signing is operationalized at pilot site with zero missed handovers or delayed escalations.

Notes

  • Forensic-panel pre-authorization is not explicitly listed as an entry condition (Entry Condition 1–7) in canonical facts; it should be elevated to Entry Condition 8 or integrated into the gate-certification process to prevent procedural gaps.
  • Shift-boundary cross-signing must be practiced before Phase One; inspectors need hands-on training to execute the ceremony reliably and avoid signing delays that defeat early-divergence detection.
  • Automatic suspension at 7 days is a powerful deterrent against concealment, but without operationalized forensic authority, it becomes a cascade that can freeze a functioning mechanism; extensive testing and rehearsal before Phase One is essential.
  • Deadlock escalation from forensic panel (no consensus within 48 hours) to co-chairs (decision within 24 hours) depends on co-chairs being available and responsive; assignment of escalation duty officers is necessary.

4. Counterintelligence Vetting and Inspector Conduct Oversight

Inspector vetting (14–16 weeks, up to 20+ weeks if deprioritized) is the critical-path entry-condition bottleneck. Delayed vetting defers Phase One clock start, accumulating USD 50–100M/month holding cost. Incomplete vetting (roster <80% by clock start) reduces coverage, increases likelihood of missed events, and signals low-credibility preparation. Conduct-oversight infrastructure (access-log audit, zone-violation investigation, three-tier escalation) is essential to prevent espionage or capture and to maintain bilateral confidence that inspectors are acting impartially. This data determines whether sufficient inspectors are cleared, deployed, and supervised to execute Phase One with full shift coverage and credible event detection.

Data to Collect

  • Counterintelligence vetting progress: number of candidate inspectors submitted per country (target 120–150 per country) and projected completion date (target 14–16 weeks from Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23, i.e., by Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23)
  • Critical-post vacancies and surge-bench fill rate (target 100% critical posts + 20–30% surge bench by Month 5 = 2027-03-08)
  • Inspector conduct-oversight infrastructure: bilateral Conduct Committee composition and authority, access-log audit procedures, zone-violation investigation protocols, three-tier infraction escalation
  • Inspector rotation schedule (quarterly cross-site rotation, no permanent site assignment >3 months) and leave coverage planning (2 weeks per quarter per inspector)
  • Zone-conduct acknowledgment and vetting-completion status: percentage of inspectors signed and cleared by 5 days before Phase One clock (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23)

Simulation Steps

  • Map counterintelligence vetting timelines per country using historical data from analogous bilateral programs (New START vetting, OPCW inspector approval, IAEA safeguards); identify bottlenecks and acceleration opportunities
  • Model three staffing scenarios: (a) on-time vetting completion (baseline), (b) 4-week vetting slip, (c) 8-week slip; calculate roster fill rate at Phase One clock start and impact on coverage gaps (night shifts, leave coverage)
  • Simulate quarterly inspector rotation across 4 sites; confirm that rotation does not create knowledge gaps or separation-of-duties violations; identify surge-pool requirements to cover rotation transitions and leave
  • Design and test a 24/7 access-log audit procedure on non-covered equipment: conduct monthly access-log review for 100 mock inspectors, comparing badge swipes against stated activities; measure detection time for boundary violations and investigate thoroughness

Expert Validation Steps

  • Consult US counterintelligence and security-clearance agencies (DCSA, IC security offices) on vetting timelines and expediting opportunities for 120–150 inspector-level clearances by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23); obtain written commitment to timeline or alert of schedule risks by Month 1 (2026-11-08)
  • Consult Chinese Ministry of State Security and equivalent vetting bodies on parallel vetting procedures and timeline for 120–150 inspectors; secure written confirmation of vetting-completion target
  • Engage bilateral legal teams to define the Conduct Committee's authority (power to veto, remove, or replace inspectors), enforce the three-tier infraction protocol, and adjudicate misconduct allegations within 72 hours
  • Consult OPCW and IAEA inspector-management programs for best practices on rotation scheduling, conflict-of-interest management, and access-log audit to inform the Consortium's procedures

Responsible Parties

  • US counterintelligence services (DCSA, FBI CI, CIA) and Chinese security agencies (MSS, equivalent)
  • Bilateral Inspector Conduct Committee with equal national co-chairs
  • Site-level counterintelligence and security personnel (access-log audit, zone monitoring)
  • Both countries' human-resources and logistics teams (rotation scheduling, leave management)

Assumptions

  • High: Both countries' counterintelligence agencies prioritize Phase One inspector vetting and complete clearances within the 14–16 week baseline (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23 to Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23); competing security priorities do not cause delays >4 weeks.
  • Medium: A roster of 80% of planned inspectors (target ~280 of 434 FTE) is sufficient for Phase One operations with reduced night-shift coverage and acceptable leave gaps; no force-protection or event-detection capability is materially degraded.
  • Medium: Neither government will use the conduct-oversight process (veto authority, Tier 2 or Tier 3 removal) to remove counterpart inspectors for political reasons; all removal decisions are substantiated by factual misconduct or security concerns.
  • Low: Inspector rotation across sites every 3 months is administratively feasible and does not create information-barrier violations, document-management issues, or security clearance complications.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 0.5 (2026-10-23 17:00), both counterintelligence agencies issue written commitment to vetting-completion target and expedited-review procedures. By Month 2 (2026-12-08), at least 60% of candidate inspectors (>70 per country) are submitted for clearance. By Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), at least 80% of planned roster (217 per country) is vetted and approved; any critical-post vacancy is filled from a pre-approved surge bench within 5 working days.
