By Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), 100% of deployed inspectors have signed zone-conduct acknowledgments and three-tier infraction protocol acknowledgments; bilateral Conduct Committee is operationalized with monthly meeting cadence.

Notes

  • Inspector vetting is subject to external delays outside the project's control; weekly steering-committee tracking and escalation protocols are essential to detect slips early.
  • A surge-bench of 20–30% pre-vetted replacements must be in place by Month 4 (2027-02-08) to accommodate vetting delays, turnover, and rotation absences; surge-bench vetting should begin in parallel with main-roster vetting, not sequentially.
  • Access-log audit monthly is resource-intensive; if audit staff are insufficient, audits will lag and zone violations will go undetected, raising espionage risk; dedicated audit personnel per country are needed.
  • Quarterly rotation is procedurally complex (handoffs, document transfer, temporary knowledge gaps); pilot the rotation process at one site in Months 5–6 (2027-03-08 to 2027-04-08) before full implementation during Phase One to identify and resolve procedural friction.

5. Pre-Test Calibration Exercise Design and Go/Modify/Stop Threshold Validation

Provisional thresholds (90% detection target, <5% false positives, <5% unverifiable equipment) are estimates used to lock the Go/Modify/Stop decision criteria before Phase One begins. Calibration exercises validate these estimates against real equipment and inspector performance; if calibration reveals that provisional targets are unrealistic (e.g., actual detection is 70%, not 90%), thresholds must be recalibrated before formal blind challenges to avoid a Modify outcome that reflects mis-set targets rather than mechanism performance. This data determines whether the final Go/Modify/Stop verdict is credible and defensible as an assessment of the mechanism's real capability, not a reflection of yardstick errors.

Data to Collect

  • Calibration-exercise scenario suite design (at least 50–100 events per site covering all 7 event types: unreported arrivals, substitutions, record falsification, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal, reluctant operators)
  • Calibration-exercise execution results: blind-challenge detection rates by event type (proposed targets: 90% unreported arrivals, 85% substitutions, 80% record falsification); false-positive rate (<5% proposed); unverifiable-equipment count (<5% proposed); confidence intervals around all estimates
  • Provisional Go/Modify/Stop threshold adjustment based on calibration evidence: if calibration results diverge >20% from provisional targets, recalibrate thresholds or document justification for keeping provisional values
  • Decision rule codification: documented rubric specifying which KPI failures are non-negotiable Stop conditions, which are Modify conditions (correctable weaknesses), and which can be waivers or conditional Go outcomes
  • Double-key co-chair signature locking all thresholds and decision rules by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) with no further amendment except via recorded protocol-change procedures

Simulation Steps

  • Commission the independent testing unit to design the full calibration-exercise scenario suite by Month 1 (2026-11-08); include realistic event scenarios that both governments' red teams deem fair and difficult enough to test detection credibly
  • Reserve 100–150 non-covered equipment units per site (surplus, refurbished, or decommissioned, not in active computational use) for calibration use; confirm operator and site-readiness for Months 4–5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) execution
  • Execute calibration exercises Months 4–5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) using blind-challenge methodology (sealed double-key schedule, minimal advance notice to inspectors and operators); score detection results using the fixed pre-agreed corroboration rule
  • Analyze calibration results: calculate detection rates, false-positive rate, unverifiable-equipment count, and 95% confidence intervals per event type; document any scenarios where detection failed and analyze root causes

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage independent testing unit leadership and both red teams to validate that calibration scenarios are realistic, representative of expected Phase One events, and fair to both countries' inspectors
  • Consult statistical experts to ensure that the calibration sample size (50–100 events per site = 200–400 total across 4 sites) is sufficient to estimate detection rates with acceptable confidence intervals (e.g., ±5% for 90% detection target)
  • Obtain bilateral agreement (signed by both co-chairs) on whether calibration-exercise data will be reused in the final Go/Modify/Stop evidence base or discarded as out-of-scope; if reused, formally integrate results into evidence base with 'validated' status
  • Commission an independent audit (third-party auditor from a neutral country) to verify that calibration-exercise methodology matches the planned Phase One exercise methodology and that detected anomalies are not artifacts of test procedure rather than mechanism weakness

Responsible Parties

  • Independent testing unit (scenario design, blind-exercise execution, scoring)
  • Both red teams (scenario fairness review, realism assessment)
  • Bilateral threshold-validation working group (threshold adjustment, decision-rule codification)
  • Both co-chairs (threshold lock-in and double-key signature)

Assumptions

  • Medium: 100–150 non-covered equipment units per site are available and reserved for calibration use (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) without disrupting Phase One operations or requiring additional facility standby.
  • High: Calibration-exercise scenarios are sufficiently representative of Phase One events that calibration results predict formal Phase One detection performance within ±10–15% accuracy; calibration is not just a rehearsal but a meaningful validation test.
  • Medium: Provisional threshold targets (90% detection, <5% false positives, <5% unverifiable) are recalibrated without triggering dispute over whether recalibration constitutes 'moving the goalposts'; both governments accept that calibration validates targets or justifies adjustment.
  • High: Calibration-exercise data can be reused in the formal Go/Modify/Stop decision (i.e., the 50–100 calibration events per site count as part of the Phase One evidence base) without muddying the distinction between calibration and formal testing; both governments agree on this in writing by Month 2 (2026-12-08).

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 1 (2026-11-08 17:00), calibration-exercise scenario suite is designed and locked; both co-chairs and red teams have reviewed scenarios and approved them as realistic and fair. By Month 5 (2027-03-08), calibration exercises are completed at all 4 sites; detection results, false-positive rate, and unverifiable-equipment counts are documented with 95% confidence intervals. By Month 5.5 (2027-03-23 17:00), all Go/Modify/Stop thresholds are double-key signed by both co-chairs; if calibration results diverged >20% from provisional targets, recalibration is documented and new thresholds are signed; all other adjustments are recorded as protocol changes with date and rationale.

Notes

  • Calibration is the only opportunity to validate provisional thresholds before formal blind challenges; skipping or rushing calibration leaves the final verdict resting on unvalidated estimates.
  • Calibration data reuse (or exclusion) must be decided by Month 2 (2026-12-08); attempting to decide after calibration execution creates the appearance of outcome-biasing.
  • If calibration reveals that false-positive rate is 10% instead of 5%, a Modify outcome may become inevitable; both governments must be prepared to accept that result without contesting the threshold or mechanism validity.
  • Calibration-exercise difficulty and scenario realism depend on independent testing unit quality and both red teams' engagement; if scenarios are too easy or too hard, calibration results will be misleading and final thresholds will be mis-set.

6. Contingency Budget Exposure and Fiscal Governance

The contingency reserve (USD 500M per canonical facts) is the only buffer for gate delays, site replacement, vendor-refusal examiner overruns, and exercise disruptions. Worst-case contingency exposure is estimated at USD 515M (per canonical facts: about USD 15M shortfall), leaving zero surge margin if multiple contingencies activate simultaneously. Contingency-governance procedures (fast-lane authority, double-key limits, fiscal escalation) determine whether contingency can be accessed fast enough to prevent operational failure when crises occur. This data determines whether the USD 500M reserve is adequate or if supplemental appropriation is required; whether contingency-governance procedures enable timely access or create decision bottlenecks; and whether fiscal tracking can detect underfunding in time to activate the withheld-funding Stop condition.

Data to Collect

  • Cost estimates for gate-delay holding cost (USD 50–100M per month x number of months deferred); worst-case gate slip from Month 6 (2027-04-08) to Month 9 (2027-07-08) = 3 months = USD 150–300M per canonical facts
  • Cost estimates for site replacement (4–8 weeks delay, USD 50–200M per canonical facts); triggered if a site is withdrawn or fails entry conditions
  • Cost estimates for late-engaged independent examiners (30–40 exams per site at USD 50–100k per exam = USD 1.5–4.0M per site vs. USD 0.6–1.2M budget; overrun USD 3.6–11.2M total per canonical facts)
  • Cost estimates for exercise-incident recovery and contingency miscellaneous (USD 4M estimate); attestation-root alternative costs if joint ceremony fails (absorbed in USD 1.25B ledger envelope, not separate)
  • Contingency reserve allocation strategy: ring-fencing (USD 200M for gate, USD 150M for site replacement, USD 100M for examiners, USD 50M for surge/incidents) vs. unified reserve; fast-lane release authority (USD 50M per side on joint signature within 5 business days per canonical facts)

Simulation Steps

  • Build a contingency-exposure model in Excel or Monte Carlo software; model 10+ scenarios combining gate delays, vendor refusals, site replacement, examiner overruns, and exercise disruptions; calculate worst-case, median, and best-case contingency burn and remaining reserve
  • For each delay scenario, calculate holding-cost accumulation: USD 50–100M/month x (number of months slipped); map holding-cost to contingency drawdown and impact on other budget envelopes
  • Model vendor-refusal cascades: if X% of Tier 1 vendors refuse, how many examiners are needed, at what cost, and is that cost within pre-allocated sub-envelope; if cost exceeds sub-envelope, calculate gap and contingency impact
  • Design three contingency-governance options: (a) unified reserve with double-key approval for any release >USD 50M; (b) ring-fenced sub-envelopes with fast-lane release authority up to USD 10M per sub-envelope; (c) tiered release authority: single-signature release up to USD 25M, double-key for USD 25–100M, co-chair political decision >USD 100M; compare governance burden and decision speed for each

Expert Validation Steps

  • Consult US Treasury, OMB, and Chinese equivalent fiscal authorities on the USD 5B appropriation and per-country USD 2.5B budgets; confirm that the 18-month appropriation window (Months 0–18 = 2026-10-08 to 2028-04-08) is enforceable and that unspent funds will not revert at fiscal-year end
  • Obtain bilateral agreement (signed by budget working group and treasuries) on contingency-governance procedures: fast-lane release authority limits, double-key decision timelines (target 5 business days), escalation to co-chairs if consensus cannot be reached within the decision window
  • Engage fiscal auditors from both countries to design the monthly contingency burn-rate reporting and variance-tracking dashboard; establish variance thresholds (e.g., variance >5% triggers escalation investigation within 5 working days)
  • Consult financial-management experts on funding-timeliness governance: design a procedure where late tranches are flagged within 5 working days, co-chairs notified within 10 days, and a 75-day total cure period applies before withheld-funding Stop is triggered (per canonical facts: 45-day disbursement window + 30-day cure = 75 days)

Responsible Parties

  • Bilateral budget working group (cost estimation, sensitivity analysis, scenario modeling)
  • US Treasury, OMB, and Chinese finance/budget authorities (appropriation governance, tranche disbursement timing)
  • Independent fiscal auditors (monthly burn-rate reporting, variance analysis, withheld-funding detection)
  • Both co-chairs (final approval of contingency-governance procedures and release authority)

Assumptions

  • Medium: Holding-cost estimates (USD 50–100M per month for gate delay) are accurate and reflect the full cost of personnel, facility, and equipment standby; no hidden costs emerge during actual delay periods.
  • Medium: Site-replacement cost estimates (USD 50–200M for 4–8 weeks) include all additional vetting, training, ledger setup, and facility standby for the alternate site; no one-time infrastructure costs exceed estimates.
  • Medium: Examiner cost estimates (USD 50–100k per exam, USD 3.6–11.2M total overrun) reflect realistic market rates for independent equipment-identity examination without vendor cooperation; bulk-discount or pre-contracting opportunities reduce actual cost.
  • Medium: Fast-lane contingency release (up to USD 50M per side on joint signature within 5 business days per canonical facts) is administratively feasible; both treasuries can authorize and transfer funds within the 5-day window without legislative or regulatory delay.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 0.5 (2026-10-23 17:00), a bilateral budget working group provides a written cost-basis analysis for all identified contingency drivers (gate delay, site replacement, examiner overrun, exercise incidents), with low, mid, and high estimates. By Month 1 (2026-11-08), contingency-governance procedures are drafted and circulated to treasuries for comment; fast-lane release authority limits and double-key decision timelines are documented. By Month 3 (2027-01-08), both governments approve the contingency-governance procedure and sign the budget accord; if the contingency-exposure gap (estimated USD 15M) cannot be closed via governance efficiency, a written decision is made to either seek supplemental appropriation or accept reduced contingency margin. By Month 6 (2027-04-08) and ongoing, monthly contingency burn-rate reports are provided to both treasuries; variance >5% triggers escalation investigation within 5 working days.

Notes

  • Contingency worst-case of USD 515M exceeds reserve by USD 15M; if gates slip 3 months (300M worst case) and a site requires replacement (200M worst case), contingency is depleted before examiner overruns (11M) can be absorbed; ring-fencing sub-envelopes can prevent exhaustion of one category but may prevent flexibility in others.
  • Holding-cost estimates assume continuous personnel and facility costs during delay; if Phase One is deferred pending entry-condition resolution, some personnel and facilities may be placed on temporary standby or reduced deployment, lowering holding cost; modeling should include a 'standby mode' cost estimate.
  • Fast-lane contingency release (USD 50M per side, 5 business days) is faster than some bilateral decision processes; ensuring treasuries can sign within 5 days may require pre-delegation to a named fiscal authority or automatic standing authorization.
  • Withheld-funding Stop trigger (75 days total: 45-day disbursement window + 30-day cure) is a powerful sanction but may not distinguish between legitimate payment-system delays and deliberate funding withholding; the procedure must include a good-faith cure-notice mechanism and a dispute-resolution path before Stop is invoked.

7. Independent Testing Unit Exercise Credibility and Blind-Challenge Fairness Validation

The Go/Modify/Stop decision rests entirely on blind-challenge detection results (proposed targets: 90% unreported arrivals, 85% substitutions, 80% record falsification). Either government could contest exercise fairness, claiming that scenarios were biased, too difficult, or unrepresentative. Without a credible, independent testing unit and a transparent fairness-comparison protocol locked before exercises begin, the final verdict will be vulnerable to post-hoc dispute over exercise validity. This data determines whether blind-challenge results are credible, symmetric, and defensible as evidence of the mechanism's real capability.

Data to Collect

  • Independent testing unit charter and governance: staffing model (neutral-country nationals, no direct national-government loyalty), reporting authority (both co-chairs jointly), conflict-of-interest policy, sealed-schedule management
  • Sealed double-key exercise schedule mechanism: how event scenarios are drawn (random, stratified, or adversarial design), how schedule is stored and revealed (encrypted, dual-key unsealing), who has access to schedule before exercises and when
  • Exercise scenario templates for all 7 event types (unreported arrival, substitution, record falsification, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal, reluctant operator): realism, complexity, difficulty parity between US and China scenarios
  • Fairness-comparison protocol: how US scenarios are compared against China scenarios for difficulty, artifact visibility, operator-knowledge assumptions; how both red teams certify fairness before each exercise runs
  • Detection-performance scoring methodology: definition of 'detection' (change recorded in ledger within 48 hours? or immediate observation?), scoring consistency across event types, false-negative and false-positive audit trail

Simulation Steps

  • Design a mock sealed double-key exercise-schedule system: define the schedule as a time-stamped list of event scenarios and timings; encrypt it with one key held by each country (neither can unseal alone); practice unsealing the schedule daily, verifying that schedule entropy and access controls prevent gaming
  • Commission independent testing unit to design representative exercise scenarios for each of the 7 event types; have both red teams review scenarios for realism and difficulty; document any fairness concerns and mitigation strategies
  • Simulate fairness comparison: present 5 unreported-arrival scenarios designed by the US red team and 5 designed by the China red team to independent auditors; score each scenario on difficulty, artifact visibility, and operator-knowledge assumptions; calculate parity metrics
  • Model three detection-scoring definitions: (a) change recorded in ledger within 24 hours, (b) within 48 hours, (c) immediate observation during physical inspection; calculate how scoring-definition choice affects false-negative rate and Go threshold achievement for each event type

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage an independent international organization (e.g., Switzerland's Federal Department of Defence, UNIDIR, or a neutral third-country government) to assess the independent testing unit's governance and conflict-of-interest policies; confirm that unit is structurally independent from both national governments
  • Consult both countries' red teams and bilateral technical leads to validate that the sealed double-key schedule mechanism prevents both inspection-side and operator-side advance knowledge; conduct a mock schedule-unsealing ceremony to confirm the procedure works in practice
  • Engage a neutral third-party auditor to review fairness-comparison protocols and certify that the fairness-audit process is transparent, documented, and produces reproducible parity assessments between US and China scenarios
  • Obtain bilateral agreement (signed by independent testing unit director and both co-chairs) on the detection-scoring definition and consistency audit procedures before the first formal blind exercise is run

Responsible Parties

  • Independent testing unit (neutral-country staffing, sealed-schedule management, scenario design, scoring)
  • Both red teams (scenario design, fairness review, bias detection)
  • Bilateral fairness-audit team (scenario comparison, parity analysis, bias certification)
  • Both co-chairs (approval of fairness protocols and scoring methodology)

Assumptions

  • High: An independent testing unit staffed by neutral-country nationals (not directly controlled by US or China) is acceptable to both governments; neither government perceives the unit as a loss of sovereign control over exercise design.
  • High: Sealed double-key schedule mechanism prevents both operator and inspector advance knowledge of exercise timing and content; neither side can engineer events or responses to optimize appearance of detection.
  • Medium: Fairness-comparison protocols produce reproducible, objective measures of scenario difficulty and parity; subjective assessments (e.g., 'this scenario is harder') can be converted to quantitative metrics that both governments accept.
  • Medium: Neither red team will deliberately design unfair scenarios (too difficult for counterpart inspectors, too easy for own inspectors) during Phase One; both teams prioritize scenario realism and testing credibility over tactical advantage.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 1 (2026-11-08 17:00), independent testing unit charter is signed by both co-chairs; unit director and staff are appointed and cleared by both governments. By Month 2 (2026-12-08), sealed double-key schedule mechanism is designed and tested on mock data; unsealing procedures are documented and both co-chairs verify the mechanism prevents advance knowledge. By Month 4 (2027-02-08), fairness-comparison protocols are operationalized; at least 2 mock scenarios per event type are presented to the fairness-audit team, and parity metrics are calculated and approved by both red teams before protocol is locked. By Month 5 (2027-03-08), the independent testing unit conducts a full mock blind exercise at one site (with live inspectors, sealed schedule, real equipment) to validate end-to-end procedures and measure detection performance; mock results are reviewed and scored by both technical teams and approved as representative before formal Phase One challenges begin.

Notes

  • Independent testing unit must be geographically separate from both governments and participating sites to prevent pressure or access by national security or intelligence agencies; location (e.g., Switzerland, UN facility) should be confirmed by Month 1 (2026-11-08).
  • Sealed double-key schedule unsealing should occur only minutes before each exercise begins, not hours or days in advance; operational details of time, location, and event type should be revealed only to site leadership, not to inspectors or operators until exercise is underway.
  • Fairness-comparison protocol must be applied to every exercise scenario, not just a sample; if one scenario is found to be unfair after the fact, the results from that exercise must be marked as questionable or excluded from the final verdict.
  • Both red teams must certify fairness before each exercise runs, not after; post-hoc fairness claims ('this scenario was unfair') should not be permitted to invalidate detection results, but pre-exercise concerns should be resolved before the scenario is executed.

Summary

The Consortium bilateral verification program faces seven critical data-collection priorities spanning domestic authority enactment, vendor pre-qualification, ledger-forensics operationalization, inspector vetting and conduct oversight, pre-test calibration, contingency fiscal governance, and independent exercise credibility. Together, these areas determine whether Phase One can start on time (Month 6 = 2027-04-08), whether the 90-day test window is credible and complete, whether the final Go/Modify/Stop decision is defensible, and whether the USD 500M contingency reserve is adequate. Immediate actions (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) focus on decomposing domestic authority enactment, securing vendor pre-binding agreements, recruiting and authorizing the forensic panel, and locking the bilateral instrument's conditional-start fallback, evidence-weighting hierarchy, and contingency-governance procedures. Critical dependencies are inspector vetting (14–16 weeks, Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23 to Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23 to 2027-02-23) and calibration-exercise execution (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08), both of which feed the threshold-lock decision by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23). Worst-case contingency exposure (USD 515M vs. USD 500M reserve, shortfall ~USD 15M) must be reconciled by Month 3 (2027-01-08) via supplemental appropriation, ring-fenced envelope allocation, or scope trade-off. Success is measured by entry-condition certification by Month 6 (2027-04-08) with zero unresolved items >4 weeks old, detection rates from calibration exercises confirming threshold realism, and independent testing unit standing by with sealed Phase One exercise schedule locked and fairness-audited. The highest-risk areas are domestic authority timing veto (no fallback if one government lags), vendor refusal cascades (no pre-bound examiners = unverifiable equipment >5% threshold), and ledger divergence procedural deadlock (no pre-authorized forensic panel = automatic suspension on technical faults). Each data-collection area requires bilateral expert validation before Month 1 (2026-11-08) to permit course correction; late discovery of gaps (e.g., vendors unwilling to pre-bind by Month 2 = 2026-12-08) compresses the remediation window and forces either Phase One deferral (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 backstop) or acceptance of reduced credibility.

Essential Information:

  • Missing deadlock resolution procedures or lack of a neutral referee panel means disputes on contested identity, asymmetric access, or funding extend beyond 7 days without escalation path; estimated 1–2 unresolved deadlocks per Phase One per site, each consuming 1–2 weeks and potentially triggering automatic suspension that appears to fail a working mechanism.

  • Ambiguity on suspension triggers or reversal procedures results in automatic suspensions firing without co-chair awareness or a path to reinstate; estimated 5–10 auto-suspensions per site per Phase One from expired discrepancy clocks or ledger divergence if no clear reversal process exists, making the mechanism appear to fail due to administrative cliffs rather than real defects.

  • Weak confidentiality or information-handling clauses allow classified technology details or operator information to leak; estimated 5–10% probability of a material IP or counterintelligence exposure per Phase One if compartmentation is not contractually enforced; exposure triggers consent-withdrawal risk (Stop) for the injured party.
  • Ambiguous dispute-escalation or arbitration procedures mean allegations of protocol violation (e.g., unauthorized zone access, evidence tampering, fabricated escalations) are litigated bilaterally without neutral arbiter; unresolved allegations escalate to political level, delaying operations by 1–3 weeks and raising risk of consent withdrawal by 10–15%.

Worst Case Scenario: The bilateral instrument is signed but with ambiguous double-key scope, weak deadlock resolution, missing forensic-panel pre-authorization, and vague suspension reversal procedures. Within Month 7 (2027-05-08), a contested equipment-identity dispute emerges: the US believes a substitution occurred undetected; China disputes the evidence and refuses to mark the equipment unverifiable. The dispute escalates through co-chairs, consuming 10 days with no neutral arbiter; the bilateral adjudication unit is asked to decide but lacks authority defined in the instrument. By day 10, an automatic suspension fires due to unresolved ledger divergence (the identity dispute triggered a divergence). China views the suspension as US-imposed, not automatic, and withdraws all inspectors. US retaliates by suspending Chinese inspectors. By Month 8 (2027-06-08), reciprocal access collapses. Go/Modify/Stop decision is impossibility. Phase One effectively fails, bilateral verification credibility is destroyed, and political escalation prevents any Phase Two restart. Estimated damage: USD 500M+ in sunk costs, geopolitical setback undermining broader bilateral cooperation.

Best Case Scenario: The bilateral instrument is detailed, signed by both co-chairs by Month 2 (2026-12-08), and clearly specifies double-key scope, pre-authorized forensic-panel authority for identity disputes (48-hour turnaround), a fixed vendor-refusal ladder (day 10 decision), tiered inspector-conduct rules, automatic-suspension triggers and reversal procedures, monthly reciprocity-parity checks, and a neutral independent adjudication panel for dispute escalation. Entry conditions are met on schedule by Month 6 (2027-04-08). Phase One clock starts on time. By Month 7 (2027-05-08), a contested identity dispute arises; the forensic panel issues a finding within 48 hours, both co-chairs accept it, and the equipment is resolved and marked unverifiable. By Month 8 (2027-06-08), one vendor refuses cooperation; the day-10 ladder is invoked, an independent examiner is engaged, and the equipment is resolved by day 12. By Month 9 (2027-07-08), all 90 days are complete. Final decision: Go. Both governments accept the verdict as principled because decision thresholds were locked in advance, exercises were blind and independently designed, and every disputed claim was resolved via the pre-agreed escalation ladder. Phase Two is authorized. Bilateral verification mechanism becomes a trusted precedent for technology confidence-building.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If negotiating a comprehensive single bilateral instrument with full detail on all decision rules, deadlock procedures, and governance proves time-intensive (estimated 8–12 weeks), adopt a modular sequencing: sign a master agreement on double-key governance, reciprocity and dispute escalation by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); defer forensic-panel authority, vendor-refusal procedures, and infraction tiers to side letters or internal standing-committee charters signed by co-chairs by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). Master agreement is binding and sufficient for entry-condition gate; side letters are binding operational detail. This reduces initial negotiation burden while preserving legal clarity.
  • If either government refuses to pre-authorize a neutral independent adjudication panel in the instrument (political resistance to third-party arbitration), adopt a bilateral co-chair adjudication model: disputes are decided by the co-chairs themselves, with a structured 7-day bilateral negotiation window before escalation. Assign a senior neutral facilitator (e.g., from a trusted international organization) to chair the co-chair meeting and help structure consensus, without issuing independent findings or overriding co-chair decision. This preserves mutual veto and national sovereignty while reducing unstructured deadlock.
  • If domestic legislative authority enactment is delayed beyond Month 3.5 (2027-01-23) in either country, trigger a provisional pre-clock dry-run on non-covered equipment (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) under interim authority.   • If pre-authorizing a single neutral adjudication panel is politically infeasible, pre-agree on panel membership and selection procedures in the bilateral instrument, with each co-chair nominating one panelist and both agreeing on a rotating third panelist from a pre-approved list of neutral nations. This distributes trust and ensures no single co-chair controls the panel; panel issues non-binding opinions, with final decisions remaining with co-chairs but informed by neutral technical input. Reduces political resistance while preserving structure.
  • If forensic-panel pre-authorization is resisted (security concern that forensics could expose classified details), defer forensic-panel authority and allow identity disputes to escalate directly to co-chairs with a structured 5-day fact-gathering period. Document each finding in the ledger to establish precedent for future disputes.
  • If a strict reciprocity-gate requirement is rejected by one country (claiming domestic conditions prevent simultaneous completion), allow a conditional provisional start (begin at each site once that site's conditions are met) but explicitly mark Phase One as 'non-binding pilot' rather than formal test, and defer the Go/Modify/Stop decision until all sites have been operating for 90 days. This removes the veto but sacrifices some evidentiary comparability; results are interpreted as indicative rather than definitive.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Failure to identify serial critical-path items leaves the plan exposed to a single-country veto; if neither country commits to expedited processing of its critical act, the other side gains negotiating leverage to demand concessions on inspection scope or zone boundaries.
  • Vague or unspecified escalation procedures mean that delays are tolerated without triggering re-planning; 4–8 week slips accumulate unnoticed until the entry-conditions steering committee is forced into crisis escalation in Month 4–5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08).
  • Absence of fallback authority routes leaves no escape if the primary legislative path is blocked by parliamentary opposition, security agency delays, or geopolitical events; the program becomes wholly dependent on both countries completing entry work simultaneously, an unrealistic assumption.
  • Undefined legal basis for inspector immunity exposes bilateral framework to liability if an inspector is sued in either country for evidence-collection activities; operator cooperation risk increases if their facility could be liable for inspector actions.
  • Unclear evidence-handling authority leads to disputes over what information can leave a site for bilateral ledger reconciliation or forensic adjudication; delays of 1–2 weeks per discrepancy resolution event while lawyers debate whether evidence transfer is authorized.

Worst Case Scenario: Legislative gridlock in either country prevents domestic access authority enactment by Month 6 (2027-04-08). Best Case Scenario: Both governments complete legislative enactment of all identified domestic acts by Month 3 (2027-01-08), 4 weeks ahead of baseline target (Month 3.5 = 2027-01-23). This acceleration unlocks Phase One clock start at Month 6 (2027-04-08) as planned, preserving the full 90-day test window (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) and the 6-week pre-test calibration window (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08). Thresholds are validated against realistic performance data before the formal decision period. Entry-conditions steering committee escalations are routine and resolve within the planned schedule, building confidence that both governments are committed to the full entry gate. Phase One starts on time and is not compressed. Holds full credible detection evidence for Go/Modify/Stop decision at Month 10 (2027-08-08).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Initiate simultaneous legislative drafting in both countries at Month 0 (2026-10-08), in parallel with bilateral instrument negotiation, rather than after instrument signature. Identify baseline legislative template from similar past bilateral agreements (IAEA, OPCW, China–US military-communications agreements); adapt templates in tandem to surface conflicts early and compress timeline by 3–4 weeks.
  • Pre-socialize controversial provisions with parliamentary and ministerial stakeholders in Month 0 (2026-10-08) via confidential consultations, before formal drafting begins. Identify and resolve points of resistance early (e.g., inspector immunity scope, evidence-handling limits, vendor enforcement powers) through working-group consensus, so legislative process moves faster by the time it reaches full committee/council.
  • Establish a bilateral legislative-process working group led by each country's legal counsel, meeting weekly from Month 0 (2026-10-08) to Month 3 (2027-01-08), with explicit milestones for each act. Track progress against milestones and trigger escalation to co-chairs within 2 working days if a single act slips >2 weeks, rather than waiting for 4-week delay threshold.
  • Define a multi-tier fallback authority chain for each country: primary legislative act → emergency executive order → provisional delegation via existing statute → conditional early-phase operation. If primary path stalls, move to next tier automatically without requiring renegotiation; document the fallback in the bilateral instrument at Month 2 (2026-12-08) so it is not treated as a crisis escalation.
  • Conduct a pre-clock dry-run gate (Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23) on non-covered equipment and non-sensitive infrastructure to test whether current domestic authority is sufficient for basic bilateral operations before formal authority enactment. This reveals authority gaps early and provides justification for accelerated or fallback enactment.
  • Engage an independent parliamentary and legal affairs consultant from a neutral third country to advise both legislatures simultaneously on best practices for verification-authority enactment, removing bilateral suspicion and helping each country learn from the other's legislative process.
  • Consider a provisional instrument taking effect only for the pre-clock calibration and dry-run phases (Months 2–5 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-03-08), with formal full-authority enactment required only for Phase One clock start (Month 6 = 2027-04-08). This allows early testing while legislative processes complete.

Create Document 3: Counterintelligence Vetting Acceleration Plan and Expedited-Clearance Request

ID: 50622309-9aa0-411d-a590-8898d75f96fd

Description: Request to both countries' counterintelligence services to vet 120–150 candidate inspectors per country on an expedited 14–16 week schedule (starting Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23, completing by Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23 at latest to support Month 5 = 2027-03-08 roster approval). Identifies vetting standards, counterpart-approval procedures (veto right), replacement-bench surge (20–30% additional pre-vetted candidates), and fallback conditional-start authority if vetting is not complete by Month 5 (2027-03-08). Document type: government process request and acceleration plan; audience: counterintelligence agencies, co-chairs, bilateral vetting coordinator; critical path bottleneck.

Responsible Role Type: Bilateral Vetting Coordinator and Counterintelligence Liaison

Primary Template: None

Secondary Template: Government Personnel Security Clearance Expedited Review Request

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 0 (2026-10-08), bilateral vetting coordinator provides both countries' counterintelligence services with the list of 120–150 candidate inspectors per country, along with justification (bilateral verification program, 14-week vetting window, start date Month 5 = 2027-03-08).
  • Request expedited vetting: provide clear vetting standards (counterintelligence, security-clearance level, polygraphy, background investigation, travel history, foreign contacts).
  • Establish counterpart-approval procedure: once vetted, candidates from Country A are sent to Country B's counterintelligence for veto-right review (5 working days); failure to object = approval.
  • Request joint designation of a vetting liaison from each country to coordinate progress and escalate bottlenecks weekly.
  • Identify a surge bench of 20–30% additional candidates per country and include them in the vetting queue; these serve as replacement pool if primary roster has attrition.
  • If vetting is not 80% complete by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), activate the conditional-start fallback: allow Phase One to begin with 80% approved roster and 20% provisional (subject to counterpart veto), with final vetted rosters catching up during Month 6 (2027-04-08).

Approval Authorities: Both countries' counterintelligence agencies execute vetting; bilateral conduct committee approves or vetoes counterpart candidates; co-chairs certify 80% roster approval by Month 5 (2027-03-08).

Essential Information:

  • Identify the critical counterintelligence vetting standards required by both governments (security-clearance level, polygraphy scope, background-investigation depth, travel-history lookback period, foreign-contact disclosure rules, disqualifying factors).
  • Specify the exact list of 120–150 candidate inspectors per country, their roles (shift inspector, technical specialist, adjudicator, support), and their proposed site assignments.
  • Define the counterpart-approval procedure: timeline for Country B to review and veto Country A's vetted candidates (propose: 5 working days; failure to object = approval); escalation path if veto is issued.
  • Detail the surge-replacement bench: identify 20–30% additional candidates per country (36–45 per country) who are pre-vetted in parallel and available as substitutes for primary-roster attrition or conditional-start gaps.
  • Document the fallback conditional-start authority: if 80% roster approval is achieved by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23) but vetting is incomplete, what double-key decision permits Phase One to begin with provisional inspectors subject to counterpart veto?
  • Establish joint bilateral vetting-liaison role: designate a counterintelligence liaison from each country with explicit authority to coordinate weekly progress, escalate bottlenecks same-week, and authorize expedited sub-processes.
  • Specify the vetting timeline milestones: candidate list submission (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23), primary-roster vetting start (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23), 50% completion (Month 2 = 2026-12-08), 80% completion (Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23), final certification (Month 5 = 2027-03-08).
  • Define escalation triggers and remedies: if vetting is <50% complete by Month 2 (2026-12-08), identify which bottleneck (background investigation, polygraphy queue, counterpart review delays) requires deputy or ministerial intervention.
  • Clarify reciprocal veto authority: if Country A's counterintelligence rejects a Country B inspector with no stated reason, what is the dispute-resolution path (appeal to co-chairs, substitute from bench, or automatic rejection)?
  • Quantify the vetting cost and resource demand: staffing (dedicated vetting coordinators, background investigators, polygraphy administrators per country), contractor support for accelerated timeline, and budget authority to hire surge vetting resources.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If vetting standards are ambiguous or unequal between countries, one side may claim the other is imposing a higher bar, creating mutual suspicion about the approval list and delaying roster certification by 2–4 weeks.
  • If the surge-replacement bench is not pre-vetted in parallel, loss of even 3–5 primary-roster inspectors to late-stage disqualifications leaves gaps at roster certification (Month 5 = 2027-03-08), forcing Phase One delay or start with unfilled critical posts.
  • If the counterpart-approval procedure lacks a time bound or escalation clause, Country A's vetted inspectors can be held indefinitely in review by Country B, creating a unilateral veto over the roster and shifting the entry-condition gate to counterintelligence discretion.
  • If the conditional-start fallback authority is not pre-agreed in the bilateral instrument, a dispute arises at Month 4–5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) over whether Phase One can start with 80% approval, consuming weeks in negotiation and deferring the clock.
  • If vetting bottlenecks (e.g., polygraphy queue, background-investigation backlog) are not identified and escalated weekly, they remain hidden until Month 4 (2027-02-08) or later, leaving insufficient time to adjust scope or activate surge capacity before Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) roster certification.
  • If the vetting plan does not account for administrative processing delays (fingerprinting, name-check clearances, database-access provisioning), realistic vetting takes 18–20 weeks instead of the planned 14–16 weeks, compressing calibration time or delaying Phase One.
  • If reciprocal-veto disputes over individual inspectors are not pre-scoped (e.g., grounds for veto, appeal process, substitute-offer timeliness), rejection of 1–2 inspectors per country late in the process triggers mutual blame and roster renegotiation.

Worst Case Scenario: Vetting does not reach 80% completion by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23) because bottlenecks (e.g., polygraphy backlog, counterpart review delays, background-investigation appeals) consume 18–20 weeks instead of the planned 14–16. The roster certification (Month 5 = 2027-03-08) is deferred to Month 6–7 (2027-04-08 to 2027-05-08), pushing Phase One clock start to Month 7–8 (2027-05-08 to 2027-06-08). The pre-test calibration (planned Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) is compressed to 1–2 weeks or skipped, forcing decision thresholds to be locked on unvalidated provisional data by Month 6 (2027-04-08). Phase One begins with only 70–75% of planned roster filled; coverage gaps emerge during night and weekend shifts, causing 1–3 unscheduled maintenance windows to be unobserved per week per site. Blind-exercise evidence quality suffers because inspector familiarity and continuity are compromised. The final Go/Modify/Stop decision at Month 10 (2027-08-08) rests on a 90-day test that ran with incomplete staffing and no validated thresholds, making the verdict appear rushed or unreliable to one or both governments. Political backing erodes, and the credibility of the mechanism is damaged even if a Go decision is issued.

Best Case Scenario: The bilateral vetting coordinator and counterintelligence liaisons meet weekly from Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), identify bottlenecks within days, and escalate to deputy or ministerial level for surge authorization. Polygraphy and background-investigation capacity is accelerated via contracted examiners and overtime staffing by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). Counterpart approval follows a 5-day review clock with automatic approval on silence; no inspector is rejected without written cause and an offer of a surge-bench substitute within 3 working days. By Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), 100% of the primary roster is vetted and approved; the surge bench (30% additional candidates) is also 100% vetted and ready as replacement pool. Roster certification is complete by Month 5 (2027-03-08). Phase One begins on schedule at Month 6 (2027-04-08) with full staffing, no coverage gaps, and every critical post filled. The pre-test calibration (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) runs for the full 6 weeks, validating all decision thresholds by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23). Blind exercises run with experienced, continuous mirrored teams; detection evidence is credible and statistically sound. The final Go decision at Month 10 (2027-08-08) is seen by both governments as the result of a well-staffed, professionally vetted, transparent process. Political confidence is sustained through Phase One and provides momentum for Phase Two site expansion.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If primary-country vetting capacity is exceeded by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), contract expedited personnel-security vetting to a third-country or international organization (e.g., a neutral vetting contractor accredited by both governments); establish reciprocal confidence through a pre-agreed vetting protocol that both sides review and approve.
  • If polygraphy or background-investigation queues extend vetting timelines beyond 16 weeks, activate a 'phased roster start': approve and deploy Tier 1 inspectors (shift leads, technical leads, data custodians) by Month 4 (2027-02-08); defer Tier 2 inspectors (support, observers) to Month 5–6 (2027-03-08 to 2027-04-08), staging them during calibration rather than primary-roster certification.
  • If counterpart veto delays approval of vetted inspectors (e.g., Country B delays Country A's roster past Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23), pre-agree on a 'conditional deployment' clause: vetted inspectors may deploy at Month 5 (2027-03-08) pending final counterpart clearance; counterpart has 10 days to issue a veto with cause, or approval is final. If a veto is issued, a surge-bench substitute deploys within 3 working days.
  • If a material gap appears in the roster late (e.g., 5–10 primary inspectors fail vetting or request withdrawal at Month 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08), activate the surge-replacement bench and extend the vetting deadline to Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) with co-chair authority to start Phase One with 80% roster if 80% threshold is reached and critical posts are filled, deferring non-critical rosters to Month 6–7 (2027-04-08 to 2027-05-08).
  • If both countries agree that the vetting timeline is unrealistic, execute a 'rolling vetting model' in which the first 30–40 FTE inspectors (Tier 1) are fully vetted by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), Phase One begins at Month 6 (2027-04-08) with this core roster, and the remaining 100–110 FTE inspectors are vetted and deployed during Months 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) via a documented on-boarding process with counterpart review windows built into the Phase-One clock.

Create Document 4: Provisional Go/Modify/Stop Thresholds and Decision Rubric

ID: 16a76b6c-f3a7-4022-a4de-e284f9dbda1b

Description: Locked decision thresholds specifying: Go requires detection ≥90% unreported arrivals, ≥85% substitutions, ≥80% record falsification, false positives <5%, reciprocal-access parity within 20%, unresolved discrepancies <10% of events, unverifiable equipment <5% per site, zero unresolved ledger divergence >7 days. Modify requires correctable weakness (detection 70–90%, unverifiable 5–10%, fixable by training/procedure); Stop requires asymmetric access, unverifiable >10%, ledger divergence unreconciled, funding withheld, or detection <70%. All thresholds documented with justification (source: calibration exercise, prior program benchmark, expert judgment), validation method, and provisional-vs.-validated status. Includes tie-breaking rule if co-chairs deadlock on Go/Modify. Document type: decision framework; audience: co-chairs, bilateral technical leads, independent testing unit, neutral referee panel; prevents post-hoc threshold reinterpretation.

Responsible Role Type: Bilateral Technical Lead and Decision-Framework Designer

Primary Template: Decision Criteria and Scoring Rubric (PMI/PRINCE2 Gate Criteria)

Secondary Template: None

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 3 (2027-01-08), compile proposed detection thresholds from prior bilateral verification programs (New START, OPCW, IAEA experience) and expert judgment on realistic detection performance against intelligent adversaries. Default proposal: 90% unreported, 85% substitution, 80% record falsification.
  • Document the source and assumption for each threshold (e.g., '90% unreported arrivals: based on IAEA prior-notice-inspection detection rates in 50+ global nuclear facilities; assumes inspectors have <2-hour arrival notification').
  • Mark each threshold as 'provisional' if not yet validated by calibration, or 'estimated' if from prior programs.
  • Execute calibration Months 4–5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08); collect actual detection data by event type.
  • By Month 5 (2027-03-08), reconcile calibration results against provisional thresholds: if actual detection is >10% above provisional (e.g., 92% vs. 90% proposed), validate the provisional value; if detection is >10% below (e.g., 78% vs. 90% proposed), flag as 'threshold mis-set' and recommend recalibration.
  • By Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), both co-chairs jointly sign the final-decision rubric confirming: Go criteria (all thresholds met), Modify criteria (correctable weakness), Stop criteria (asymmetry, funding, >10% unverifiable, <70% detection). Include a tie-breaking rule: if one co-chair votes Go and the other Modify, the more conservative Modify outcome is adopted unless the neutral referee panel votes unanimously for Go within 48 hours.
  • Lock the rubric in the bilateral instrument; mark as 'calibrated and validated' in the ledger.

Approval Authorities: Both co-chairs jointly sign the rubric by double-key by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23); no changes to thresholds or criteria thereafter except through recorded protocol amendment.

Essential Information:

  • Define and justify the three Go/Modify/Stop decision outcomes with explicit criteria: Go (all thresholds met), Modify (correctable weakness), Stop (asymmetric access, funding withheld, unverifiable >10%, detection <70%). Include a detailed rubric for each outcome.
  • Specify the five detection-performance thresholds by event type with sources and assumptions: unreported arrivals (proposed baseline 90%), substitutions (proposed 85%), record falsification (proposed 80%), false-positive rate (<5% proposed), and latency benchmarks. Document whether each is provisional (unvalidated) or validated against calibration data.
  • Establish and document the corroboration rule for equipment identity confirmation: state the minimum number of independent evidence layers required, which layers count (attestation, physical inspection, records, identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure, movement), and what happens if layers disagree.
  • Define all other Go thresholds numerically: reciprocal-access parity (within 20% proposed), unresolved discrepancies (<10% of events proposed), unverifiable equipment (<5% per site proposed), unresolved ledger divergence (zero >7 days proposed), material asymmetric-access or IP/CI incidents (zero proposed).
  • Describe the validation method for each threshold: source (prior bilateral programs, expert judgment, calibration exercise results, benchmark, assumption), confidence level, and any sensitivity ranges (e.g., 'detection ±10% from target = Go still holds; ±15% = Modify; >20% = Stop').
  • Include a tie-breaking rule for deadlock between co-chairs on Go vs. Modify outcome (e.g., 'more conservative Modify is adopted unless neutral referee panel votes unanimously for Go within 48 hours').
  • Specify which thresholds are locked by double-key signature before the first formal blind exercise (Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23) and which may be adjusted only through a recorded protocol-change procedure documented in the ledger.
  • Detail the Modify-outcome criteria: specify the upper and lower bounds of acceptable performance that trigger Modify rather than Go or Stop (e.g., detection 70–90%, unverifiable 5–10%). Include the types of correctable weaknesses (training, procedure adjustment, evidence-layer enhancement) that justify Modify.
  • Detail the Stop-outcome criteria and non-negotiable failure modes: list which failures are automatic Stop conditions (e.g., funding withheld >30 days, unresolved ledger divergence >7 days, operator shielding, detection <70%).
  • Provide a sample scoring sheet or checklist showing how the bilateral technical team evaluates each KPI against the rubric at final decision (Month 10 = 2027-08-08), including how edge cases are handled and who has decision authority if a KPI falls between defined bands.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Vague or post-hoc threshold justification invites goalpost disputes: if thresholds appear to be set after results are known, the defeated co-chair can claim the outcome was predetermined rather than principled, undermining mutual acceptance of the Go/Modify/Stop verdict and potentially triggering bilateral escalation or consent withdrawal.
  • Provisional thresholds locked without calibration validation: if the calibration exercise (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) reveals that actual detection is 2–3 standard deviations away from the proposed baseline (e.g., actual 60% vs. 90% proposed), the locked threshold becomes inappropriate. A Go decision on an unvalidated threshold is indefensible; a Modify outcome driven by threshold mis-calibration rather than mechanism defect wastes the test.
  • Unclear corroboration rule enables disputed identity findings: if the document does not specify how many layers must agree and which layers are sufficient, contested identities (estimated 5–10 per site) escalate to co-chair negotiation for each case, consuming time within the discrepancy clock and risking automatic suspension triggered by administrative deadlock rather than real mechanism failure.
  • Ambiguous Modify vs. Stop boundary: if the gap between Modify criteria (detection 70–90%) and Stop criteria (detection <70%) is not clearly documented, a mechanism at 71% detection faces dispute over whether it is correctable or terminal, delaying the final decision and creating opportunity for either co-chair to claim the outcome was predetermined.
  • Missing tie-breaking rule for Go/Modify deadlock: if the document does not specify what happens when co-chairs split equally, negotiation defaults to co-chair pressure and political bargaining rather than a pre-agreed neutral process, inviting accusations of weaker government accepting a worse outcome under duress.
  • No sensitivity analysis for threshold interdependence: if two thresholds are slightly mis-set in opposite directions (e.g., detection threshold too low, false-positive threshold too high), the combined effect can distort the Go decision even though each individual threshold appears acceptable. Absent sensitivity ranges, this risk is not transparent.
  • Incomplete documentation of sources and assumptions: if thresholds are adopted from prior programs (New START, OPCW, IAEA) without documenting the operational context of those programs (e.g., IAEA inspections assume sovereign state cooperation; New START inspectors have diplomatic immunity), the threshold is transplanted without justifying its applicability to a frontier-computing environment under mutual distrust.
  • Unspecified handling of partial or borderline KPI performance: if a site achieves 89% detection (1% below the 90% Go threshold) but all other thresholds are met, the document does not specify whether this is Go, Modify or Stop, requiring emergent interpretation and creating dispute risk.

Worst Case Scenario: Thresholds locked without calibration validation and later revealed as fundamentally mis-set. At Month 9 (2027-07-08), the bilateral technical team reports actual blind-challenge detection of 65% unreported arrivals (vs. 90% proposed threshold), but the locked rubric requires 90% for Go. The co-chairs must choose between: (1) Stop, claiming the mechanism failed; (2) Modify, admitting the threshold was mis-set; (3) unilateral reinterpretation of the rubric, claimed by one co-chair as justified correction and by the other as goalpost-moving. If neither co-chair agrees and the neutral referee panel cannot break the deadlock, the 90-day test ends without a mutually accepted verdict. One government claims the verification mechanism is fundamentally inadequate; the other claims the test was prejudiced by poor threshold-setting. Political trust collapses, Phase Two is cancelled, and bilateral verification is abandoned for years. This outcome is plausible if the calibration exercise is incomplete, delayed, or not permitted to inform threshold adjustment before the formal clock starts. Estimated probability: 15–25% if calibration is compressed to <3 weeks or data cannot be reused.

Best Case Scenario: A clear, pre-validated, numerically defined rubric enables the bilateral technical team to evaluate Phase One results against explicit criteria without ambiguity or reinterpretation. The calibration exercise (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) confirms that detection rates are 88% unreported, 83% substitution, 79% record falsification—all within ±2% of the proposed thresholds. The rubric is locked by double-key signature at Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) with every threshold, source and sensitivity range documented. At Month 9 (2027-07-08), the 90-day blind challenges yield detection of 91%, 84%, 81% respectively, false positives 3.8%, parity 18%, zero unverifiable >5%. The technical team applies the rubric without judgment: all KPIs meet Go criteria. Co-chairs sign the Go decision by Month 10 (2027-08-08) within 48 hours, both citing the same documented rubric. The decision is accepted by both governments as defensible and principled. This enables Phase Two authorization, expanded site coverage, and sustained bilateral verification credibility. Estimated probability: 30–40% if calibration runs as planned and thresholds are validated before formal clock starts.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If calibration exercise cannot be completed by Month 5 (2027-03-08), use a pre-test sensitivity exercise (compressed 2-week schedule on non-covered equipment in Month 3.5 = 2027-01-23) to test detection performance at the proposed thresholds and adjust by ±5–10% if clear bias is found. Lock thresholds by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23) with an explicit 'unvalidated, sensitivity-tested' label; include in the final decision document a caveat that thresholds were set with limited calibration data, reducing confidence in the Go outcome proportionally.
  • If either co-chair objects to a specific threshold (e.g., claims 90% detection is unattainable for a reasonable mechanism), invoke a structured co-chair negotiation: each presents data or precedent supporting their case; a neutral technical referee panel issues a non-binding opinion within 5 days; co-chairs then vote; if still split, adopt the lower (more conservative) threshold as the presumptive Go criterion, with the option to achieve a higher threshold as a 'Gold-level' Go. Lock this compromise by double-key.
  • If detection-rate calibration data is statistically thin (<50 events per site in the calibration exercise), define the locked threshold as a 'range' rather than a point (e.g., Go if detection is 85–95%, TBD within that band) and specify that the final decision uses the midpoint of the observed range; avoid single-point thresholds that appear rigidly arbitrary.
  • If the bilateral instrument does not permit calibration-exercise data to be reused in the formal Go/Modify/Stop decision, run two separate evidence streams: (1) calibration on non-covered equipment to validate thresholds, (2) formal blind challenges on the covered-equipment roster to generate the decision evidence. Use calibration to 'shape' the thresholds (justified by pilot data), then lock them before formal challenges. Document that calibration is methodological validation, not evidence reuse.
  • If co-chairs deadlock on Go vs. Modify (each met one version of the threshold), invoke the tie-breaking rule immediately: neutral referee panel votes within 24 hours (not 5 days) and the result is binding. If referee is split, apply the 'more conservative Modify' rule by document default, allowing either co-chair to appeal within 48 hours; if both appeal, escalate to co-chairs' political leadership for a one-time override decision documented in the bilateral instrument as exceptional.
  • If a KPI falls between defined bands (e.g., 89.5% detection vs. 90% Go threshold), use a rounding rule: apply standard mathematical rounding (89.5% rounds to 90% and meets Go) and document that KPIs within ±0.5% of threshold boundaries are treated as meeting the criterion. Publish this rounding policy with the threshold rubric to avoid dispute.
  • If either co-chair wants to adjust a threshold after the formal clock starts (months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), define a 'single-adjustment protocol': (1) that co-chair submits written justification citing new evidence within 48 hours; (2) the other co-chair and neutral referee panel review within 5 days; (3) if approved by consensus, the adjustment is recorded in the ledger with full provenance; (4) the adjusted threshold applies only to that KPI's final evaluation, with a clear note in the decision document explaining the in-test adjustment. No threshold can be adjusted twice.

Create Document 5: Funding Timeliness and Contingency-Release Governance Framework

ID: 884edf00-d432-4d4e-b08b-1dcfbc53b36c

Description: Bilateral governance structure and procedural rules governing the USD 5.0B appropriations, USD 2.5B per country, and USD 500M contingency reserve. Specifies: each government must fund its tranche within 45 days of fiscal-year start; variance >5% in Months 0–3 (2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08) triggers escalation; tranche late beyond 75 days (45 + 30-day cure) counts as funding withheld (a Stop trigger). Contingency release requires double-key co-chair authorization; fast lane up to USD 50M per side on joint signature within 5 business days. Contingency sub-envelopes: USD 200M for gate delay, USD 150M for site replacement, USD 100M for vendor fallbacks, USD 50M for surge/exercises. Monthly fiscal-accountability reporting to both treasuries. Document type: financial governance and accountability framework; audience: both countries' treasuries, co-chairs, budget working group, auditors; ensures continuous funding and contingency visibility.

Responsible Role Type: Bilateral Budget Director and Fiscal Accountability Officer

Primary Template: Government Budget Execution and Contingency Management Procedures

Secondary Template: None

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 0 (2026-10-08), establish a bilateral budget working group with representatives from both countries' finance ministries, co-chairs' offices, and the Consortium program manager.
  • Draft the funding-timeliness governance procedures specifying: tranche schedule (each government obligates its USD 2.5B by 45 days into the fiscal year), variance thresholds (>5% variance in Months 0–3 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08 triggers escalation to co-chairs), cure period (30 days to correct variance), and Stop trigger (funding withheld >75 days total).
  • Design contingency-release procedures: (a) fast-lane release up to USD 50M per side (USD 100M total) on joint co-chair signature within 5 business days, no veto; (b) releases >USD 50M per side require formal co-chair agreement within 48 hours; (c) if co-chairs deadlock on a release decision >USD 50M, escalate to neutral referee panel for a non-binding opinion within 5 days, then co-chairs re-vote.
  • Define contingency sub-envelopes within the USD 500M reserve: (1) gate delay costs (USD 200M, released on monthly assessment if entry conditions slip); (2) site replacement (USD 150M, released if operator withdraws); (3) vendor-refusal fallbacks/examiners (USD 100M, released if vendors exceed quota; (4) surge/exercises (USD 50M, released for contingency exercises or emergency personnel).
  • Establish monthly fiscal-accountability reporting: by the 10th of each month, both countries' finance teams submit a spending report (actual vs. planned, variance analysis, contingency burn) to the bilateral budget working group and both co-chairs.
  • Lock the governance framework in the bilateral instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08); publish financial reporting timelines to both treasuries by Month 2 (2026-12-08).

Approval Authorities: Both co-chairs jointly authorize contingency releases >USD 50M per side; both countries' finance ministries authorize their tranches; bilateral budget working group monitors timeliness and variance monthly.

Essential Information:

  • Define the funding-timeliness mandate: each government must obligate its USD 2.5B tranche within 45 days of the fiscal-year start (Month 0 = 2026-10-08); specify the cure period (30 days) and the Stop trigger (funding withheld if not obligated by Day 75).
  • Specify variance thresholds and escalation: budget variance >5% in Months 0–3 (2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08) triggers escalation to co-chairs for corrective action; document the review process and authority to reallocate between sub-envelopes.
  • Detail the contingency-release governance: USD 500M reserve (USD 250M per country) released only by double-key co-chair authorization; fast-lane releases up to USD 50M per side on joint signature within 5 business days (no individual veto); releases >USD 50M per side require formal agreement within 48 hours; deadlock escalates to neutral referee panel for non-binding opinion within 5 days.
  • Define contingency sub-envelopes with release triggers: (1) gate-delay costs (USD 200M, released on monthly assessment if entry-condition milestones slip); (2) site replacement (USD 150M, released if operator withdraws or site is unsuitable); (3) vendor-refusal fallbacks and independent-examiner overage (USD 100M, released if vendor-cooperation rates exceed quota); (4) surge capacity and additional exercises (USD 50M, released for contingency exercises or emergency personnel deployment).
  • Establish monthly fiscal-accountability reporting format: by the 10th of each month, both countries' finance teams submit a report including actual vs. planned spending, variance analysis, contingency burn-rate, pending commitments, and any projected envelope shortfalls or overruns; report delivered to the bilateral budget working group and both co-chairs.
  • Specify the bilateral budget working group structure and responsibilities: establish the group by Month 0 (2026-10-08) with representatives from both countries' finance ministries, co-chairs' offices, and the Consortium program manager; meeting cadence (at minimum bi-weekly), decision authority (consensus-based escalation to co-chairs if disagreement), and documentation of all decisions in the ledger.
  • Define operator and vendor compensation administration rules: compensation is administered by each government and charged to that government's USD 2.5B contribution within the USD 1.0B site-preparation envelope; no shared or commingled compensation pool; each government is responsible for ensuring timely payments to domestic operators and vendors within the allocated budget.
  • Lock the governance framework in the bilateral instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08): the funding-timeliness rules, contingency-release procedures, and fiscal-accountability requirements must be formally signed by both co-chairs and incorporated into the bilateral instrument; no unilateral changes permitted without documented amendment.
  • Calculate and document contingency worst-case exposure: estimated worst-case scenario combines gate-delay holding costs (USD 300M if Phase One delayed to Month 9 = 2027-07-08), site replacement (USD 200M if one site withdraws and replacement is needed), and vendor-examiner overages (approximately USD 11M across all sites if independent examiners are engaged late), totalling approximately USD 511M against the USD 500M contingency reserve, exposing a potential USD 11M shortfall.
  • Establish escalation and override authorities: define who has authority to authorize spending from each sub-envelope within the contingency (e.g., co-chairs for amounts >USD 50M per side, bilateral budget director for routine reconciliation items); document escalation authority if either government objects to a contingency release; clarify that no unilateral freeze of contingency is permitted without documented co-chair sign-off.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Undefined variance thresholds or escalation timelines allow unaccountable budget drift: if variance >5% is not escalated within 5 business days, corrective reallocation becomes impossible and the program lacks transparency, increasing risk of late or withheld funding.
  • Ambiguous contingency-release procedures lead to deadlock: without a clear fast-lane (USD 50M requiring 48-hour agreement), contingency funds sit uncommitted while urgent needs (vendor fallbacks, exercise escalation, site replacement) go unfunded, compressing the test window.
  • Missing sub-envelope definitions leave contingency unallocated: without explicit sub-envelopes for gate delay, site replacement, vendor fallbacks, and surge, co-chairs face ambiguous allocation decisions at crisis moments, delaying deployment by 1–2 weeks per contingency decision.
  • No monthly fiscal-accountability reporting creates blind spots: without standardized monthly reporting by both countries' finance teams, variance and spending patterns are not visible to co-chairs until late (e.g., Month 3 or 4 = 2027-01-08 or 2027-02-08), leaving insufficient time to adjust spending before gate completion.
  • Unclear operator-and-vendor compensation split invites disputes: if it is not explicit that each government funds its own domestic operators and vendors within its USD 2.5B share, both governments may claim the other should pay, creating payment delays and operator withdrawal risk.
  • Vague Stop trigger for funding withheld undermines the dual-key commitment: without a clear definition (funding not obligated by Day 75 = Stop) and no cure mechanism, either government could claim withheld funding and collapse the agreement prematurely.
  • Missing contingency worst-case analysis leaves no margin for simultaneous fallbacks: if the document does not quantify that a gate slip (USD 300M) plus a site replacement (USD 200M) plus examiner overage (USD 11M) totals approximately USD 511M against the USD 500M reserve, neither government sees the USD 11M shortfall exposure and cannot plan surge capacity or reduce scope.
  • Absent ledger documentation of budget decisions creates no audit trail: if budget disputes, contingency releases, or variance escalations are not recorded in the tamper-evident ledger, later questions about fiscal accountability cannot be resolved with evidence that both countries accepted the decision.

Worst Case Scenario: One country delays its appropriations beyond the 75-day Stop trigger (Month 0 = 2026-10-08 + 75 days ≈ Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23), claiming domestic budgetary constraints or parliamentary delay. The other country, having obligated its USD 2.5B on time, claims funding is withheld and invokes the Stop clause, halting Phase One before the 90-day test can begin. The funding-timeliness framework, having no documented variance-escalation or cure pathway, provides no mechanism for the delayed country to remediate without withdrawing consent entirely. The bilateral instrument is terminated; the program collapses with USD 1–2 billion in committed personnel, site preparation, and facility costs already incurred and unrecoverable. Alternatively, both countries obligate their tranches but neither fully releases contingency sub-envelopes for gate-delay holding costs (if entry conditions slip by 3 months = USD 150–300M needed); critical personnel are furloughed, facilities contracts are cancelled, and when entry conditions are finally certified at Month 6+ (2027-04-08+), surge reactivation takes 4–8 weeks, compressing Phase One to 50–60 days and eliminating the pre-test calibration window. Final Go/Modify/Stop decision is based on incomplete evidence and unvalidated provisional thresholds, forcing a default Modify outcome that does not reflect mechanism credibility. (160 words)

Best Case Scenario: Both countries obligate their USD 2.5B tranches by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), well within the 45-day fiscal-year window, with zero variance >5% in Months 0–3 (2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08). Monthly fiscal-accountability reports show spending aligned to plan, with contingency reserves remaining stable at approximately USD 500M through Month 4 (2027-02-08). Entry-condition delays are modest (2–3 weeks in inspector vetting or site selection); the bilateral budget working group approves contingency releases within the fast-lane (USD 50M per side on joint signature within 5 business days) to cover gate-delay holding costs, operator compensation and independent-examiner pre-qualification. Phase One begins on schedule at Month 6 (2027-04-08), with full staffing deployed and all facilities operational. The 90-day test window is uncompressed; calibration exercises validate thresholds by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23); Go/Modify/Stop decision at Month 10 (2027-08-08) is based on clean evidence and locked criteria, enabling a credible Go or defensible Modify verdict. Contingency reserve at end of Phase One is approximately USD 200M, providing surge capacity for Phase Two or sustained operations. (160 words)

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the bilateral budget working group cannot reach consensus on variance thresholds or contingency sub-envelope allocations by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), establish a pre-agreed tiered default governance: Tier 1 variance (0–5%) requires no escalation; Tier 2 variance (5–10%) requires co-chair review and reallocation within 5 days; Tier 3 variance (>10%) triggers contingency release within the relevant sub-envelope. Codify these tiers in the bilateral instrument so both governments accept them in advance rather than negotiating them as disputes.
  • If contingency-release deadlock persists >5 days on a decision affecting Phase One's critical path, invoke an automatic escalation: activate a neutral independent referee panel (a senior finance official from a third country or international organization) to issue a non-binding recommendation within 48 hours on the optimal allocation; the co-chairs then must re-vote; if still deadlocked after the re-vote, the lower-cost option automatically activates (e.g., pay the independent examiner now rather than defer, releasing the funds).
  • If either government cannot obligate its full USD 2.5B tranche by Day 45, allow an interim 50% partial release by Month 1 (2026-11-08) so personnel deployment and site prep can begin; defer the final 50% tranche release to Day 60, giving the delayed country an additional 15-day cure window; if funding remains incomplete at Day 75 (Stop trigger), the other country has the option to propose a reduced-scope Phase One (fewer sites, shorter test window) that the delayed country can still fund, or trigger Stop.
  • If contingency reserves are depleted faster than forecast (e.g., gate delay >3 months = >USD 300M), activate a contingency-supplementation process: either government may request a bilateral review of program scope and timing; both countries jointly agree whether to (a) extend appropriation authority for an additional USD 100–200M, (b) reduce Phase One scope (from 4 to 2 sites, shorten test window to 60 days), or (c) pause Phase One to preserve remaining contingency for Phase Two.
  • If operator compensation disputes arise (e.g., an operator claims it was not fully compensated by its government and threatens to withdraw), establish a bilateral operator-dispute fund (USD 25M from contingency) administered by the bilateral budget director with both co-chairs' approval; this fund covers shortfalls when an operator files a verified claim that it was underpaid despite contractual obligation, up to a cap of USD 5M per operator per country.
  • If monthly fiscal-accountability reporting reveals recurring variance or contingency burn not anticipated in the plan, schedule an emergency trilateral (US co-chair, Chinese co-chair, bilateral budget director) review within 5 business days; the trio jointly decide whether to reallocate across envelopes (e.g., reduce site-prep spending by USD 50M to fund examiner overage), extend the appropriation timeline, or adjust program scope to stay within the USD 5.0B cap.

Documents to Find

Find Document 1: US Congressional Authorization and Ratification Precedents (New START, IAEA, Chemical Weapons Convention)

ID: ff059db5-2e5d-478f-b507-6ba11dfd9a24
