Description: Enacted US Congressional resolutions, treaties, and implementing legislation from comparable bilateral or international verification programs (New START Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, US obligations under IAEA safeguards, Chemical Weapons Convention ratification). Source material type: legislative text and procedural records; purpose: informing US domestic authority decomposition, identifying legislative committees and timelines, understanding inspector immunity and access authority language. Intended audience: bilateral legal team, US State Department, US Congress co-chair staff.

Recency Requirement: Current enacted law; New START ratified 2010, still in effect; CWC ratified 1997; IAEA safeguards agreements executed by country (ongoing). Identify most recent Congressional action amending or extending authority (e.g., New START extension 2021, CWC amendments 2019+).

Responsible Role Type: Bilateral Legal Counsel and US Legislative Counsel

Steps to Find:

  • Access US Congress.gov; search for New START Act (Public Law 111-129, 2010), IAEA protocols/agreements, and Chemical Weapons Convention Implementation Act (Public Law 105-277, 1998).
  • Identify the legislative committees (US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, House Armed Services Committee) that handled ratification; review committee reports and floor debates for statutory language on inspector access, immunity, and evidence handling.
  • Request the State Department's Arms Control, Verification, and Compliance Bureau for copies of bilateral agreements with IAEA and OPCW on inspection scope, inspector immunity, and evidence preservation.
  • Consult the Congressional Research Service for legislative procedure guides and typical timelines for treaty ratification and implementing legislation (typically 4–8 weeks for ratification, 4–12 weeks for implementing bills).

Access Difficulty: Easy. US Congress.gov is a public website; legislative text, committee reports, and floor records are publicly available. State Department materials are public or available via FOIA request (10–20 business days). CRS reports are available to Congress members or via their offices; can be obtained through Freedom of Information Act request.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the specific Congressional committees (US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, House Armed Services Committee) with jurisdiction over bilateral verification agreements and inspector-access authorization; map their typical review timelines (4–8 weeks) and procedural requirements.
  • Document the exact statutory language and precedents from New START (Public Law 111-129, 2010), IAEA safeguards protocols, and Chemical Weapons Convention Implementation Act (Public Law 105-277, 1998) that define inspector immunity, access authority, evidence handling, and domestic-government enforcement mechanisms.
  • Extract the procedural pathway and typical duration for US ratification of a bilateral instrument: committee review, floor debate, adoption, entry into force (4–12 weeks for implementing legislation).
  • Identify which US executive agency (State Department, Defense Department, Commerce Department) holds export-control or technology-transfer authority for classified computing-equipment evidence and whether additional approvals or delegations are required before foreign inspectors can access such evidence.
  • Specify the domestic legal mechanisms in US law that compel operator and vendor participation in inspection, evidence preservation, and binding agreements; determine whether existing law is sufficient or new legislation is required.
  • Document inspector-immunity and conduct-rule precedents from comparable programs to inform the bilateral conduct code and disciplinary procedures.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or vague precedent documentation leaves the bilateral legal team uncertain about which Congressional committees must approve domestic access authority, extending entry-condition timeline by 4–8 weeks and deferring Phase One clock start.
  • Missing statutory language on inspector immunity, evidence handling, or vendor-binding authority results in new legislation being drafted from first principles rather than adapted from proven templates, increasing legislative risk and timeline uncertainty.
  • Lack of procedural-pathway clarity causes the legal team to miss critical deadlines (e.g., committee markup schedules, floor-debate windows), compressing the 8-week entry-condition window and pushing Phase One start past Month 6 (2027-04-08).
  • Absence of export-control precedent forces the bilateral team to request new Commerce or State Department delegations, introducing a third regulatory agency and potential interagency disputes that delay evidence-handling authority by 4–6 weeks.
  • Unclear operator-and-vendor-binding mechanisms mean domestic implementing legislation must invent enforcement tools rather than adapt them, increasing Congressional scrutiny and amendment risk.

Worst Case Scenario: The bilateral legal team discovers, at Month 3 (2027-01-08), that the required Congressional authorization pathway differs from precedents (e.g., requires a new statute rather than delegated authority), and the appropriate Congressional committee cannot schedule a markup until after the planned Phase One start date. Implementing legislation stalls in committee or faces floor amendments that reopen core provisions (inspector access, evidence filtering, vendor binding). The entry-condition gate pushes to Month 8 (2027-06-08) or later, compressing the 90-day Phase One window or cancelling it entirely. This cascades into loss of political will, contingency-budget consumption (USD 100M+ in holding costs), and failure to reach a Go decision.

Best Case Scenario: The bilateral legal counsel rapidly adapts proven New START and Chemical Weapons Convention statutory language and procedural templates, finding that existing US law (Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, export-control delegations, treaty-implementation authorities) is sufficient or requires only a narrow implementing order from the President. Congressional approval proceeds on the expedited timeline of a past bilateral verification agreement (4–6 weeks). Domestic access authority is enacted by Month 3.5 (2027-01-23) as planned, enabling full certification of entry conditions by Month 6 (2027-04-08) and Phase One start on schedule.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Engage the Congressional Research Service immediately (Month 0 = 2026-10-08) to produce a rapid legislative-pathway memo comparing New START, IAEA, and CWC precedents; identify the fastest committee and the minimum statutory language required, permitting legal counsel to front-load Congressional staff negotiations.
  • Request a joint State Department–bilateral legal team review of whether existing Presidential authorities (e.g., treaty power, Commander-in-Chief, export-control delegations) are sufficient to authorize domestic access and inspector immunity without new legislation; if yes, pursue a delegated executive order or National Security Memorandum (2–4 weeks), avoiding the full legislative process.
  • Pre-socialize the draft bilateral instrument and implementing-authority language with key Congressional committee staff (Senate Foreign Relations, House Armed Services, Intelligence committees) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), before formal submission, to surface objections early and permit revision before formal legislative drafting.
  • Prepare a 'minimum viable statute' that addresses only inspector access, immunity, and evidence handling, deferring operator-binding and vendor-enforcement provisions to administrative regulations or operator contracts, reducing legislative scope and approval time.
  • Identify a lead Congressional sponsor in advance (Month 0 = 2026-10-08) and negotiate with committee leadership to secure a floor slot no later than Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), ensuring the bill can pass in time for Month 3 (2027-01-08) entry-condition certification.

Find Document 2: China State Council Directive and Ministerial Governance Structure (Comparable Programs)

ID: e13c34ae-f828-453f-a706-f5808d8f4622

Description: Examples of State Council administrative directives or notices (guiding documents) delegating authority to ministries to compel enterprise participation in bilateral programs or international verification. Source material type: official Chinese government documents; purpose: understanding China's administrative process for delegation, identifying approving authorities (MIIT, NDRC, State Council), and realistic enactment timelines. Intended audience: bilateral legal team, Chinese co-chair staff, Chinese Ministry of Industry & Information Technology.

Recency Requirement: Current or recent (2015+) State Council directives related to international verification, technology regulation, or export control. IAEA safeguards agreements with China (current). Any bilateral verification arrangements with Russia, EU, or IAEA (current implementations).

Responsible Role Type: Chinese Legal Counsel and Ministry Liaison

Steps to Find:

  • Request the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) for precedents of bilateral verification agreements with other governments (e.g., IAEA agreements, Russia bilateral protocols) and the State Council directives authorizing Chinese participation.
  • Contact the Ministry of Industry & Information Technology (MIIT) for any existing directives or regulations on technology verification, equipment tracking, or enterprise cooperation with government programs.
  • Query the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) for economic coordination directives that compel enterprise participation (precedents for authorizing operator participation in interstate programs).
  • Consult Chinese legal counsel with experience in State Council administrative processes; estimate typical timeline for a directive (2–4 weeks drafting, 1–2 weeks interagency coordination, 1–2 weeks State Council approval process = 4–8 weeks total).

Access Difficulty: Medium. Official State Council directives and MOFA materials are not systematically published online; access requires direct government liaison. IAEA agreements may be available via IAEA (iaea.org) or China's MOFA website. NDRC directives are sometimes published on ndrc.gov.cn. Bilateral legal teams with prior government relationships can request these materials via formal diplomatic note.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the specific Chinese government authority (State Council, MIIT, NDRC, or other ministry) competent to delegate verification participation and equipment-tracking obligations to Chinese operators and vendors, and confirm its precedent for issuing such directives.
  • Document the legal mechanism (State Council notice, ministerial regulation, or bilateral instrument provision) by which China compels domestic operator participation, vendor cooperation, and evidence disclosure in international verification programs.
  • Quantify the typical timeline for State Council directive enactment: drafting (weeks), interagency coordination (weeks), and approval (weeks); identify any expedited pathways or statutory fast-track procedures.
  • List precedents: IAEA safeguards agreements with China, any bilateral verification arrangements with Russia, EU or other governments, and the State Council directives or ministerial notices that authorized Chinese participation in each.
  • Specify required content: statutory authority to access declared equipment, inspect staging and maintenance areas, collect evidence, enforce vendor reporting, and authorize inspector presence; identify any domestic legislative gaps.
  • Confirm domestic legal barriers: do current Chinese laws permit the participation model (mirrored foreign inspectors on-site, ledger transparency, evidence redaction audits), or does the directive need to modify existing security or trade-secret law?
  • Detail the approval chain: which agencies must coordinate (State Council, MOFA, MIIT, MSS, NDRC), in what sequence, and what are realistic interagency timelines?

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or vague directive authority leaves ambiguity over which operators and vendors can be compelled to participate, delaying binding agreements by 2–4 weeks and deferring operator commitment until Month 4.5 (2027-02-23) instead of Month 4 (2027-02-08).
  • Lack of precedent or prior enactment delays legal analysis and creates false starts if the chosen authority mechanism has never been used, extending the domestic authority critical-path task by 4–8 weeks.
  • Unidentified statutory gaps (e.g., current law does not permit foreign inspectors in certain facility types, or trade-secret law restricts evidence sharing) force last-minute legislative amendment, deferring entry certification past Month 6 (2027-04-08).
  • Vague timeline estimates (e.g., 'approval takes 1–3 months') leave no margin and fail to trigger escalation if the process slips; without specific week-level milestones, slippage is not detected until Month 4–5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08), too late to recover.
  • Failure to identify the responsible ministry and point of contact delays the drafting process by 2–4 weeks while the legal team searches for the correct authority.

Worst Case Scenario: The bilateral legal team discovers at Month 3 (2027-01-08) that China's domestic authority must be enacted via a new legislative act (not a State Council notice), requiring parliamentary ratification. Timelines extend to 4–6 months. Phase One entry certification, originally planned for Month 6 (2027-04-08), shifts to Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08). The 90-day test window is compressed or eliminated. If certification is deferred past the Month 9 (2027-07-08) backstop, co-chairs must invoke the extend-or-stop decision, risking Phase One cancellation or indefinite deferral. Political will erodes during the delay. Contingency funds (USD 500M) are consumed by holding costs (USD 50–100M per month × 3 months = USD 150–300M). Surplus contingency shrinks to USD 200–350M, eliminating surge margin for vendor fallbacks, site replacement or late-discovered ledger issues. Estimated cost: USD 150–300M; estimated probability: 20–30% if the directive authority and timeline are not confirmed by Month 1 (2026-11-08).

Best Case Scenario: By Month 1 (2026-11-08), the bilateral legal team confirms that a State Council notice (precedent: IAEA safeguards directive of 2015, or NDRC economic-coordination directive for Sino-foreign joint projects) is the appropriate mechanism, with a typical 6–8 week enactment timeline. The team identifies the lead ministry (MIIT or NDRC), outlines the notice's required content (compelled operator participation, vendor reporting, inspector access), and maps an expedited path (parallel drafting and interagency coordination in Months 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08). The directive is signed and enacted by Month 3 (2027-01-08), entering the entry-conditions critical path on schedule. Operators and vendors are bound by Month 4 (2027-02-08). Domestic authority is certified by Month 3.5 (2027-01-23). Phase One entry certification is completed by Month 6 (2027-04-08). Calibration runs on schedule Months 4–5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08). Phase One starts Month 6 (2027-04-08) with full 90-day window. Contingency remains at USD 500M, sustaining surge capacity and fallback options. Bilateral momentum is strong.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If State Council directive authority cannot be confirmed by Month 1 (2026-11-08), initiate parallel-path legislative drafting: simultaneously prepare both a State Council notice and a standalone law, with bilaterally agreed fallback to whichever achieves approval first. This expands options if the primary mechanism stalls.
  • Engage the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) to provide historical precedents and timelines for similar bilateral verification agreements (e.g., IAEA cooperation, nuclear arms-control precedents with Russia); use MOFA's experience to validate or adjust the enactment timeline.
  • Request direct liaison with the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) to explore whether authority can be delegated via an existing economic-coordination framework or joint committee, rather than a new directive; this may compress the timeline to 4 weeks if piggyback authority already exists.
  • Negotiate a provisional bilateral instrument clause that allows Phase One to start on 'non-covered equipment' under a pre-clock dry run (Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23) using observers rather than inspectors, deferring full domestic authority enactment until Month 4–5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08); this keeps momentum and surfaces implementation gaps before the formal clock.
  • If legislative timelines slip beyond Month 3.5 (2027-01-23), invoke the conditional-start fallback: allow each country's sites to begin Phase One independently once its own domestic authority is enacted, deferring the Go/Modify/Stop decision until both have completed 90 days; this removes either government's unilateral veto over timing.

Find Document 3: Counterintelligence Personnel Security Clearance Processing Timelines and Standards (US and China)

ID: 50d5de66-55cd-40a8-ac34-a55ee69a2fc1

Description: Published standards and estimated timelines for counterintelligence vetting of government and contractor personnel, specific to US and Chinese processes. Source material type: government procedure manuals, clearance timelines, expedited-review options; purpose: validating the 14–16 week vetting target for 120–150 candidate inspectors per country, identifying bottleneck agencies (US DoD CI, FBI, Chinese Ministry of State Security), and fallback acceleration options. Intended audience: bilateral vetting coordinator, US counterintelligence liaisons, Chinese security-service liaisons.

Recency Requirement: Current (2024–2026) clearance timelines and procedures. US: DoD 5220.22-M, Office of Personnel Management (OPM) clearance processing guides. China: not publicly documented; estimate from IAEA inspector-vetting experience and comparable bilateral programs (New START).

Responsible Role Type: Bilateral Vetting Coordinator and Counterintelligence Process Specialist

Steps to Find:

  • Contact US Office of Personnel Management (OPM) directly for current clearance-processing timelines for Secret and Top Secret/SCI level personnel (typical US timeline: 6–12 months for TS/SCI, accelerated pathways 3–4 months for priority requests).
  • Request the US Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) for guidance on expedited contractor-personnel vetting (may be available through 5–10 week expedited reviews if priority is confirmed).
  • Consult prior bilateral programs (New START inspection teams, IAEA safeguards inspectors) for actual vetting timelines experienced; research publications and Congressional records on inspector deployment timelines.
  • For China: request diplomatic liaison to Chinese Ministry of State Security through the Chinese co-chair office; inquire about typical timelines for security vetting of government-appointed personnel (estimated 4–8 weeks based on comparable IAEA experience).
  • Identify fallback acceleration options: surge vetting capacity (hiring additional security investigators), parallel vetting (multiple agencies working simultaneously), and conditional approval (provisional approval pending final background checks).

Access Difficulty: Medium. US OPM and DCSA guidance is public or accessible via FOIA request (2–4 week turnaround). Prior bilateral-program timelines may be in public Congressional testimonies or negotiated agreements. China's security-vetting timelines are not publicly available; requires direct diplomatic request to Chinese co-chair office or Ministry liaison.

Essential Information:

  • Current US counterintelligence clearance timelines for Secret and Top Secret/SCI personnel, including OPM processing windows (baseline 6–12 months for TS/SCI, expedited 3–4 months for priority requests).
  • Expedited vetting pathways available through DCSA for contractor personnel (5–10 week expedited reviews if priority is confirmed).
  • Actual vetting timelines from prior bilateral programs (New START inspection teams, IAEA safeguards inspectors) to validate the 14–16 week plan target for 120–150 inspectors per country.
  • Chinese security-vetting timelines and procedures for government-appointed personnel, estimated at 4–8 weeks based on comparable IAEA experience (not publicly available; requires diplomatic request).
  • Fallback acceleration options: surge vetting capacity (additional investigators), parallel vetting (simultaneous agencies), conditional approval (provisional pending final checks).
  • Documented bottleneck agencies: US DoD CI, FBI, OPM; Chinese Ministry of State Security.
  • Current US standards: DoD 5220.22-M, OPM clearance-processing guides; recency requirement: 2024–2026 standards.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Clearance timelines underestimated by >2 weeks: Phase One clock start slips from Month 6 (2027-04-08) to Month 7+ (2027-05-08), compressing the formal 90-day test window and eliminating pre-test calibration time (originally Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08).
  • Fallback acceleration options not identified in advance: if vetting stalls, no expedited pathway is available, and inspector roster remains unfilled (critical path blocker for entry-gate certification at Month 6 = 2027-04-08).
  • Chinese timeline estimates inaccurate: if Chinese vetting takes >8 weeks instead of baseline 4–8 weeks, asymmetric roster fill creates reciprocity imbalance (one country deploys at 60% strength, the other at 100%), triggering asymmetric-access disputes.
  • Bottleneck agencies not pre-identified: late discovery that a specific CI unit (e.g., FBI) is deprioritizing the program due to competing national-security caseload adds 4–8 weeks delay with no mitigation path.

Worst Case Scenario: Counterintelligence vetting timelines for 120–150 inspectors per country take 20+ weeks instead of planned 14–16 weeks, due to deprioritization by domestic security agencies or underestimated Chinese processes. Inspector approval, a mandatory entry condition, does not complete until Month 7–8 (2027-05-08 to 2027-06-08) instead of Month 5 (2027-03-08). This extends the reciprocity gate past the Month 6 (2027-04-08) entry-certification deadline and defers Phase One clock start to Month 7–8 (2027-05-08 to 2027-06-08), compressing the formal 90-day test window to 30–60 days. Pre-test calibration exercise (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) is eliminated, forcing decision thresholds to be locked on provisional, unvalidated data. Probability of Modify outcome increases by 15–25% due to threshold mis-calibration. One country's roster remains <80% filled at clock start, triggering asymmetric-access dispute and potential consent withdrawal by the disadvantaged side. Phase One fails to start credibly, or starts late with degraded evidence quality.

Best Case Scenario: Current clearance timelines from OPM and DCSA (6–12 months baseline, 3–4 months expedited, 5–10 weeks for priority contractors) are confirmed by diplomatic liaison to Chinese counterpart, with Chinese vetting matching the 4–8 week estimate for government-appointed personnel. Expedited vetting pathways (surge capacity, parallel processing, conditional approval) are negotiated in advance with US and Chinese security agencies by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23). Bottleneck agencies (DoD CI, FBI, MSS) are identified and pre-briefed on the program's strategic importance. All 120–150 inspectors per country complete clearance by Month 4.5 (2027-02-23), ahead of the Month 5 (2027-03-08) entry-gate requirement. Roster fill rate reaches 95%+ at clock start (Month 6 = 2027-04-08), with surge pool (15% above baseline) pre-positioned. Pre-test calibration exercise runs on schedule (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08), validating thresholds before formal blind challenges. Entry certification completed by Month 6 (2027-04-08); Phase One clock starts on schedule. Reciprocal-access parity is maintained throughout, and final Go decision is reached with high confidence in detection and threshold validity.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Initiate bilateral vetting coordination by Month 0 (2026-10-08): each government designates a vetting-process lead; both co-chairs issue a strategic-priority directive to their domestic security agencies (DoD CI, FBI, OPM for US; MSS for China) confirming expedited timelines as a national priority; establish weekly vetting-status tracking with escalation to co-chairs if slippage >1 week.
  • Request and document current clearance timelines directly from OPM and DCSA by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); commission an independent assessment of expedited-vetting capacity (surge investigators, parallel-agency models) from a trusted contractor or academic center with clearance experience.
  • Engage diplomatic liaison to Chinese counterpart (through the Chinese co-chair office or Ministry of State Security) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) to confirm Chinese vetting timelines, identify any bottlenecks (e.g., interagency coordination delays), and negotiate parallel-processing options; document Chinese timelines in a bilateral memorandum of understanding (MOU) by Month 1 (2026-11-08).
  • Establish a fallback vetting model if standard timelines cannot be met: conditional approval (provisional clearance pending final background checks, with interim restrictions on certain access areas) by Month 4 (2027-02-08); allow Phase One to start with an 80% roster and pre-approve a rapid-replacement bench so that vacancies are filled within 1 week of discovery.
  • Pre-identify and pre-approve candidate inspector lists by Month 1 (2026-11-08), so vetting can proceed in parallel with other entry-condition work; segregate vetting into tranches (critical inspectors first, surge pool second) to stagger approval and ensure continuous filling.
  • If domestic vetting capacity is insufficient, negotiate with a third-country security service (e.g., a trusted Five Eyes partner for US inspectors, or a trusted partner state for Chinese inspectors) to conduct expedited background checks and clearance interviews by Month 3–4 (2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08), accelerating domestic final approval.
  • Document and publish vetting timelines and any delays in the bilateral ledger monthly, so both governments have transparent visibility into the critical path and can escalate obstacles early rather than discovering timeline slippage in Month 5 (2027-03-08) when gates are already past due.

Find Document 4: IAEA Safeguards Bilateral Agreements and Layered-Evidence Protocols

ID: 3c1048cf-a497-406a-b278-ee3fa78d44c7

Description: Bilateral safeguards agreements between the IAEA and participating states (including US and China) specifying inspection rights, equipment-identity verification using layered evidence, containment and surveillance procedures, and dispute-resolution mechanisms. Source material type: bilateral international agreements and technical procedures; purpose: informing the evidence-weighting hierarchy (attestation, physical inspection, records, third-party logs), equipment-identity confidence measures, and forensic-panel decision procedures. Intended audience: bilateral technical team, forensic-panel designers, evidence-weighting specialists.

Recency Requirement: Current (2020+) IAEA Safeguards Agreements and IAEA Safeguards Implementation Reports (annual). Bilateral agreements with US and China negotiated in prior years but reviewed annually.

Responsible Role Type: Bilateral Technical Lead and Evidence-Weighting Specialist

Steps to Find:

  • Visit the IAEA website (iaea.org) to access the Safeguards Agreements database; retrieve agreements between IAEA and China, IAEA and US (unclassified summaries).
  • Request the IAEA Department of Safeguards for technical procedures on equipment-identity verification, layered evidence, and sample cross-checking (publicly available or via IAEA liaison channels).
  • Access the IAEA Safeguards Implementation Reports (annual, unclassified summary, classified full report); request classified version via bilateral legal channels.
  • Contact the IAEA Office of Information for academic publications on layered-evidence methodology and safeguards design (IAEA publishes technical papers on Detection Methods).
  • Interview IAEA safeguards specialists via the IAEA's public affairs office for guidance on evidence-weighting rules and forensic methodology (no classification barrier; staff are often available for consultation).

Access Difficulty: Easy–Medium. IAEA Safeguards Agreements and Implementation Reports (unclassified portions) are published on iaea.org. IAEA technical procedures and papers are available via IAEA Publications Catalogue. Classified full reports require bilateral diplomatic request (2–4 weeks) or direct IAEA liaison (same clearance as the requesting governments).

Essential Information:

  • Identify the specific bilateral safeguards agreements between the IAEA and both the US and China, including inspection rights, equipment-identity verification procedures, and containment/surveillance methods applicable to frontier computing equipment.
  • Detail the IAEA's layered-evidence methodology for equipment identity confirmation, including which evidence sources (cryptographic attestation, physical inspection, customs records, identifiers, maintenance logs, infrastructure changes, witnessed movement) are weighted and how corroboration rules are applied.
  • Document the IAEA's forensic-panel procedures for resolving disputed equipment-identity findings, including decision timelines, evidence standards, and how factual disagreements between inspection teams are adjudicated.
  • List the IAEA's dispute-resolution mechanisms for cases where bilateral partners disagree on equipment status, including escalation paths, neutral-referee authority, and how contested findings are recorded.
  • Specify the IAEA's containment and surveillance procedures (seals, access logs, video recording, chain-of-custody documentation) that could inform the design of narrow inspection zones and tamper-evident ledger requirements.
  • Quantify historical baseline performance metrics from IAEA safeguards operations: detection rates for unreported arrivals by equipment class, false-positive rates in identity verification, time to resolve equipment-identity disputes, and unverifiable-equipment thresholds that have caused site suspension.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or outdated IAEA agreements fail to identify provisions already accepted by both governments (US and China), requiring unnecessary legal renegotiation and delaying bilateral-instrument signature by 4–8 weeks.
  • Layered-evidence methodology from IAEA safeguards differs materially from the plan's corroboration rule (e.g., IAEA requires 3+ layers; the plan proposes 2 layers); misalignment forces evidence-weighting redesign by Month 3 (2027-01-08), compressing calibration time.
  • IAEA forensic-panel procedures are not retrieved, forcing the plan to invent forensic authority and timelines without precedent; if the invented procedures prove impractical, ledger divergence clocks expire and trigger automatic suspensions prematurely.
  • Missing IAEA dispute-resolution mechanisms mean the plan's deadlock escalation (neutral referee panel, 7-day limit) lacks proven design; disputes consume co-chair time, delay closure, and risk producing contested verdicts.
  • Containment and surveillance procedures differ from the plan's narrow-zone model; if IAEA zones are wider or procedures more intrusive, the plan's IP-protection boundary becomes indefensible, raising consent-withdrawal risk.
  • Historical IAEA performance baselines (detection rates, false positives, unverifiable thresholds) are not retrieved; provisional thresholds remain unvalidated against precedent, increasing probability of Modify outcome due to mis-calibration by 15–25%.

Worst Case Scenario: The plan adopts a forensic-panel procedure and dispute-resolution mechanism without reference to IAEA precedent, and the invented procedures prove operationally unworkable (e.g., forensic panel cannot reach consensus within 48 hours on contested equipment identity; disputed findings consume >7 days to adjudicate). Unresolved divergences trigger automatic site suspensions at Months 6.5, 7, and 8 (2027-04-23 to 2027-06-08), appearing to fail the verification mechanism when it is actually working. The bilateral co-chairs perceive the mechanism as too fragile, and one government withdraws consent by Month 8 (2027-06-08), halting Phase One before the 90-day window closes. The plan has no credible verdict; political trust collapses; Option 2 (extend or stop) defaults to Stop. The USD 5 billion investment yields no Go decision and no reusable evidence standards for future bilateral verification.

Best Case Scenario: The IAEA safeguards agreements reveal that split-custody attestation root ceremonies, shift-handover cross-signing between national teams, and a 48-hour forensic-panel timeline are already proven procedures accepted by both governments in nuclear safeguards contexts. The plan adopts these precedents verbatim, giving both co-chairs confidence that forensic authority is legitimate and tried. IAEA historical baselines (e.g., 95% detection of unreported arrivals, <2% false positives, 99% of disputes resolved within 5 days) validate the plan's provisional thresholds or show required adjustments early in the pre-test calibration. By Month 3 (2027-01-08), the bilateral-instrument language on evidence weighting and forensic procedures is finalized using IAEA language, avoiding renegotiation. Phase One completes with automatic suspensions rare (<5% of events) because forensic procedures are trusted and decisive. The final Go decision is accepted by both governments as principled rather than tuned, establishing a template for extended verification.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If current IAEA Safeguards Agreements are not available or are classified, request a briefing from the IAEA Department of Safeguards (via the bilateral-program legal lead) on the unclassified framework of equipment-identity methodology and forensic procedures, allowing 2–3 weeks for response; use the briefing to inform the design, marking all thresholds as provisional until bilateral legal review is complete.
  • If IAEA forensic-panel procedures cannot be retrieved, convene a technical panel (3–5 senior nuclear-safeguards inspectors from each country, selected by mutual agreement) to document the forensic methodology they have used in prior bilateral disputes; incorporate their documented procedures into the bilateral instrument by Month 2 (2026-12-08).
  • If historical IAEA performance baselines are classified or not available, conduct a 4-week expert-elicitation exercise (Months 0.5–1.5 = 2026-10-23 to 2026-11-23) with IAEA and national safeguards specialists to estimate detection rates, false-positive rates, and unverifiable thresholds for frontier computing equipment as a proxy; use the estimates to validate provisional thresholds during pre-test calibration (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08).
  • If bilateral safeguards agreements with the US and China are not accessible through the IAEA, request them via bilateral diplomatic channels (State Department to Chinese Foreign Ministry) as classified documents; allow 4–8 weeks for release; import language on inspection rights, equipment identity, and dispute resolution into the bilateral instrument.
  • If containment and surveillance procedures differ materially from the plan's narrow-zone design, convene a reconciliation workshop (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) with bilateral technical and legal leads to align the zone model with proven IAEA procedures; document any deviations and mark them as added risk in the bilateral instrument.

Find Document 5: Frontier Computing Equipment Manufacturer Specifications and Equipment-Roadmap Data

ID: 2d2b4388-1c20-4c2e-982b-5b7fff42c278

Description: Technical specifications and equipment roadmaps from major manufacturers of frontier computing equipment (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, TPU/Google, custom ASICs). Source material type: manufacturer data sheets, product specifications, performance metrics; purpose: defining the covered-equipment schedule, classifying equipment as frontier-relevant (top 5% by performance metric), and forecasting equipment obsolescence during the 30+ month project lifecycle. Intended audience: bilateral technical lead, covered-equipment-schedule custodian, independent testing unit.

Recency Requirement: Current (2026) manufacturer specifications and roadmap data; any public 2025–2027 announcements of new product lines or performance improvements.

Responsible Role Type: Equipment-Schedule Custodian and Technical Specification Lead

Steps to Find:

  • Visit manufacturers' official websites: NVIDIA.com (GPU specifications), AMD.com (GPU/EPYC specifications), Intel.com (CPU/GPU specifications), Google.com (TPU technical documentation).
  • Consult published product data sheets and performance benchmarks (TensorFlow Performance Benchmarks, MLPerf, standard GPU benchmarks like SPECrate).
  • Query industry databases (top500.org for supercomputer rankings, which track high-performance accelerators; IDC, Gartner reports on data-center equipment trends).
  • Interview equipment specialists at participating datacenters to understand current inventory and equipment-refresh cycles (timelines for new equipment arrivals, typical lifecycle of frontier equipment = 18–36 months before obsolescence).
  • Consult industry research reports (Gartner, IDC, Mercury Research) on AI accelerator market trends and performance forecasts for 2026–2028 (available via subscription or academic institution access).

Access Difficulty: Easy. Manufacturer specifications and public roadmap data are freely available on official websites. Industry reports require subscription (USD 500–5,000 per report) or access through institutional subscriptions (universities, think tanks, government libraries may have access).

Essential Information:

  • Identify the complete list of frontier computing equipment classes (GPUs, TPUs, custom ASICs, CPUs, accelerators) relevant to the declared participating sites, with current 2026 manufacturer specifications and performance metrics (compute, memory bandwidth, power consumption) that define 'frontier-relevant' (top 5% by performance)
  • Document the equipment roadmaps for 2026–2028 from NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Google/TPU, and custom ASIC manufacturers, including announced product-release dates, performance improvements, and estimated obsolescence timelines for each current-generation product line
  • Define the performance thresholds and benchmarking standards (e.g., MLPerf, TensorFlow, SPECrate) used to classify equipment as frontier-relevant for covered-equipment schedule inclusion; establish which equipment classes are explicitly in vs. out of scope
  • Provide a manufacturer-neutral equipment taxonomy with technical identifiers (model number, architecture, release date, performance metrics, security/attestation capabilities) that can be used to author the confidential covered-equipment schedule
  • Specify current equipment lifecycles and obsolescence predictions: expected time-to-replacement for each equipment class during the 30+ month project (Month 0 = 2026-10-08 through Month 30 = 2029-04-08), including refresh cycles at participating sites
  • Detail manufacturer attestation and cryptographic-identity capabilities (e.g., NVIDIA Attestation Service, AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX, Google Titan security keys) for each equipment class, to support the attestation trust-root decision and fallback routes when vendors refuse cooperation
  • Quantify the estimated market share and prevalence of each equipment class at typical frontier datacenters (US and China), to inform site-selection matching and calibration of detection thresholds (e.g., are NVIDIA GPUs 70% of frontier infrastructure, or 50%?)

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or outdated manufacturer specifications result in the covered-equipment schedule excluding or mis-classifying frontier equipment, leaving real-world arrivals or departures unmonitored and undetected in blind exercises
  • Missing equipment roadmap data leads to premature obsolescence of thresholds; equipment scheduled as 'frontier-relevant' becomes commodity mid-test, invalidating detection results and forcing a Modify outcome to recalibrate the schedule
  • Inadequate attestation-capability documentation prevents the independent testing unit from designing challenge exercises that test attestation fallbacks; vendor-refusal scenarios become unrealistic, overstating the mechanism's robustness
  • Manufacturer-neutral taxonomy is weak or inconsistent, causing inspectors to misidentify equipment during intake verification, creating false-identity disputes that trigger escalation clocks and potential site suspension
  • Equipment-lifecycle predictions are inaccurate (e.g., predicting 18-month obsolescence when actual is 36 months), causing the schedule to become out-of-sync with real equipment-refresh cycles, reducing the practical effectiveness of the verification regime
  • Missing data on China-specific equipment (custom ASICs, domestic GPUs) results in asymmetric coverage: US sites have clear, comprehensive specifications while China sites have incomplete data, collapses reciprocal-access parity and triggers asymmetry disputes

Worst Case Scenario: A critical equipment class (e.g., 80% of frontier AI accelerators globally) is omitted or severely mis-specified in the covered-equipment schedule because manufacturer specifications were outdated or incomplete. During Phase One, multiple unmonitored equipment arrivals and substitutions occur at both sites. Blind-challenge exercises fail to detect these changes because they were designed against incomplete specifications. The final Go/Modify/Stop decision relies on a false-positive blind-detection rate, appearing to show >85% detection when true detection was <40%. A post-Phase-One audit discovers the equipment-schedule gap, invalidating the entire Go decision and forcing an expensive Phase Two recalibration or termination of the program. Reputational damage undermines bilateral trust; one government claims the other deliberately withheld equipment-specification data to game the test. Estimated cost and delay: Phase restart in Month 15+ (2028-01-08+), USD 500M+ in sunk costs, 12+ month delay.

Best Case Scenario: Complete, current manufacturer specifications and equipment roadmaps are integrated into an accurate, manufacturer-neutral covered-equipment schedule adopted at Month 3 (2027-01-08). The schedule clearly defines frontier-relevant thresholds and includes 95%+ of frontier equipment deployed at participating sites. Attestation capabilities are well-documented, enabling strong fallback routes for vendor-refusal scenarios. Equipment-lifecycle predictions align with real refresh cycles, keeping the schedule synchronized with actual equipment evolution through the entire project lifecycle. Blind-exercise design is grounded in accurate specifications, detecting real substitutions and arrivals with >85% accuracy, validating the mechanism's credibility. Final Go decision is supported by clean, reproducible detection evidence. The equipment-schedule custodian maintains the data as a reusable asset for future bilateral verification efforts, accelerating Phase Two execution and demonstrating the mechanism's value to both governments.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If current publicly available manufacturer specifications are incomplete, conduct confidential bilateral interviews with equipment specialists and procurement leads at each participating datacenter to document actual equipment inventory, performance metrics, and upcoming refresh cycles, then synthesize this datacenter-specific data into a schedule covering 95%+ of deployed equipment at participating sites by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23)
  • Engage each major manufacturer directly (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Google, custom ASIC vendors) via bilateral government channels, requesting confidential technical briefings and future-product roadmaps to fill specification gaps; secure non-disclosure agreements allowing use of sensitive roadmap data for verification purposes only
  • Substitute manufacturer specifications with equipment-performance benchmarking conducted on-site at participating datacenters: deploy standard benchmarks (MLPerf, TensorFlow, SPECrate, industry-specific workloads) on actual equipment to derive performance baselines and lifecycle predictions empirically rather than relying on vendor datasheets
  • If equipment-lifecycle prediction is uncertain, adopt a conservative approach: expand the frontier-relevant threshold downward by one performance tier to include higher volumes of equipment, accepting lower specificity but higher coverage and reduced risk of unmonitored arrivals
  • Pre-qualify the independent testing unit to conduct their own equipment-specifications audit by Month 2 (2026-12-08), using a subset of sites' actual inventory; use this audit to validate or revise the covered-equipment schedule before final adoption at Month 3 (2027-01-08), catching gaps before the clock starts
  • Establish a standing bilateral equipment-specifications working group (2–3 specialists per country, plus independent testing-unit representation) to maintain and refine the schedule through Phase One; schedule formal review points at Month 2.5 (2026-12-23), Month 5 (2027-03-08), and Month 8 (2027-06-08) to catch and correct specification drift before it impacts verification credibility

Strengths

  • Narrow, bounded mission (declared-equipment change verification only) with explicit exclusions limits scope creep and IP exposure.
  • Both leaders' political backing and domestic authority to compel participation (user constraint).
  • Double-key governance with equal co-chairs, no casting vote, and defined deadlock, impaired-confidence and suspension procedures.
  • Layered evidence with no single decisive source; replicated tamper-evident ledger with independent national copies.
  • Fully funded design: USD 5.0B (user constraint), 50/50, every expense mapped to an envelope; USD 500M contingency.
  • Strict entry gate keeps setup failures from being logged as verification failures.
  • Pre-clock calibration on non-covered equipment and blind exercises run by an independent unit give credible, pre-committed Go/Modify/Stop criteria.
  • Mirrored full-time staffing (about 434 FTE, estimate) avoids single-person critical functions.

Weaknesses

  • No killer application yet: no single compelling flagship use-case (e.g., a visible, high-value event such as verified intake of a large new accelerator shipment) shows both governments and the public why the mechanism matters. Value is currently procedural and abstract.
  • Strict gate with no conditional start gives the slower government an effective timing veto; Month 9 (2027-07-08) backstop only forces an extend-or-stop decision.
  • Inspector counterintelligence vetting (14-16 weeks, 20+ if deprioritised) is the critical-path bottleneck.
  • Most thresholds are provisional (TBD); a mis-set value could force a Modify verdict reflecting the yardstick, not the mechanism.
  • Narrow fixed zones create blind spots; fixed corroboration rules can be learned and gamed.
  • Contingency worst case about USD 515M (estimate) exceeds the USD 500M reserve by about USD 15M.
  • Staffing envelope covers at most about 3 years (estimate), so scaling beyond Phase One is unfunded.
  • Split between site preparation and operator compensation within the USD 1.0B envelope is not fixed.

Opportunities

  • Killer application: develop a flagship 'verified intake-to-exit chain' for one high-consequence equipment class (new-arrival intake with identity confirmed by 2+ layers, then verified disposition at exit). A clean public-to-leadership demonstration that a declared shipment was verified by both sides without exposing IP could catalyze adoption. Obstacles: identity must be convincing without attestation hooks or vendor cooperation; sensitive details cannot be disclosed; the 90-day window offers few high-value real events; the schedule is frozen and manufacturer-neutral; exercises must not touch live computation.
  • Reusable evidence standards and ledger design for bilateral technology verification, extendable to more sites after Go.
  • Lessons from New START, OPCW managed access and IAEA/Euratom layered safeguards (analogues; not verified as directly transferable).
  • Pre-qualified independent examiner and clean-room pools can become a standing neutral verification capacity.
  • A successful Phase One strengthens reciprocal confidence and political insulation for later steps.
  • Vendors gain assured, bounded, reciprocal tracking, a reason to cooperate rather than refuse.

Threats

  • Geopolitical deterioration reducing political will or reinterpreting the instrument; New START inspection suspensions show reciprocity can fail.
  • Domestic legislative or administrative delays; holding cost USD 50-100M per month (estimate).
  • Vendor refusal cascades leaving over 10% of equipment unverifiable at a site, a Stop condition.
  • IP or counterintelligence incidents triggering consent withdrawal.
  • Ledger divergence or cyberattack on ledger and attestation roots; compromised key ceremony.
  • Asymmetric access or a government shielding an operator collapsing reciprocity.
  • Automatic suspension clocks turning administrative lag into spurious Stop triggers.
  • Export-control, environmental (e-waste) and data-protection rules delaying evidence handling and disposition.
  • Disputes over exercise fairness delaying the final decision.

Recommendations

  • Define and test the killer application: by Month 2 (2026-12-08), the independent testing unit and both technical leads draft a flagship intake-to-exit scenario for one covered class; rehearse it in calibration (Months 4-5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) and stage it as the lead demonstration in Phase One.
  • Run weekly co-chair entry-gate reviews from Month 0 (2026-10-08), with each country's named domestic-authority lead decomposing required legal acts; escalate any item over 4 weeks late to co-chairs within 2 working days.
  • Start inspector counterintelligence vetting at Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) with a pre-approved bench of 15% surge; owner: both counterintelligence units; target at least 80% roster filled and all critical posts filled by Month 5 (2027-03-08).
  • Pre-bind the top 8-12 vendors per site and sign examiner and clean-room agreements by Month 4 (2027-02-08); owners: operators and bilateral legal units; publish the day-10 refusal ladder.
  • Stand up the joint forensic panel (3-5 per country) and ledger stress test on non-covered equipment by Month 4 (2027-02-08); owner: ledger operations and the panel.
  • Run calibration in Months 4-5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) and double-key lock thresholds by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23); owner: independent testing unit with co-chairs.
  • Raise the contingency exposure gap (about USD 15M, estimate) at the Month 3 (2027-01-08) appropriations review; owner: treasuries and the budget working group.

Strategic Objectives

  • Certify all 7 entry conditions by both sides by Month 6 (2027-04-08), with no unresolved item older than 4 weeks.
  • Lock all Go/Modify/Stop thresholds by double-key signature by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), each with documented justification and validation method.
  • Fill at least 80% of the planned roster and 100% of critical posts with approved inspectors by Month 5 (2027-03-08).
  • In Phase One (Months 6-9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), reach blind detection of at least 90% unreported arrivals, 85% substitutions and 80% record falsification (provisional) with false positives under 5%.
  • Execute at least one end-to-end flagship intake-to-exit demonstration per site by Month 9 (2027-07-08), with zero active-computation interruptions, and issue the Go/Modify/Stop decision by Month 10 (2027-08-08).

Assumptions

  • Both leaders sustain political backing through Month 10 (2027-08-08); trust is not assumed.
  • Four participating sites (2 US, 2 China) (estimate); named regions are illustrative.
  • Phase One runs Months 6-9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) under a strict gate; calibration data is excluded from the decision evidence base.
  • Staffing about 434 FTE (estimate); thresholds are proposed and provisional.
  • Success covers only monitored changes at participating declared sites.
  • Revenue, investors, customers and ROI are Not applicable; value is mission justification and fiscal accountability.

Missing Information

  • Specific domestic legal acts, approving bodies and realistic enactment timelines in each country.
  • Which flagship use-case leadership would find most compelling, and whether enough real events will occur in 90 days.
  • Vendor willingness and attestation-hook availability by equipment class.
  • Empirical detection and false-positive baselines to validate provisional thresholds.
  • Split of the USD 1.0B envelope between site preparation and operator compensation.
  • Actual loaded staff costs and vetting capacity of the security agencies.
  • Referee panel membership and trusted host for the key ceremony.

Questions

  • Which single use-case would make both leaderships say the mechanism is indispensable, and can Phase One demonstrate it without exposing IP?
  • If one government's authority lags past Month 6 (2027-04-08), are both sides truly willing to let the Month 9 (2027-07-08) extend-or-stop decision decide?
  • Are the provisional detection and parity thresholds defensible, and how will calibration prove they are not tuned?
  • What blind spots do the narrow fixed zones leave, and could an operator exploit them without detection?
  • How would the program handle a USD 15M contingency shortfall or a vendor refusal at a hard site, and who decides?

Roles Needed & Example People

Roles

1. Bilateral Co-Chair (Equal National Leadership)

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Bilateral co-chairs require continuous, non-substitutable oversight of all strategic decisions throughout the entire project lifecycle (Months 0-10 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-08-08). They hold double-key authority over budgets, protocol changes, findings and suspension. This is a permanent, full-time leadership role with no phase-out and cannot be delegated to contractors or temporary staff. Essential governance continuity demands exclusive, long-term commitment.

Explanation: Two equal national co-chairs (one per country) with double-key authority over budgets, protocol changes, site findings, sanctions and suspension. No casting vote; deadlock escalates to neutral referee panel after 7 days. Own entry-condition steering, gate certification, and final Go/Modify/Stop decision. Critical from Month 0 (2026-10-08) through Month 10 (2027-08-08). This role is foundational; without reciprocal, mutually accountable leadership, governance deadlock and consent withdrawal are unavoidable.

Consequences: No reciprocal governance or decision-making authority; unilateral authority by one country collapses the bilateral mechanism. Deadlock becomes unresolvable. Budget and protocol changes lack legitimacy. Operator and vendor compliance becomes impossible to enforce reciprocally. Phase One is not credible.

People Count: 2 (one per country, equal rank, non-substitutable)

Typical Activities: Dr. Chen convenes weekly co-chair steering meetings with her Chinese counterpart to track entry-condition milestones (instrument signature, appropriations, domestic authority enactment, site selection, inspector approval, vendor binding). She holds decision authority over all budgets, protocol changes, site findings and sanctions through double-key signature. She escalates deadlocked disputes to the independent referee panel after 7 days and issues the final Go/Modify/Stop decision by Month 10 (2027-08-08). She maintains continuous liaison with domestic US agencies (State, DoD, Treasury) to ensure legal authority and funding timelines. She signs every significant finding and coordinates with media and Congress on progress.

Background Story: Dr. Margaret Chen serves as the US Co-Chair, a career diplomat and arms-control negotiator based in Washington, DC. She holds a PhD in international law from Yale and 22 years' experience in multilateral treaties, including 8 years leading US verification initiatives at the IAEA. Her expertise spans bilateral governance structures, double-key authority mechanisms and escalation protocols under mutual distrust. She was appointed to this role by the US State Department in recognition of her reputation for principled negotiation and her ability to maintain trust with counterparts even in high-stakes disputes. Her familiarity with the challenge of verifying frontier technologies comes from her prior work on nuclear-fuel-cycle verification and her deep understanding of how inspection regimes balance national security with transparency.

Equipment Needs: Secure communications infrastructure (encrypted video conferencing, dedicated secure phone lines), double-key signature hardware and cryptographic tokens, access to bilateral treaty archives and classified documents, real-time dashboards showing project KPIs (ledger sync status, discrepancy aging, threshold trackers), meeting facilities with classified handling capability.

Facility Needs: Secure executive conference rooms in Washington DC and equivalent Chinese government facility, both with SCIF (Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility) classification capability, 24/7 operational status. Weekly co-chair meetings from Month 0 (2026-10-08) through Month 10 (2027-08-08) require real-time audio/video with cryptographic protection, document archival capability, and witness/recording equipment for bilateral decisions. Backup secure communication sites at alternate locations.

2. Inspection and Verification Unit (Full-Time Mirrored National Teams)

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Inspectors conducting 24/7 shift coverage at participating sites require continuous deployment from Month 5 (2027-03-08) through final decision (Month 10 = 2027-08-08), with pre-deployment vetting and training from Month 0 (2026-10-08). The plan explicitly states 'full-time mirrored national inspectors' and 'no single-person critical functions, part-time or temporary-agency inspectors.' Separation of duties, shift continuity, security clearance and counterintelligence vetting are incompatible with part-time or contractor status. The 24/7 shift model, surge coverage and leave rotation require dedicated, vetted full-time staff.

Explanation: About 144 full-time inspectors per country (36 per site across 4 sites), deployed 24/7 in shifts with separation of duties, leave coverage and surge reserves. Conduct intake verification using layered evidence, equipment-identity confirmation, maintenance audits, third-party escort, exit-disposition witnessing. Operate within bounded marked zones, perform shift-handover cross-signing for ledger reconciliation, and document all events in real time. Critical from Month 5 (2027-03-08) deployment through Month 10 (2027-08-08) final decision, with training and pre-clock vetting from Month 0 (2026-10-08).

Consequences: No on-ground presence to verify equipment or witness events. Identity verification depends entirely on records and third-party claims. Maintenance and third-party access cannot be monitored. Exit dispositions are unwitnessed. Exercise blind-challenge scenarios cannot be executed. Entire Phase One evidence base collapses.

People Count: min 288, max 350 (144–175 per country, ~36 per site team, with 20–30% surge and leave buffer; may scale with site count or shift model)

Typical Activities: Okafor oversees intake verification of arriving computing equipment at his assigned participating site, confirming identity through cryptographic attestation, physical inspection, customs records and equipment identifiers. He leads shift-handover cross-signing with his Chinese counterpart inspectors, comparing ledger entries and flagging any divergences within 2 hours for forensic review. He conducts maintenance-event audits and escorts third-party vendor visits to ensure vendor-provided evidence is preserved. He witnesses equipment departures and assigns exit dispositions (destruction, disablement, transfer, release or unresolved). He investigates zone-boundary infractions and escalates tier-2 or tier-3 violations to the bilateral conduct committee within 48 hours.

Background Story: Thomas Okafor is a Senior Inspection Officer based in Northern Virginia with 16 years of on-site verification experience. A former US Department of Defense counterintelligence officer, he led inspection teams under the New START treaty, verifying strategic delivery vehicles in Russia (pre-2020) and managing inspector conduct under conditions of mutual suspicion. He holds a master's degree in arms-control policy from Georgetown and speaks Mandarin at professional proficiency. His expertise spans intake-protocol execution, equipment-identity verification using layered evidence, and maintaining inspector discipline in contested environments. He was selected as a senior inspector lead for The Consortium because of his demonstrated ability to document findings impartially and his experience managing 24/7 shift coverage under separation-of-duties constraints.

Equipment Needs: Field inspection kits: cryptographic attestation readers (manufacturer-certified), portable physical-inspection equipment (calibrated scales, dimensional gauges, spectroscopic analyzers for material identification), high-resolution photography and video equipment with tamper-evident sealing, access-badge readers and real-time ledger terminals (air-gapped for security), chain-of-custody documentation binders. Personal protective equipment and hazmat gear for maintenance-area access. All devices encrypted end-to-end.

Facility Needs: Secure on-site inspection offices at each of the 4 participating datacenters, operating 24/7 with shift-rotation capacity. Each office requires: secure ledger workstation, evidence-storage lockers with cryptographic sealing, interview rooms for witness statements, redaction/audit workspace for operator-provided evidence filtering, secure communications links to national ledger facilities, and shift-briefing areas. Marked physical inspection zones with access-control gates, video recording, and badge-swipe logging. Comfortable quarters for shift rotations and emergency recall capability.

3. Ledger Operations and Cryptographic Custody (Full-Time Mirrored Technical Teams)

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Ledger operations and cryptographic custody is a critical path function requiring continuous on-duty personnel from Month 1 (2026-11-08) through final decision (Month 10 = 2027-08-08). Ledger integrity, bounded synchronization, divergence detection within 2 hours, and cryptographic root-key management are non-delegable functions that demand dedicated, cleared full-time technical specialists. Monthly failover tests and quarterly resilience drills require permanent institutional knowledge and uninterrupted custody chain. Part-time or contractor engagement introduces continuity breaks and custody-chain risk unacceptable in a bilateral verification mechanism.

Explanation: About 30–50 full-time technical staff per country (systems engineers, cryptographic specialists, database administrators) maintaining two independent national ledger copies, implementing bounded sync (<1 hour target), conducting continuous integrity verification, managing offline cryptographic root-key custody, and operating secure communications links. Detect divergence within 2 hours and alert forensic team. Run monthly failover tests and quarterly resilience drills. Critical from Month 1 (2026-11-08) through Month 10 (2027-08-08). Ledger integrity is non-delegable; a single cryptographic or sync failure triggers automatic suspension.

Consequences: Ledger divergence is undetected or unresolved; automatic suspension triggers for technical failures rather than real concealment. Evidence base cannot be reconciled. Both governments lose confidence in the ledger as a neutral record. Phase One Go decision lacks evidentiary foundation.

People Count: min 60, max 100 (30–50 per country, with rotation for 24/7 ops and surge)

Typical Activities: Dr. Sharma designs and operates the US national ledger copy, a replicated, cryptographically signed record of all Phase One events. She implements the bounded-synchronization protocol targeting <1-hour sync latency with the Chinese ledger and monitors divergence continuously. She conducts automated integrity verification every 4 hours, comparing ledger hashes and alerting the forensic team within 15 minutes if a divergence exceeds tolerance. She manages offline cryptographic root-key custody and participates in bilateral key ceremonies. She leads monthly failover-recovery tests and quarterly resilience drills, simulating network outages and system crashes to validate recovery time meets <4-hour targets. She maintains offline encrypted backups and documents all cryptographic procedures for bilateral audit.

Background Story: Dr. Priya Sharma is a cryptographic systems engineer and ledger-operations specialist based in Washington, DC, with 14 years' experience in distributed-ledger design and high-assurance systems. She earned her PhD in computer science from MIT, focusing on Byzantine-fault-tolerant consensus and tamper-evident logging. She was principal architect for the IAEA's safeguards digital-transition project and brings deep expertise in cryptographic key management, offline backup procedures and rapid-recovery protocols. She was recruited specifically for her experience designing ledgers where no single actor can unilaterally insert or modify records and where divergence is detected within hours rather than days.

Equipment Needs: Two independent ledger systems (one per country): redundant server infrastructure with cryptographic signing hardware, air-gapped offline backup systems, secure communications appliances (dedicated fiber and radio frequency terminals), cryptographic root-key storage hardware with physical tamper-evidence seals, high-assurance clock synchronization (GPS-backed, accurate to <1 second), network monitoring and anomaly-detection appliances, backup power (uninterruptible supplies, diesel generators), and rapid-recovery tape or drive systems.

Facility Needs: Secure ledger operations centers in each country, geographically separated from co-chair offices and participating sites to prevent single-point-of-failure espionage. Each center requires: 24/7 staffed operations floor with isolated network segments, climate-controlled server rooms, offline cryptographic key-storage vault with multi-factor physical access controls, isolated disaster-recovery facility reachable within 6 hours, secure communications room with redundant links, and monthly failover-test staging area.

4. Forensic Equipment-Identity Panel and Adjudication Authority

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Forensic panel members issuing binding or co-chair-delegated findings within 48 hours on contested equipment identity require continuous availability from Month 1 (2026-11-08) through final decision. The plan designates them as pre-authorized decision-makers with no appeal override except co-chair escalation, making their role permanent and non-substitutable. 48-hour response requirements and the need to maintain a shared knowledge base on evidence patterns and corroboration rules across 90+ days of operations demands full-time commitment and institutional continuity. A contractor or part-time arrangement creates gaps in availability and institutional memory incompatible with forensic authority.

Explanation: 3–5 senior technical specialists per country (total 6–10 members) with equal national membership and pre-authorized authority to issue binding or co-chair-delegated findings on contested equipment-identity disputes within 48 hours. Apply pre-agreed corroboration hierarchy (attestation > physical inspection + chain-of-custody > maintenance records > third-party logs). Investigate ledger divergences and discrepancy escalations. Issue findings documented in the ledger. If consensus fails, escalate to co-chairs within 24 hours. Active from Month 1 (2026-11-08) through final decision; critical to preventing divergence clocks from expiring and triggering automatic suspension.

Consequences: No authority to resolve contested identity disputes. All divergence escalations default to co-chair negotiation, consuming 7–10 days and exhausting the 7-day suspension clock. Automatic suspensions fire for legitimate forensic disputes. The mechanism appears to fail when it is functioning. Bilateral trust collapses.

People Count: 6–10 (3–5 per country, equal membership, no casting vote; non-delegable expertise)

Typical Activities: Whitmore chairs the US side of the bilateral forensic panel (3-5 specialists per country), issuing findings on contested equipment-identity disputes within 48 hours. He applies the pre-agreed corroboration hierarchy: cryptographic attestation agreement > physical inspection + chain-of-custody > maintenance records > third-party logs. He investigates every ledger divergence flagged by the ledger-operations team, comparing national copies and determining which one is correct. If the forensic panel cannot achieve consensus within 48 hours, he escalates to the co-chairs for decision within 24 hours. He maintains a log of all identity disputes and resolutions for the bilateral record and testifies to the Go/Modify/Stop decision by documenting which threshold criteria were met.

Background Story: Dr. Robert Whitmore is a forensic equipment-identity specialist and senior adjudication authority, based in Maryland. He holds a PhD in materials science and 20 years' experience authenticating high-value equipment, including 8 years as a US Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency investigator focusing on microelectronics supply-chain integrity. He has testified before Congress on equipment-substitution vulnerabilities and authored technical standards on cryptographic-attestation validation. He was selected as a forensic-panel lead because of his ability to synthesize layered evidence (attestation, physical inspection, maintenance records, third-party logs) into a binding identity finding within 48 hours and his reputation for principled judgment even under adversarial disagreement.

Equipment Needs: Forensic analysis laboratory equipment: equipment-identity verification tools (teardown and inspection stations), cryptographic-attestation validation hardware and software, independent spectroscopy and material-analysis instruments, high-resolution imaging for identifier and serial-number authentication, database systems for maintaining corroboration-evidence hierarchies, secure document storage and access-controlled case files.

Facility Needs: Secure bilateral forensic office(s) or co-located facilities in each country (or a shared neutral third location if governments permit), operational during regular business hours with 48-hour rapid-response capability. Must have isolated evidence-handling area, secure communications to the ledger and co-chairs, case-file archives under dual custody, and monthly coordination meetings. If decentralized, requires identical facility specifications at both national sites.

5. Bilateral Legal and Treaty Implementation Unit

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Bilateral legal and treaty-implementation unit must be on permanent staff from Month 0 (2026-10-08) through final decision (Month 10 = 2027-08-08), with front-loaded effort in Months 0-3 (2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08) for domestic-authority decomposition and bilateral-instrument drafting. These specialists maintain continuity on treaty language interpretation, operator/vendor agreement terms and escalation protocols, which cannot be effectively handed off mid-project. The need for domestic-government coordination and direct access to legislative contacts requires permanent, security-cleared legal staff with institutional knowledge of bilateral obligations. Contract or temporary legal support may be supplemented for surge drafting, but core treaty and authority counsel must be full-time.

Explanation: About 15–25 full-time bilingual legal specialists per country (including treaty lawyers, domestic-authority counsel, contract drafters) responsible for drafting and ratifying the bilateral instrument, decomposing domestic access authority into specific legislative acts, pre-binding operator and vendor participation agreements, establishing escalation protocols and deadlock procedures, managing inspector conduct rules and discipline, and documenting all decisions in the ledger. Coordinate with domestic legislatures and governments on authority enactment. Critical from Month 0 (2026-10-08) through Month 3 (2027-01-08) (entry-condition phase) and ongoing through final decision for dispute resolution.

Consequences: Bilateral instrument lacks clear language on double-key governance, deadlock resolution and automatic suspension triggers. Domestic access authority is not decomposed into specific acts; domestic legislatures and governments lack clear approval templates. Operator and vendor binding agreements are unsigned or ambiguous. Escalation and discipline procedures are undefined. Entry-condition delays are unmanaged. Phase One starts without legal foundation.

People Count: min 30, max 50 (15–25 per country, with translation and domestic-coordination support)

Typical Activities: Rodriguez drafts and coordinates bilateral-instrument language governing double-key governance, deadlock resolution, automatic-suspension triggers and reciprocity rules. She decomposes mandatory entry conditions into specific US legislative acts (e.g., Congressional ratification, domestic access authority, inspector immunity) and coordinates with the State Department, DoD and domestic agencies on timelines. She negotiates operator and vendor binding agreements, ensuring US operators and vendors are contractually obligated to cooperate. She documents all procedural changes via recorded protocol amendment signed by both co-chairs and maintains a confidential bilingual treaty archive. She provides legal interpretation of instrument language when disputes arise and advises co-chairs on whether a proposed action violates bilateral commitments.

Background Story: Alicia Rodriguez is a bilateral treaty counsel and legal implementation specialist, based in Washington, DC, with 19 years in arms-control law and international agreements. She holds a Juris Doctor from Columbia Law School and was a senior attorney in the US State Department's Legal Advisor's office, where she drafted bilateral instruments with Russia, China and the IAEA. She led the legal team for the Obama-era Iran nuclear agreement verification provisions and negotiated inspector-immunity clauses and dispute-resolution procedures. She was recruited for this role because of her ability to decompose complex bilateral requirements into specific domestic legislative language and her experience navigating both US Congressional approval and Chinese government coordination processes.

Equipment Needs: Secure document management systems (hard-copy and digital archives with cryptographic indexing), treaty-language databases (bilateral instrument, domestic legislation, operator/vendor agreements), legal research tools and access to international treaty repositories, secure email and communications for domestic agency coordination, cryptographic signing software for protocol amendments and bilateral correspondence.

Facility Needs: Secure bilateral legal offices in Washington DC and equivalent Chinese government location (or shared neutral third location), operational from Month 0 (2026-10-08) through Month 10 (2027-08-08). Each office requires: treaty archive with classified document storage, secure conference rooms for domestic-government coordination meetings, real-time access to the bilateral instrument and protocol-change ledger, multilingual (English-Mandarin) document production and review capability, and encryption infrastructure for secure correspondence with co-chairs and operators.

6. Independent Testing Unit and Red Team (Challenge Exercise Design and Scoring)

Contract Type: independent_contractor

Contract Type Justification: Independent testing unit and red-team personnel must be explicitly independent from both national governments to prevent exercise bias and maintain credibility of blind-challenge results. The plan requires them to be 'equally staffed from neutral countries or internationally vetted experts, not national teams.' This architecture is incompatible with full-time employment by either the US or Chinese government. Independent contractors from third countries or international organizations preserve the neutrality required for uncontested Go/Modify/Stop verdicts. Red-team work is phase-specific (Months 1-9 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-07-08 for design, calibration, and formal challenges), with defined deliverables (scenario design, scoring, fairness peer review), making contractor engagement appropriate.

Explanation: About 20–30 full-time challenge-design and red-team specialists (equally staffed from neutral countries or internationally vetted experts, not national teams) responsible for designing blind-challenge scenarios (unreported arrivals, substitutions, record falsification, vendor refusal, reluctant operators), scheduling them on a sealed double-key schedule, and scoring detection results. Maintain independence from national governments to prevent exercise bias. Design calibration exercise (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) on non-covered equipment and validate thresholds. Run formal blind challenges during Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). Active from Month 1 (2026-11-08) through final decision; critical to the credibility of Go/Modify/Stop verdict.

Consequences: Challenge exercises are designed by national red teams, introducing bias. One government can design tests favoring its own inspectors. Blind-challenge results are contested as unfair. Final Go/Modify/Stop decision lacks credible detection evidence. Neither government accepts the verdict.

People Count: min 20, max 40 (neutral-country or third-party specialists, no direct national loyalty; rotation to manage independence)

Typical Activities: Larsson designs blind-challenge exercise scenarios covering all seven event types: unreported arrivals, equipment substitutions, record falsification, vendor refusal, reluctant operators, maintenance delays and emergency access. He maintains a sealed double-key schedule shared only with the co-chairs, so inspectors and operators have minimal advance notice. He coordinates with the independent testing unit to implement scenarios at each participating site without disrupting active computation.
