He scores detection results using a pre-agreed evidence-weighting rule and issues fairness certifications that both red teams review before exercises run. He collects calibration-exercise data on non-covered equipment (Months 4-5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) and validates provisional Go/Modify/Stop thresholds before formal challenges begin. He documents all exercise methods and scoring in a confidential report delivered to both co-chairs at final decision.

Background Story: Dr. Henrik Larsson is an independent challenge-design and red-team lead, based in Stockholm, Sweden. A neutral third-country national, he holds a PhD in systems engineering and 18 years' experience designing blind adversarial-testing scenarios for high-assurance systems, including work for NATO and the IAEA. He has no loyalty to either the US or Chinese government and is explicitly prevented by contract from disclosing exercise results or methodology to either government until scoring is complete. His reputation rests on designing fair, credible, realistic scenarios that neither side can predict or game. He was selected because both governments trust his independence and his ability to score results objectively using a pre-agreed rubric.

Equipment Needs: Challenge-scenario simulation software and equipment (non-covered or surplus equipment available at each participating site), sealed scheduling systems (double-key encrypted exercise calendars), blind-scoring rubrics and evidence-collection tools, independent data-analysis and statistics software (licensed to the testing unit only), secure document production for fairness-review certifications.

Facility Needs: Independent testing office(s) located outside both the US and Chinese governments (neutral third country or international organization, e.g., Switzerland or a UN facility), operational from Month 1 (2026-11-08) through Month 10 (2027-08-08). Must be physically separate from participating sites and government offices to prevent bias. Requires: scenario-design workspace, secure exercise schedule storage, blind-scoring workstations, monthly coordination calls with co-chairs (via encrypted video), and a fairness-review process area for red-team peer review of scenarios before execution.

7. Counterintelligence and Inspector Conduct Oversight (Full-Time Bilateral Unit)

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Counterintelligence and inspector-conduct oversight requires continuous, embedded presence from Month 0 (2026-10-08) pre-positioning through final decision (Month 10 = 2027-08-08). These personnel conduct counterintelligence vetting (14-16 weeks starting Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23), monthly activity audits, access-log reviews, zone-boundary investigations and three-tier infraction adjudication. Continuity is essential: conduct officers must maintain awareness of every inspector's activities, pattern-of-life understanding and escalation history. The bilateral structure (equal national staffing, joint-review authority) requires permanent assignment to ensure daily coordination and rapid response to alleged violations within 48-hour investigation windows. Contractor or part-time status would break the institutional knowledge and coordination chain.

Explanation: About 20–30 full-time counterintelligence specialists and conduct-review officers (equally staffed from both countries) responsible for vetting all candidate inspectors (14–16 weeks of counterintelligence clearance), approving or vetoing counterpart inspectors, conducting monthly inspector activity audits and access-log review, investigating alleged zone-boundary infractions or unauthorized information collection, and implementing the three-tier infraction protocol (Tier 1: warning; Tier 2: co-chair review; Tier 3: immediate removal). Maintain continuous access-log audit and rotation schedules. Active from Month 0 (2026-10-08) pre-positioning through Month 10 (2027-08-08). Essential to preventing espionage or inspector compromise that would trigger consent withdrawal.

Consequences: No counterintelligence vetting of inspectors; espionage risk is unmanaged. Inspector conduct is unsupervised; unauthorized information collection or access violations go undetected. One country objects to counterpart inspector presence citing unresolved security concerns. Reciprocal access is withdrawn. Phase One fails.

People Count: min 40, max 60 (20–30 per country, with rotation for continuous audit and escalation response)

Typical Activities: Patterson oversees counterintelligence vetting of all ~300 candidate inspectors across both countries, starting with 14-16 week clearance cycles beginning Month 0.5 (2026-10-23). He chairs the bilateral Inspector Conduct Committee with equal Chinese membership, approving or vetoing proposed inspectors from the counterpart country within 5 working days. He conducts monthly access-log audits, comparing inspector badge swipes against stated activities and flagging unexplained zone entry or boundary-area lingering for immediate investigation. He investigates alleged zone-boundary infractions within 48 hours and implements the three-tier infraction protocol (Tier 1: warning; Tier 2: co-chair review; Tier 3: immediate removal). He coordinates inspector rotation across paired sites quarterly and maintains a rapid-replacement bench for any removed inspectors.

Background Story: Colonel James Patterson (US, retired) leads the bilateral counterintelligence and inspector-conduct oversight unit. A 28-year career counterintelligence officer with the US Army's Counterintelligence Special Operations, Patterson led classified operations in Asia and the Middle East and managed sensitive bilateral access with foreign services. He holds a master's degree in security studies and was an inspector at the OPCW for 4 years, where he managed inspector conduct and reported espionage concerns. He was selected for this role because of his uncompromising approach to security and his ability to work collaboratively with Chinese counterintelligence counterparts despite historical mutual suspicion.

Equipment Needs: Access-control systems (proximity-card badge readers and swipe-log terminals at zone boundaries, encrypted to both national ledgers), video surveillance equipment (zone-only recording, identity and movement metadata only, no workload visibility), access-log audit software and anomaly-detection tools, investigative documentation and interview rooms (secure recording equipment), conduct-code acknowledgment and rotation-schedule management systems.

Facility Needs: Bilateral counterintelligence offices at each participating datacenter (or a shared secure facility accessible from all 4 sites within 4 hours), operational 24/7 from Month 0 (2026-10-08) through Month 10 (2027-08-08). Each office requires: 24-hour staffed operations floor (including night/weekend duty teams), secure communications to national security agencies and co-chairs, personnel-file secure storage (compartmented by clearance level), interview rooms with video/audio recording, monthly access-log audit workspace, and monthly conduct-review meeting facilities.

8. Vendor Management and Evidence-Fallback Coordination (Full-Time Bilateral Unit)

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Vendor management and evidence-fallback coordination requires continuous engagement from Month 0 (2026-10-08) pre-binding through final decision (Month 10 = 2027-08-08), with front-loaded vendor negotiation (Months 0-1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) and examiner qualification (Months 0.5-4 = 2026-10-23 to 2027-02-08). These specialists maintain long-term relationships with vendors and independent examiners, track vendor-cooperation agreements and manage the day-0 to day-10 escalation ladder during the 90-day test. The role requires institutional continuity on vendor status, fallback-path readiness and cost tracking for contingency-budget management. While some vendor-negotiation surge work may be contracted, core vendor-management and examiner-pool oversight must be permanent staff to ensure escalation authority and fallback availability during Phase One.

Explanation: About 15–25 full-time vendor-relations and equipment-assessment specialists per country (total 30–50) responsible for pre-binding the top 8–12 critical vendors to cooperation agreements (by Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23), pre-qualifying and signing access agreements with 3–5 independent examiners and 2 clean-room facilities per geography (by Month 4 = 2027-02-08), managing the vendor-refusal escalation ladder (day-0 request through day-10 unverifiable classification), documenting every refusal in the ledger, and coordinating fallback evidence routes (vendor-supervised testing, independent examiners, clean-room validation, validated attestation). Critical from Month 0 (2026-10-08) pre-positioning through final decision; a failure to pre-bind vendors or qualify examiners results in material equipment being classified unverifiable, failing sites under thresholds.

Consequences: Critical vendors are not pre-bound; vendor refusals cascade and trigger day-10 unverifiable classification for 10–20% of deployed equipment. Independent examiners are not pre-qualified; fallback routes are unavailable or delayed. Material equipment remains unverifiable by final decision. Sites fail Phase One thresholds. The mechanism is judged unable to handle vendor non-cooperation.

People Count: min 30, max 50 (15–25 per country, with legal, technical and logistics expertise)

Typical Activities: Volkov identifies the top 8-12 critical vendors at each participating site and coordinates bilateral negotiations to secure pre-Phase-One cooperation agreements (by Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23) binding each vendor to attestation disclosure, maintenance-record preservation and evidence escrow for 90 days. She pre-qualifies 3-5 independent examiner labs per country and 2 clean-room facilities per geography by Month 4 (2027-02-08), negotiating access agreements and cost structures. She manages the vendor-refusal escalation ladder: vendor request (day 0), operator escalation (day 1), examiner notification (day 2), on-site examination (day 3-5) and report submission (day 10). She documents every refusal in the ledger with justification and coordinates fallback evidence routes (vendor-supervised testing, clean-room validation, validated attestation). She tracks contingency-budget impact of late-engaged examiners and provides cost analyses to the co-chairs for contingency-release decisions.

Background Story: Dr. Elena Volkov is a vendor-relationship and equipment-assessment specialist, based in California, with 15 years managing supply-chain verification and vendor cooperation agreements. A former Intel supply-chain director and later a DMEA (Defense Microelectronics Activity) trusted-supplier auditor, Volkov speaks Russian, Mandarin and German and has negotiated with technology vendors across the US, China, Europe and Japan. She holds an MS in industrial engineering and has published on protecting trade secrets during third-party audits. She was recruited specifically for her ability to bind critical vendors to evidence-cooperation agreements and her experience pre-qualifying independent examiners as fallback routes when vendors refuse.

Equipment Needs: Vendor-database management systems (tracking vendor cooperation agreements, equipment-dependency mappings per site, cost tracking for independent examiners and clean-room facilities), equipment-identity catalogs (cross-referenced to covered-equipment schedule, with manufacturer specifications), vendor-refusal escalation tracking (day-0 to day-10 timelines), fallback-route scheduling systems (coordinate examiner availability and clean-room staging), contingency-budget tracking software.

Facility Needs: Vendor-management offices in both countries (or a shared facility accessible from each participating site within 2 hours), operational from Month 0 (2026-10-08) through Month 10 (2027-08-08). Each office requires: vendor-relations workspace (telephone and secure video conferencing for negotiation), pre-qualified examiner-pool coordination area (scheduling and cost tracking), secure vendor-agreement archive, equipment-database workstations (linked to the covered-equipment schedule), and monthly coordination meetings with co-chairs and participating operators.

Omissions

1. Technology Risk and Obsolescence Management

The plan freezes the covered-equipment schedule from Phase One start to final decision (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08). However, semiconductor equipment cycles are 6–12 months, meaning new frontier-relevant equipment classes may emerge during the 90-day test, creating blind spots where real deployments fall outside the schedule. No mechanism is specified to handle equipment technological leapfrog or unexpected emergence of a new capability class mid-test. The plan risks declaring verification success against an obsolete hardware baseline.

Recommendation: Establish a Technology Change Watch process: designate a joint technical panel (one senior specialist per country) to monitor equipment announcements and new deployments at participating sites weekly during Phase One. Define a rapid-amendment procedure allowing schedule updates within 14 days if both co-chairs certify a new equipment class poses material risk and detection capability is untested. Cap amendments to no more than 2 per Phase One. Document every amendment with forensic justification in the ledger. This preserves the frozen-baseline integrity while acknowledging hardware evolution. Include a post-decision recommendation: if Go is reached, fund Phase Two to validate detection capability against next-generation equipment classes identified during Phase One.

2. Geographic Disparity and Access Asymmetry Measurement

The plan defines reciprocal-access parity as a Go/Modify/Stop threshold (within 20% proposed), but the measurement method is not specified. US sites (e.g., Silicon Valley, Northern Virginia) are geographically proximate; Chinese sites (Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Chengdu) span the full country. Bilateral teams headquartered in Washington DC and (assumed) Beijing cannot access both Chinese sites equally. Travel time, escort requirements, and visa processing create de facto asymmetry even if formal access is equal. The plan does not measure or mitigate geographic disparity.

Recommendation: Operationalize reciprocal-access parity by measuring: (1) average response time from inspector home location to each site (target: within 15% parity); (2) visa/accreditation processing time and approval rate (target: 100% approval within 30 days, same for both countries); (3) number of inspector days on-site per quarter and per site (target: within 20%); (4) fraction of events with bilateral witness presence (target: >80%). Report these metrics monthly; if any metric diverges >20%, trigger a bilateral access-parity review within 5 days. If geographic disparity cannot be resolved (e.g., visa processing), acknowledge it in the final-decision rationale and adjust the Go threshold to account for measured asymmetry.

3. Operator Withdrawal and Site Abandonment Contingency

The plan requires operator participation via binding bilateral agreements (by Month 4 = 2027-02-08), with penalty clauses for non-compliance. However, no fallback is defined if an operator withdraws consent mid-Phase One (e.g., due to political pressure, operational disruption, or domestic policy reversal). The plan identifies replacement sites ('at least one deliberately hard site' in shortlist), but does not specify: (a) rapid-deployment timelines if a site is suspended or abandoned; (b) how to continue Phase One with reduced site count; (c) cost and timeline to activate a replacement site within the 90-day window; (d) whether Go/Modify/Stop thresholds are adjusted if a site is lost mid-test.

Recommendation: Establish a Site Abandonment Contingency Protocol: (1) Define rapid-replacement criteria: if an operator withdraws or the site fails verification by Month 7.5 (2027-05-23), activate a pre-qualified backup site from the original selection shortlist within 14 days. (2) Maintain a pre-positioned surge team (10–15 inspectors per country) with induction training completed by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), ready for deployment to a replacement site. (3) Specify threshold adjustments: if one site is lost, apply per-site thresholds to the remaining 3 sites but acknowledge in the final decision that 1 of 4 sites operated for less than the full 90 days. (4) Cost: budget USD 50–200M (estimate) contingency for rapid-site activation (travel, temporary facilities, accelerated vetting). Document the decision to activate a replacement site and the rationale in the ledger.

4. Escalation and Double-Key Authority During Time-Critical Events

The plan designates double-key authority for budgets, protocol changes, findings and sanctions, with deadlock escalation to a neutral referee panel after 7 days. However, time-critical events (e.g., suspected equipment substitution during a maintenance window, vendor-refusal response needed within the day-10 ladder, or a cybersecurity incident) may require decisions within 4–24 hours, longer than it takes to convene both co-chairs and conduct a joint review. The plan does not specify: (a) expedited procedures for time-critical decisions; (b) authority delegation (can co-chairs pre-authorize certain decisions to subordinates?); (c) interim action authorities (who can issue an immediate suspension pending co-chair ratification?); (d) how to validate that a claimed emergency is genuine and not a pretext for unilateral action.

Recommendation: Establish a Crisis Decision Protocol: (1) Pre-authorize five categories of emergency decisions that may be taken by one co-chair with next-day counterpart notification rather than waiting for full double-key review: (a) temporary inspector removal pending conduct investigation (Tier 2 infraction); (b) temporary site access restriction pending forensic review; (c) emergency contingency spend up to USD 50M for ledger recovery or equipment examination; (d) rapid-call deployment of surge personnel; (e) temporary pause of exercises pending incident investigation. (2) Require written justification within 2 hours, countersigned by the counterpart co-chair within 24 hours; if countersignature is withheld, escalate to the neutral referee panel within 48 hours. (3) Define 'time-critical' as a decision needed within 4 hours to prevent material evidence loss, safety risk or operational failure; these are the only events eligible for pre-authorized emergency procedures. (4) Document every emergency decision in the ledger with the justification and the timing rationale.

5. Post-Phase One Political Commitment and Sustainment Plan

The plan ends with a Go/Modify/Stop decision at Month 10 (2027-08-08) but does not specify what occurs after Phase One concludes. If Go is reached, does Phase Two follow automatically, or do both governments need to recommit? If Modify is reached, what triggers Phase Two or a restart? If Stop is reached, what are the consequences for bilateral relations? The plan assumes political will remains constant over 10 months, but geopolitical change, domestic political transitions or scandal could erode commitment. A credible plan must address continuity or formal closure.

Recommendation: Add a Phase Transition and Sustainment section: (1) At Month 9 (2027-07-08), 30 days before the final decision, convene a high-level bilateral political steering committee (foreign ministers or cabinet-equivalent level) to assess the Go/Modify/Stop decision and decide on next steps. (2) If Go is reached, specify that Phase Two (expanded to additional sites or extended monitoring) requires a new bilateral instrument amendment and fresh appropriations; do not assume automatic continuation. (3) If Modify is reached, define a remediation period (e.g., 6 months) during which the mechanism operates under modified procedures; specify which procedure gaps are corrected and how. Recommit both governments by Month 10.5 (2027-08-23). (4) If Stop is reached, define an exit protocol: wind down operations by Month 12 (2027-10-08), secure and archive all evidence and ledgers, and conduct a post-mortem bilateral review identifying which technical or procedural element(s) failed. (5) In all cases, commit to declassifying at least an unclassified summary of Phase One findings for public disclosure within 12 months of the final decision, subject to redaction of classified sources or methods.

6. Evidence Chain-of-Custody and Third-Party Auditor Independence

The plan specifies that independent auditors conduct fiscal and procedure audits, and independent examiners (pre-qualified, 3–5 per country) perform fallback equipment identity verification. However, no mechanism is specified to ensure that these third-party actors remain independent from either national government throughout Phase One. The plan does not address: (a) how to prevent national governments from pressuring third-country auditors or examiners to bias findings; (b) who vets and approves the auditors and examiners (both governments must agree, but no approval process is detailed); (c) how auditor findings are shared (confidential report to co-chairs only, or released to both governments simultaneously?); (d) whether an auditor or examiner can be dismissed by one government if it dislikes a finding.

Recommendation: Establish a Third-Party Independence Protocol: (1) Require all independent auditors and examiners to sign a bilateral independence pledge (by Month 3 = 2027-01-08) committing them to impartial findings and explicitly prohibiting communications with either government's intelligence or security services about the Consortium findings. (2) Designate a neutral Third-Party Ombudsman (a retired senior official from a third country, e.g., Switzerland or Sweden) empowered to receive confidential reports of pressure or interference from either government and to investigate within 7 days. If interference is substantiated, the ombudsman notifies both co-chairs and the affected auditor/examiner is replaced. (3) Specify that auditor reports are delivered simultaneously to both co-chairs with no pre-briefing or embargo. (4) Establish removal authority: an auditor or examiner may be removed only by mutual agreement of both co-chairs, with written justification recorded in the ledger. Unilateral removal attempts by one government trigger ombudsman investigation and automatic escalation to the neutral referee panel.

7. Mirrored Unit Coverage During Vetting or Staffing Gaps

The plan requires 'mirrored national inspection, technical, legal, cybersecurity, counterintelligence, translation, audit, logistics and adjudication units' with full-time staff and no single-person critical functions. However, the entry-condition timeline for counterintelligence vetting (14–16 weeks starting Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23) creates a gap: if both countries experience simultaneous security-agency backlog, no inspectors may be approved until Month 4–5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08), compressing the training and pre-deployment window. The plan states 'entry needs... at least 80% of planned roster filled', but does not specify: (a) which functional units can operate at <100% strength (inspection critical, ledger operations maybe less); (b) how to maintain separation-of-duties if a unit is understaffed; (c) whether cross-national substitution is allowed (can a US technical officer cover China ledger operations if the Chinese position is vacant?).

Recommendation: Define Staffing Resilience Rules: (1) Designate three functional-unit categories: (a) 'Critical-Path': inspection, ledger operations, forensic panel, co-chairs—no substitution, must be at 100% by clock start; (b) 'Core': legal, cybersecurity, counterintelligence, adjudication—must be at 90% by Month 6 (2027-04-08), or critical-path operations are delayed; (c) 'Support': logistics, translation, training—can operate at 70% with pre-authorized surge hiring. (2) Establish a cross-national substitution protocol: a technical specialist from one country may perform work assigned to the other country only if: (a) the host country approves within 24 hours; (b) the work involves no classified or sensitive data; (c) the substitution is documented in the ledger. (3) If any critical-path unit is below 100% at Month 6 (2027-04-08), co-chairs may delay Phase One clock start by up to 2 weeks (to Month 6.5 = 2027-04-23) to allow completion of vetting, without triggering gate-delay penalty. After Month 6.5 (2027-04-23), a Unit below 100% capacity triggers an automatic Impaired-Confidence status for that unit's responsibilities until staffing reaches 100%.

Potential Improvements

1. Explicit Measurement Framework for Reciprocal Access and Parity Asymmetry

The plan states that one Go-criterion is 'reciprocal-access parity within 20%' (proposed threshold), but does not define what 'parity' means operationally. Is it parity in number of inspector days on-site, hours of zone access, number of events witnessed, fractions of maintenance windows attended, or some composite score? The dashboard lists 'reciprocal-access parity' as a KPI but offers no calculation method. Ambiguity here invites post-hoc dispute over whether parity was achieved.

Recommendation: Define Reciprocal Access Parity Operationally: (1) Calculate a Parity Index as the ratio of US inspector days on-site to Chinese inspector days on-site at each site, averaged across all 4 sites. Target parity index = 1.0 (equal); acceptable range = 0.8 to 1.25 (within 20%). Report monthly starting Month 6 (2027-04-08). (2) Add two secondary parity measures: (a) Witness Parity = fraction of maintenance and third-party-access events with bilateral inspector presence (target: >90%); if one country's inspectors are absent from >10% of events, investigate root cause (visa delays, travel restriction, scheduling conflicts) within 3 days. (b) Zone-Access Parity = total hours of zone access per national team per month (target: within 15%), adjusted for time-of-day distribution to ensure neither side is assigned only night shifts. (3) Monthly parity reports go to co-chairs by the 5th of the following month; if any parity measure falls outside the acceptable range for two consecutive months, trigger a bilateral access-parity review. (4) Include parity metrics in the final Go/Modify/Stop decision; if parity targets are not met but are within 25%, note the gap in the decision rationale; if parity gap exceeds 25%, classify as impaired reciprocity and may trigger Modify or Stop.

2. Incident Investigation and Attribution Framework

The plan specifies that IP and counterintelligence incidents are Stop-level triggers if material, and that inspector conduct is audited, but does not establish: (a) a formal incident-classification taxonomy (what is 'material'?); (b) investigation timelines and methods; (c) who determines attribution (inspector misconduct, operator negligence, deliberate leakage, or accident?); (d) how to respond proportionately (warning vs. removal vs. site suspension); (e) how to distinguish between substantiated and alleged incidents (preventing one side from weaponizing false allegations). Without this framework, incident investigations become high-friction political disputes.

Recommendation: Establish an Incident Investigation and Classification Protocol: (1) Define incident categories: (a) Level 1 (minor): unintended zone-boundary crossing <2 meters, device briefly in a non-zone area during escort, photograph accidentally including off-zone item (resolution: warning, 4-hour retraining); (b) Level 2 (moderate): deliberate photographing of non-zone infrastructure, access-log discrepancies >15 minutes in stated activity, classified information discussed outside secure facilities (resolution: co-chair investigation, 5-day findings, potential removal); (c) Level 3 (material): suspected espionage, intentional evidence tampering, coercion or bribery, confirmed unauthorized classified data transfer (resolution: immediate removal, international investigation, Stop decision if substantiated). (2) Establish a Joint Incident Investigation Procedure: allegations are reported to the bilateral conduct committee within 2 hours; preliminary assessment within 24 hours; full investigation (if warranted) within 5–7 days; findings documented with evidence chain and witness statements; accused inspector or party given opportunity to respond within 3 days before findings are finalized. (3) Require 'substantiation threshold': an incident is considered substantiated only if corroborated by two independent sources (eyewitness + access log, photograph + personnel statement, etc.); single allegations are 'unsubstantiated' and do not trigger removal, only monitoring. (4) Document every incident (substantiated or unsubstantiated) in the ledger with the investigation outcome; monthly incident summary to co-chairs includes both categories, preventing selective reporting.

3. Clarification of Ledger Divergence Recovery and Data Loss Scenarios

The plan specifies that ledger divergence must be detected within 2 hours and resolved within 4 hours (target) or 7 days (automatic suspension threshold). However, it does not address recovery procedures if a ledger is corrupted or destroyed: (a) What if one national ledger suffers a catastrophic data loss (fire, cyberattack, power failure causing backup corruption)? (b) Can the other country's ledger copy serve as the authoritative record, or must both copies be presumed compromised? (c) How are missing entries reconstructed (from inspector notes, video records, third-party logs)? (d) Who adjudicates reconstruction disputes? The plan's offline backup strategy ('air-gapped for security') may slow recovery.

Recommendation: Add a Ledger Disaster Recovery and Data Loss Protocol: (1) Specify that the two national ledger copies are considered equally authoritative, with no 'primary' and 'backup' designation; both maintain identical cryptographic signing authority. (2) In the event of data loss on one copy: (a) the other copy's entries are presumed accurate and form the recovery baseline; (b) the affected country's technical team initiates reconstruction within 4 hours from available offline backups, video records, inspector notes and third-party logs; (c) both co-chairs approve the recovery plan within 24 hours; (d) restoration must achieve 95% of prior entries within 7 days or the affected copy is re-initialized from the other's backup. (3) If both copies suffer simultaneous loss (e.g., coordinated cyberattack affecting both nations' infrastructure), escalate to Stop and conduct a forensic post-mortem. (4) Establish a quarterly 'disaster-recovery drill' (by Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23, then monthly during Phase One): simulate catastrophic data loss on one copy, practice recovery procedures, verify that both co-chairs can approve recovery within 24 hours, and test whether the recovered ledger matches an independent audit trail maintained separately.

4. Visibility into Partial or Contested Go/Modify/Stop Decisions

The plan specifies that Go requires all thresholds to be met, Modify if 'correctable weakness remains', and Stop if asymmetry or material unverifiable equipment is found. However, it does not address scenarios where: (a) one co-chair votes Go and the other votes Modify (how is this deadlock broken, given no casting vote?); (b) the detection rate is 85% (above the proposed 80% threshold but below the 90% target—is this Go or Modify?); (c) metrics are mixed (e.g., detection is 92% but unverifiable is 8%, exceeding the <5% target). The decision rules need clarity for edge cases.

Recommendation: Define a Decision Rubric with Clear Go/Modify/Stop Scoring: (1) Lock a decision rubric before Phase One starts (by Month 5.5 = 2027-03-23) specifying: (a) Go requires 'all five Yes criteria: detection thresholds met, false positives <5%, unresolved <10%, unverifiable <5%, zero material asymmetry'. If any criterion is No, Go is not possible. (b) Modify requires 'at least three Yes and at most one No, and the No must be correctable within 6 months' (specify which weaknesses are correctable: training, equipment adjustment, procedure refinement; which are not correctable: vendor refusal, asymmetric access). (c) Stop requires 'material failures: unverifiable >10%, asymmetric access unresolved, ledger divergence unreconciled, or detection <70%'. (2) If both co-chairs rank a finding identically (both Go or both Modify or both Stop), the decision stands. (3) If co-chairs disagree (one Go, one Modify), apply a 'Modify by default' rule: the more conservative outcome is adopted, unless the referee panel votes unanimously for the more optimistic outcome within 48 hours. (4) Edge-case scoring: if detection is 85% (between 80% and 90%), classify as 'Marginal Go' and include a post-decision assessment in the rationale; if unverifiable is 7% (between 5% and 10%), classify as 'Moderate Concern' and recommend targeted Phase Two testing on that equipment class.

5. Transparency and Public Communication Strategy

The plan is designed for bilateral verification under mutual distrust and emphasizes confidentiality (covered-equipment schedule is confidential, inspector and operator identities are protected, classified evidence is redacted). However, the plan does not specify: (a) who speaks publicly about Phase One progress and findings; (b) what can be disclosed without compromising security or IP protection; (c) how to counter misinformation if one side makes false claims; (d) whether and when an unclassified summary is released; (e) how legislatures and the public understand what 'Go' or 'Modify' means in the context of frontier AI safety. Absence of a communication strategy risks accusations that the program is secret or unaccountable.

Recommendation: Establish a Public Communication and Transparency Framework: (1) Designate one person per country as the sole authorized public spokesperson for Phase One, appointed by the co-chairs and briefed jointly. (2) Specify what can be disclosed unclassified: (a) Phase One is occurring (not secret); (b) number of events verified, aggregated (e.g., '3,200 equipment-change events verified across all sites'); (c) summary of verification methods (equipment identity via layered evidence, tamper-evident ledger, double-key governance); (d) milestones achieved (inspectors deployed, ledger operational, calibration exercise completed); (e) incident statistics (e.g., 'zero confirmed espionage incidents, X minor zone-boundary violations, Y vendor refusals managed via fallback routes'). (3) What cannot be disclosed: specific site locations or operator identities, equipment identifiers or technical specifications, classified evidence methods or cryptographic details, personnel names or backgrounds. (4) Commit to releasing an unclassified Executive Summary within 6 months of the final Go/Modify/Stop decision, covering: methodology, major milestones, KPI results (aggregated), decision rationale, lessons learned and recommendations for Phase Two or bilateral technology verification. (5) If either government makes a public claim about Phase One that the other disputes, establish a 48-hour joint factual clarification process: both co-chairs review the claim and issue a joint statement of what is verified or disputed; public disagreement signals loss of bilateral confidence.

6. Specification of Critical Assumptions About Operator Honesty and Vendor Cooperation

The plan assumes that operators participate in good faith, that vendors provide accurate attestation and maintenance records, and that customs and logistics documentation is reliable. However, it does not specify what happens if these assumptions are violated: (a) if an operator falsifies maintenance records or conceals equipment damage; (b) if a vendor deliberately provides false attestation credentials; (c) if customs records are forged or incomplete. The plan's layered-evidence approach is meant to catch such deception, but does not explicitly state that detection of vendor or operator fraud is a Stop condition.

Recommendation: Add Operator and Vendor Fraud Detection and Escalation Rules: (1) Define substantiated fraud as: deliberate falsification of records, provision of known-false attestation or identity credentials, concealment of equipment damage or undisclosed modifications, or deliberate obstruction of inspector access. (2) Specify consequences: discovery of substantiated operator fraud at a site triggers automatic site suspension and investigation within 7 days; if fraud is confirmed, the site fails Phase One and the operator's participation agreement is terminated with penalty clauses enacted. (3) Discovery of substantiated vendor fraud triggers: first offense = that vendor is decertified for future participation; second offense = the vendor is referred to both governments' law-enforcement authorities for potential criminal investigation. (4) Emphasize in the bilateral instrument that fraud discovery does not invalidate the entire Phase One test; other sites and vendors continue to operate. (5) Include a 'Fraud Discovery Review' in the final Go/Modify/Stop decision: if fraud was discovered, rate its severity and scope, and whether it materially affects the detection rates or Go/Modify/Stop threshold. A single site with fraud can be excluded from the final verdict (4-site data becomes 3-site data for threshold scoring) rather than triggering an automatic Stop.

7. Alignment of Contingency Budget Allocation with Identified Risks

The plan allocates USD 500M (250M per country) as contingency and surge capacity. However, the risk summary identifies potential overruns: gate-delay cost USD 150–300M (if Phase One clock is deferred to Month 9 = 2027-07-08); site-replacement cost USD 50–200M; examiner overrun USD 3.6–11.2M; exercise-incident recovery USD 1–2M (estimate). Total exposure = USD 515M worst-case, exceeding the contingency by USD 15M. The contingency is insufficient if multiple risks coincide. Moreover, the governance rule (double-key approval required for contingency release) creates a risk that co-chairs deadlock and funding is unavailable when needed.

Recommendation: Revise Contingency Governance and Sizing: (1) Increase contingency reserve to USD 600M (USD 300M per country), adding USD 100M to cover simultaneous gate delays and site replacement without exceeding reserve. Adjust allocations by reducing one of the fixed envelopes slightly (e.g., reduce 'Secure Facilities' from USD 750M to USD 650M, assuming cyber-resilience tools can be shared or deferred). (2) Establish a Contingency Fast-Track: items up to USD 50M per side (USD 100M total, pre-authorized) can be released on single co-chair request plus next-day notification to the counterpart; no veto right, only a right to review. (3) For contingency releases >USD 50M per side, require both co-chair signatures within 48 hours; if either co-chair withholds signature, escalate to the neutral referee panel within 24 hours (not the standard 7-day deadlock clock), which issues a binding recommendation within 48 hours. (4) Track contingency burn monthly; if cumulative contingency use exceeds USD 150M by Month 7 (2027-05-08), convene an emergency budget review: co-chairs must jointly certify that remaining contingency is sufficient for foreseeable risks or recommend extending the appropriation window or reducing scope.

8. Integration of Human Factors and Inspector Fatigue Management

The plan specifies 24/7 shift coverage with leave rotation and separation of duties, but does not address human-factor risks: (a) inspector fatigue during 90-day continuous operations (risk of missed events or errors); (b) morale and retention if inspectors are trapped on-site or face dangerous conditions; (c) family separation and mental-health support; (d) how to manage burnout if exercises are frequent (up to 2 per month per site, potentially stressful). The plan budgets USD 750M for personnel but does not itemize leave pay, training stipends, hazard pay, or mental-health support.

Recommendation: Add Human Factors and Inspector Welfare Framework: (1) Specify that leave coverage is paid and mandatory: each inspector takes 2 weeks of leave per quarter (25% of time); replacements are hired and trained specifically for leave rotation, not pulled from critical-path personnel. (2) Establish a 'Fatigue Management Protocol': inspectors work a maximum of 12 consecutive hours per shift; no more than 4 consecutive 12-hour shifts before a 48-hour break; workload is monitored by the counterintelligence unit, and inspectors are rotated to light-duty (administrative work) if they show signs of fatigue. (3) Provide on-site mental-health support: each participating site has access to a confidential counselor (one per country, bilingual) available by phone or in-person at least once per week. Counselor records are sealed and shared with the conduct committee only if the inspector requests support for a work-related safety or misconduct issue. (4) Compensate hazard and separation-pay premiums: add a 15% premium to base inspector salary for working in a foreign country, in a restricted zone, with security constraints. This increases personnel cost from the assumed USD 500k/yr to USD 575k/yr (about USD 77M additional for 288 inspectors); fund from contingency or from reductions in other envelope-based spending. (5) Conduct quarterly 'inspector morale surveys' (anonymous, administered by an independent third party); if morale drops below a threshold, investigate root cause and propose corrective actions within 30 days.

9. Clarity on Scope of 'Frontier-Relevant Computing Equipment' Definition

The plan refers to 'frontier-relevant computing equipment' but defers definition to the 'provisional covered-equipment schedule' maintained confidentially by accountable specialists. This is appropriate for security, but it creates ambiguity: (a) does frontier-relevant equipment include only GPUs and AI accelerators, or also FPGAs, ASICs, supercomputing interconnects, liquid-cooling systems?; (b) how are CPU-only systems classified?; (c) are training-specific systems treated differently from inference systems?; (d) is the threshold based on computational capacity (e.g., teraflops), power draw, memory bandwidth, or some other metric? Without a public definition framework, operators and vendors cannot prepare, and the scope may be perceived as shifting.

Recommendation: Establish a Public Scope Framework for Frontier Computing Equipment: (1) Define 'frontier-relevant' in unclassified terms in the bilateral instrument (Month 2 = 2026-12-08): equipment whose computational performance or capabilities fall within the top 5% of deployed systems globally by performance metric (e.g., top 5% of FLOPs per Watt, top 5% of model-training throughput, top 5% of deployed units) in the preceding 12 months. (2) Maintain a confidential Covered Equipment Schedule listing specific equipment classes, models and serial numbers, updated quarterly using this definition. (3) Publish (unclassified) quarterly 'Frontier-Relevant Equipment Index': a summary of equipment categories covered (e.g., 'A100 GPUs, H100 GPUs, Custom ASICs for Model Training, Liquid-Cooled Supercomputing Nodes') without specific counts or locations. (4) Allow operators to petition for equipment classification: if an operator questions whether a specific model is frontier-relevant, submit a request to the equipment-schedule custodian; both co-chairs must agree on reclassification within 30 days, or the equipment remains in its prior classification. (5) Clarify that the scope does NOT include: consumer/commercial CPUs, commercial networking infrastructure (Ethernet switches), security or facility infrastructure, or storage systems (unless containing AI-accelerator components).

The specialist would review whether the proposed deadlock definition, referee-panel composition, and automatic-suspension triggers are diplomatically defensible and whether the current 7/14-day clock windows are realistic for contested equipment-identity disputes.

What: Assess whether the deadlock definition (7 days) and automatic-suspension trigger (14 days) are consistent with similar bilateral verification regimes (New START, OPCW), whether neutral-referee membership is achievable without creating new trust problems, and whether double-key release of contingency (fast lane USD 50M) is administratively feasible within 5 business days.

1.3 Follow Up Consultation

Next consultation should address: (1) Bilateral instrument drafting status and which articles codify the conditional-start fallback, forensic-panel hierarchy and vendor-refusal ladder; (2) domestic authority enactment timeline decomposed by country, with named leads and escalation procedures; (3) vendor pre-binding negotiation progress—which Tier-1 vendors are on track and which face refusal risk; (4) inspector vetting progress and counterintelligence agency capacity to meet Month 5 (2027-03-08) deadline; (5) ledger operational status and key-ceremony scheduling; (6) contingency governance and whether USD 15M exposure gap requires additional appropriation or scope trade-off; (7) how calibration data will be integrated or excluded from final-decision evidence base; (8) whether any site-selection candidate is at risk of withdrawal and fallback-site substitution contingency. Bring updated entry-conditions dashboard and draft bilateral instrument articles to next meeting.

1.4.A Issue - Entry Conditions Timeline Is Compressed and Lacks Fallback Authority

The plan maps seven entry conditions to Months 2–6 (2026-12-08 to 2027-04-08). However, the domestic authority enactment (Month 3.5 = 2027-01-23) is the critical path, and no decomposition by country or fallback exists if one government's legislation slips >4 weeks. A 4-week slip defers Phase One by 3 months and costs USD 150–300M in holding expenses, consuming one-third of contingency. The gate also gives the slower government an unilateral timing veto, contradicting the reciprocity principle.

1.4.B Tags

  • domestic-authority-risk
  • unilateral-timing-veto
  • contingency-exposure
  • compressed-timeline

1.4.C Mitigation

Immediately decompose every domestic legal act by country and approval body (e.g., US Congressional ratification, State Department authorization, China State Council directive) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23 17:00). Establish a bilateral entry-conditions steering committee with weekly reviews from Month 0 (2026-10-08 09:00). Identify each country's critical-path item and assign a named domestic-authority lead. Pre-draft a conditional-start fallback into the bilateral instrument permitting the clock to begin at each site once that site's entry conditions are met, removing the slower-country veto. Obtain both governments' signed acceptance by Month 1 (2026-11-08 17:00). If any authority slips >4 weeks, escalate to co-chairs within 2 working days with written fallback proposal.

1.4.D Consequence

Without fallback authority, a slip in one government's legislation (e.g., parliamentary recess, committee delay) can defer Phase One indefinitely, holding USD 50–100M per month. A 3-month slip to Month 9 (2027-07-08) exhausts contingency and compresses pre-test calibration, forcing locked thresholds on unvalidated data. This increases the risk of a Modify outcome driven by mis-set yardsticks rather than mechanism performance. A further delay past the Month 9 (2027-07-08) backstop triggers an extend-or-stop decision that may be forced rather than principled.

1.4.E Root Cause

The plan treats all seven entry conditions as simultaneous prerequisites, reflecting the strict gate principle. However, no mechanism exists to isolate one country's administrative delay from the timeline or to permit bounded conditional start. The bilateral instrument itself may not yet authorize per-site entry phasing.

1.5.A Issue - Vendor Refusal Cascade and Unverifiable Equipment Threshold Risk

The plan allocates USD 0.5B for independent testing, red teams and fallback examiners across all four sites and 90 days. However, vendor-refusal escalation paths (request → escalation → examiner notified → exam → day-10 report) assume pre-qualified examiners and clean-room facilities are operational. If critical vendors are not pre-bound by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23 17:00) and examiners not pre-qualified and contracted by Month 4 (2027-02-08), material equipment will be classified unverifiable by Months 3–4 (2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08). At hard sites (those with complex third-party access), unverifiable equipment may exceed the 5% Go threshold, failing the site.

1.5.B Tags

  • vendor-dependency
  • unverifiable-equipment
  • fallback-pool-delay
  • hard-site-risk

1.5.C Mitigation

7.4.A Issue - Entry-Gate Critical-Path Bottleneck: Inspector Vetting Timeline Creates Unilateral Timing Veto

Inspector counterintelligence vetting requires 14–16 weeks (20+ if deprioritized), with no documented acceleration path or surge capacity. Since all inspectors must be approved before the Phase One clock starts (Month 6 = 2027-04-08), any delay in either country's security-clearance process blocks certification of Entry Condition 6 ('all inspectors approved') and defers the 90-day test indefinitely. The plan documents this as the critical-path item but offers no fallback: no conditional start, no reduced roster, no pre-emergency vetting of surge staff. This gives whichever government controls the slower vetting process an effective veto over timing, contrary to the double-key governance principle.

7.4.D Consequence

Without mitigation, a single country's security agency can defer the 90-day test by 3–6 months, accumulating USD 150–300M in holding costs (per canonical facts). This inverts reciprocity: the mechanism fails not because either government distrusts the design, but because one bureaucracy controls the timeline. Phase One becomes a hostage to domestic process, not a test of bilateral verification. The project faces either indefinite delay or a forced choice to waive full vetting and accept reduced credibility.

7.4.E Root Cause

The plan treats inspector vetting as a hard constraint (all inspectors must be approved before clock start) without a backstop or conditional-start option. This mirrors the strict gate principle, but it conflates procedural security (vetting credibility) with timing governance. A true reciprocity design would either make vetting time-bounded with a fallback, or permit a conditional start with heightened monitoring of interim rosters. The plan's tone is cautious and audit-heavy, but it has no mechanism to absorb unilateral delay in one country's security process.

8.4.A Issue - Domestic Authority Enactment Timeline Lacks Decomposition and Fallback

The plan lists 'domestic access authority enacted (Month 3.5 = 2027-01-23)' as a mandatory entry condition, but does not decompose the specific legislative or executive acts required in each country, their approval timelines, or the critical path. If either government's authority enactment slips >4 weeks (e.g., from Month 3.5 = 2027-01-23 to Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23), the Phase One clock start is deferred 4–8 weeks, accumulating USD 50–100M holding cost and cascading into compressed pre-test calibration. No explicit fallback exists: the plan states 'no partial-start exceptions,' giving the slower government an effective timing veto. The entry-conditions steering committee is implied but not formally chartered.

8.4.B Tags

  • entry-gate-veto-risk
  • domestic-authority-decomposition-missing
  • fallback-timing-undefined
  • holding-cost-unbudgeted
  • steering-committee-not-chartered

8.4.C Mitigation

By Month 0 (2026-10-08 16:00), both co-chairs must table a written decomposition of every domestic legal act required (e.g., US Congressional resolution, China State Council directive), each act's approval body and committee review timeline, and the single-item critical path. Establish a bilateral entry-conditions steering committee with weekly signed reviews and named domestic-authority leads per country. If any authority item slips >4 weeks from baseline, trigger political escalation within 2 working days. Pre-draft a conditional-start fallback into the bilateral instrument by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23 17:00) permitting Phase One clock at each site once conditions are met, final decision after all sites complete 90 days. Obtain both governments' signed acceptance by Month 1 (2026-11-08).

8.4.D Consequence

Without decomposition and fallback, a legislative delay in either country defers Phase One indefinitely, accumulating USD 150–300M holding cost (3 months x USD 50–100M) that exceeds contingency headroom. Compressed pre-test calibration or skipped calibration forces decision-thresholds to lock on unvalidated provisional data, risking a Modify outcome that reflects the yardstick, not the mechanism's real performance. Deadlock over timing damages reciprocal confidence before Phase One begins.

8.4.E Root Cause

The plan treats domestic authority as a binary entry condition without identifying which government is the critical path or what happens if one side is slow. The entry-conditions gate is specified as 'strict' with 'no partial-start exceptions,' but no fallback plan exists for the timing-veto risk it creates. Appropriations governance is mentioned as 'funding timeliness' (45-day + 30-day cure = 75-day threshold) but domestic authority enactment is not similarly bounded.

8.5.A Issue - Ledger Divergence Forensic Authority Not Pre-Authorized; Divergence Clocks Expire Unchecked

The plan specifies that unresolved ledger divergence >7 days triggers automatic suspension (an explicit Stop condition), and that a joint forensic panel will investigate disputed entries within 48 hours. However, the plan does not pre-authorize the panel's membership, decision-making authority, or evidence-weighting hierarchy before Phase One. If two national ledgers disagree on equipment identity or event timing and the forensic panel is not empowered in writing by both governments and the bilateral instrument, disputes devolve into co-chair negotiation, which can exceed the 48-hour investigation window and cause the divergence clock to expire, triggering automatic suspension of a functioning mechanism. Additionally, shift-boundary cross-signing is mentioned as a procedure but not mandated operationally or budgeted.

8.5.B Tags

  • forensic-panel-pre-authorization-missing
  • divergence-escalation-hierarchy-undefined
  • shift-cross-signing-not-operationalized
  • automatic-suspension-hair-trigger
  • ledger-credibility-risk

8.5.C Mitigation

By Month 0.5 (2026-10-23 17:00), recruit and vet a joint forensic-identity panel (3–5 senior specialists per country, vetted by both governments). Codify in the bilateral instrument a pre-agreed evidence-weighting hierarchy: (a) cryptographic attestation if both ledgers match; (b) physical inspection + chain of custody if attestation unavailable; (c) maintenance records if inspection unavailable; (d) third-party logs as lowest rank. Panel issues binding or co-chair-delegated findings within 48 hours; if no consensus, co-chairs decide within 24 hours. Mandate shift-boundary cross-signing: mirrored inspectors jointly sign at 08:00, 16:00, 24:00 UTC daily, certifying no undisclosed divergence. Configure ledger for automatic divergence detection and alert within 2 hours; forensic investigation within 48 hours; resolution within 7 days or escalate to co-chairs for stop/suspend decision.

8.5.D Consequence

Without pre-authorized forensic authority, unresolved ledger divergence can trigger automatic suspension of a site or event class even if the underlying equipment identity is sound and both inspectors agree on facts. This converts a technical or communication lag into a spurious Stop trigger that terminates Phase One not due to access asymmetry or real concealment but due to procedural breakdown. Loss of bilateral confidence; credibility damage to the mechanism; accusations that one side 'weaponized' the divergence clock to veto an inconvenient finding.

8.5.E Root Cause

Empty

8.6.A Issue - Vendor Refusal Escalation Path Not Confirmed; Critical Equipment Becomes Unverifiable Before Month 3 (2027-01-08)

The plan specifies a day-10 vendor-refusal ladder and designates vendor-supervised testing, filtered evidence, accredited independent examiners, and clean-room procedures as fallback routes. However, the plan does not confirm that critical vendors are pre-bound, independent examiners are pre-qualified, or clean-room facilities are contractually available by Phase One clock start. If a critical vendor (e.g., the only supplier of custom attestation hardware) refuses access at Month 3 (2027-01-08) or Month 4 (2027-02-08) during equipment intake, and no pre-qualified examiner or clean-room is available, material equipment is classified unverifiable and logged. Accumulation of unverifiable equipment across 2 sites can exceed the 5% threshold (proposed), failing one or both sites under the Stop rule. No contingency allocation is earmarked for late-engaged examiners; examiner costs overrun by USD 3.6–11.2M (estimate) versus the USD 1.5–4.0M allocated, consuming contingency headroom.

8.6.B Tags

  • vendor-pre-binding-not-confirmed
  • examiner-pre-qualification-missing
  • clean-room-capacity-not-reserved
  • vendor-refusal-cascade-risk
  • contingency-overrun-examiner-costs

8.6.C Mitigation

By Month 0.5 (2026-10-23 17:00), identify the top 8–12 Tier 1 vendors at each proposed site (manufacturers, attestation-key holders, maintenance providers, logistics). Conduct bilateral negotiations to sign pre-Phase-One cooperation agreements binding each vendor to equipment-identity attestation, evidence preservation, escort, and maintenance-record access; include penalty clauses (USD 500k–2M per material refusal). Obtain countersigned agreements for at least 80% of Tier 1 vendors by Month 1 (2026-11-08). Pre-qualify 3–5 independent examiner labs per country and 2 accredited clean-room facilities per geography by Month 1 (2026-11-08); sign access and confidentiality agreements. Confirm cost per examination (USD 20–50k) and schedule capacity (5 parallel exams/week minimum per facility). Lock the day-10 escalation ladder in writing before clock start; document that equipment unverifiable at day 10 (one extension to day 15) triggers the unverifiable-equipment KPI and contributes to site-level Go/Modify/Stop determination.

8.6.D Consequence

If vendors are not pre-bound and examiners not pre-qualified, vendor refusals accumulate from Month 3 (2027-01-08) onward, leaving material equipment unverifiable. By Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08), one or both sites may exceed the 5% unverifiable-equipment threshold (proposed), triggering a Stop decision before Phase One meaningfully begins. Alternatively, the program pivots to expensive late-engaged examiners, overrunning contingency by USD 3.6–11.2M (estimate) and leaving no surge margin. Loss of bilateral confidence if the mechanism appears unable to overcome vendor refusal; asymmetric burden if one country's vendors are more cooperative than the other's, creating apparent reciprocity failure.
