Review 1: Critical Issues

  1. Domestic Authority Enactment Timeline Lacks Decomposition and Creates Unilateral Timing Veto: The plan identifies 'domestic access authority enacted Month 3.5 (2027-01-23)' as a mandatory entry condition but provides no country-specific legislative decomposition, approval bodies, or fallback if one government's process slips >4 weeks. A 4-week slip costs about USD 50–100M (estimate); a 3-month delay to Month 9 (2027-07-08)—the backstop decision window—accumulates USD 150–300M holding cost and eliminates pre-test calibration, forcing threshold lock-in on unvalidated provisional data. This cascades into increased Modify-outcome probability (from a 15–25% baseline (estimate) to 30–40% (estimate)) driven by yardstick error, not mechanism failure. Recommendation: Immediately decompose each country's required legislative acts and establish a bilateral steering committee with weekly milestone tracking; keep the strict entry gate and rely on the Month 9 (2027-07-08) double-key extend-or-stop backstop; a pre-clock dry run on non-covered equipment may be used, but it does not start the 90 days.

  2. Vendor Refusal Escalation Paths and Independent-Examiner Pre-Qualification Are Not Confirmed Before Clock Start: The plan specifies a day-10 vendor-refusal ladder and designates 3–5 examiner labs per country and 2 clean-room facilities per geography as fallback infrastructure, but agreements are targeted for Month 4 (2027-02-08)—after entry-condition certification (Month 6 = 2027-04-08). If vendors refuse cooperation at Month 3–4 (2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08) and examiners are not pre-qualified, material equipment will accumulate unverifiable status, exceeding the <5% Go threshold (canonical fact), forcing Modify at 5–10% and failing the site above 10%. Contingency worst-case already exposes USD 515M against USD 500M reserve (about USD 15M shortfall per canonical facts); late-engaged examiners add USD 3.6–11.2M overrun (estimate). Recommendation: Begin generic (non-site-specific) vendor soundings and obtain letters of intent from 80% of Tier-1 vendors by Month 1 (2026-11-08) (early-warning indicator only, draft text, not locked; per-site vendor lists follow the Month 2 = 2026-12-08 ratification), and gather examiner/clean-room cost (USD 20–30k per exam) and capacity (5 parallel exams/week) commitments by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); binding agreements remain due by Month 4 (2027-02-08).

  3. Ledger Divergence Forensic Authority Not Pre-Authorized; Automatic Suspension Clocks Turn Technical Faults into Stop Triggers: The plan defines automatic suspension at 7 days of unresolved divergence as an explicit Stop condition but does not pre-authorize the joint forensic-identity panel (3–5 per country) or lock the evidence-weighting hierarchy before Phase One clock start. Without pre-committed forensic authority and an operational shift-boundary cross-signing protocol, disputed equipment identity or sync delays will consume the 7-day divergence clock without resolution, triggering automatic suspension of a functioning mechanism and converting administrative gridlock into a spurious Stop outcome. This cascades with vendor-refusal delays: if both divergence deadlock and vendor refusal occur simultaneously at a site, overlapping Tier 2 (72-hour) and Tier 3 (14-day) clocks will interact, accelerating site suspension risk. Recommendation: From Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), start vetting the forensic panel (provisional appointment pending clearance); by Month 1 (2026-11-08), codify the evidence-weighting hierarchy in the bilateral instrument and operationalize shift-boundary cross-signing procedures on non-covered equipment, with ledger divergence detection and forensic escalation tested by Month 4 (2027-02-08).

Review 2: Implementation Consequences

  1. Successful Go Decision Establishes Precedent for Bilateral Frontier-Technology Verification, Enabling Phase Two Expansion and Long-Term Reciprocal Confidence: A credible Go verdict (detection ≥90% unreported arrivals, ≥85% substitutions, ≥80% record falsification per canonical thresholds) at Month 10 (2027-08-08) positions the Consortium as a replicable model for reciprocal verification of critical technology. Phase Two expansion to additional sites or equipment classes requires new bilateral-instrument amendment and fresh appropriations but leverages the existing USD 750M personnel envelope and USD 1.25B ledger infrastructure (already amortized). Long-term impact: reduced geopolitical friction on frontier-AI controls and a shared verification standard transcending US–China bilateral scope. Interaction: a Go outcome depends entirely on pre-test calibration (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) validating provisional thresholds; compressed or skipped calibration cascades into mis-set yardsticks, forcing Modify or Stop and eliminating Phase Two option. Recommendation: lock calibration completion and threshold validation by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), with explicit co-chair sign-off that thresholds are 'validated' before formal blind challenges begin.

  2. Contingency Worst-Case Depletion (USD 515M Against USD 500M Reserve) Leaves Negative Surge Margin and Eliminates Fault Tolerance for Concurrent Fallbacks: The plan's contingency exposure—gate delay USD 150–300M + site replacement USD 50–200M + examiner overrun USD 3.6–11.2M + incident recovery USD 4M—totals about USD 515M (canonical fact), exceeding the USD 500M contingency by about USD 15M. If gate slip and vendor refusal cascade occur simultaneously (moderate probability per risk analysis), contingency is exhausted before examiner costs are fully absorbed, forcing either scope compression (reduced site count or exercise cap) or supplemental appropriation request at Month 3 (2027-01-08). This interacts with domestic-authority delays: a 4-week legislative slip costs USD 50–100M/month holding; if coupled with a site replacement (USD 50–200M) triggered by operator withdrawal, contingency is depleted by Month 4 (2027-02-08), leaving no buffer for Phase One operational incidents. Recommendation: by Month 3 (2027-01-08), conduct a bilateral contingency-exposure review and either approve supplemental funding (USD 25–50M), pre-bind 100% of Tier 1 vendors to reduce examiner-overrun risk, or propose a double-key budget change to the USD 50M fast-lane cap (25M per side) to accelerate recovery if concurrent fallbacks activate.

  3. Strict Entry Gate with No Conditional-Start Fallback Transfers Timing Risk Entirely to Bilateral Domestic Processes, Creating Indefinite Delay Exposure and Potential Phase One Cancellation: The entry-gate design (all 7 conditions certified simultaneously, no per-site partial start per canonical facts) means a single country's domestic-authority delay >4 weeks defers the entire 90-day clock indefinitely. A slip from Month 6 (2027-04-08) to Month 9 (2027-07-08) backstop window consumes pre-test calibration and locks thresholds unvalidated; further slip past Month 9 (2027-07-08) triggers co-chair extend-or-stop decision with no technical justification (calibration not completed), risking Stop from procedural gridlock rather than mechanism failure. Political cost: the slower-moving government gains unilateral timing veto, inverts reciprocity, and erodes bilateral trust before Phase One begins. This cascades with inspector-vetting delays (14–16 weeks, Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23 to Month 4.5 = 2027-02-23): if vetting slips 4 weeks in one country, entry certification is blocked even if other conditions are complete, compounding the timing-veto risk. Recommendation: keep the strict gate (no per-site or conditional start) and rely on the Month 9 (2027-07-08) double-key extend-or-stop backstop; track domestic-authority milestones weekly to give early warning. Any conditional start would be a change to the gate design that must be decided explicitly by double-key.

Review 3: Recommended Actions

  1. Secure Letters of Intent from 80% of Tier-1 Vendors by Month 1 (2026-11-08); Binding Agreements by Month 4 (2027-02-08): Expected impact: eliminates vendor-refusal cascade risk and reduces contingency examiner-overrun exposure (USD 3.6–11.2M in total, estimate) by pre-negotiating cost, capacity, and penalty clauses (USD 500k–2M per refusal). Priority: Critical. Implementation: by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), run generic vendor soundings and draft a standardized binding-agreement template (draft text, not locked); after the Month 2 (2026-12-08) site ratification, identify top 8–12 vendors per site; operators and legal counsel execute negotiations in parallel across all 4 sites; target 80% letters of intent by Month 1 (2026-11-08) as an early-warning tripwire, with binding agreements signed by Month 4 (2027-02-08).

  2. Operationalize Shift-Boundary Cross-Signing and Forensic-Panel Authority by Month 1 (2026-11-08); Stress-Test on Non-Covered Equipment by Month 4 (2027-02-08): Expected impact: reduces automatic-suspension risk from unresolved ledger divergence by pre-authorizing forensic decision-making within 48 hours, eliminating the 7-day clock expiry that converts technical sync faults into spurious Stop triggers. Risk reduction: 30–40% of potential false-stop cascades prevented. Priority: Critical. Implementation: start vetting forensic panel (3–5 per country) at Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), with provisional appointment pending clearance; codify evidence-weighting hierarchy in bilateral instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08); operationalize and stress-test shift-handover procedures on non-covered equipment by Month 4 (2027-02-08).

  3. Conduct Pre-Test Calibration (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) and Lock Thresholds by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23): Expected impact: validates provisional Go/Modify/Stop thresholds (detection ≥90% unreported arrivals, ≥85% substitutions, ≥80% record falsification) against real equipment and inspector performance, reducing Modify-outcome probability driven by mis-set yardsticks from 15–25% to <5% (estimate). Time saving: eliminating unvalidated threshold lock-in preserves calibration window even if domestic authority enactment slips. Priority: Critical. Implementation: reserve 100–150 non-covered equipment units per site by Month 3 (2027-01-08); execute 50–100 blind-challenge scenarios per site Months 4–5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08); document detection rates by event type; recalibrate if >20% divergence detected; issue double-key signed locked-threshold document by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23).

Review 4: Showstopper Risks

  1. Operator Withdrawal or Non-Compliance Mid-Phase-One Cascades Site Failure and Contingency Depletion: Operator refusal to bind vendors, allow inspectors, or participate in exercises (estimated 5–10% probability per site per canonical facts) forces site suspension and cascades with entry-condition delays. If an operator withdraws after Month 6 (2027-04-08) clock start, a 4–8 week replacement-site activation (USD 50–200M) depletes contingency; simultaneous gate-delay holdover (USD 150–300M) and examiner overrun (USD 3.6–11.2M) total USD 515M worst-case, exhausting the USD 500M reserve by approximately USD 15M. Likelihood: Medium. Interaction: operator withdrawal at a hard site (high third-party access, vendor-refusal risk) compounds vendor-refusal cascades, accelerating unverifiable-equipment accumulation. Mitigation: Lock operator participation via legally binding bilateral agreement (by Month 4 = 2027-02-08) with penalty clauses (USD 1–10M per material breach); pre-identify and pre-vet a standby alternate operator at a nearby site. Contingency: If primary operator withdraws, activate the alternate within 2 weeks and the Month 10 (2027-08-08) decision applies only to an on-time Month 6 (2027-04-08) start; a replacement delays the clock start rather than lengthening Phase One, absorbing replacement-site cost from contingency sub-envelope ring-fenced at Month 3 (2027-01-08).

  2. Geopolitical Deterioration or Political-Will Withdrawal During Entry-Condition Phase Halts Domestic Authority Enactment and Collapses Bilateral Commitment: A significant geopolitical incident or domestic political transition (estimated 15–25% probability per risk analysis) between Month 0 (2026-10-08) and Month 6 (2027-04-08) can cause one government to reinterpret the bilateral instrument, withdraw inspector vetting support, or withhold appropriation tranche release. Holding cost accumulates USD 50–100M/month; withheld funding triggers Stop condition at 75 days total (45-day + 30-day cure per canonical fact), terminating Phase One before calibration or clock start. Political cost: reciprocal confidence collapses; Phase Two extension becomes impossible. Likelihood: Medium. Interaction: political pressure cascades with domestic-authority legislative delays (already 4+ weeks likely), compounding the timing-veto and entry-gate bottleneck into indefinite stall. Mitigation: Secure high-level (presidential or cabinet-equivalent) political commitment to Phase One at project kick-off (Month 0 = 2026-10-08); establish a bilateral political steering committee (foreign ministers, quarterly) to reinforce commitment and preempt reinterpretation. Contingency: If political support wanes, invoke a 6-month pause clause in the bilateral instrument (negotiated by Month 1 = 2026-11-08) allowing Phase One to suspend and resume without termination; hold appropriations in escrow during pause, preserving the 18-month availability window (Month 18 = 2028-04-08).

  3. Attestation Trust Root Provenance Compromise or Rejection Forces Cryptographic Redesign and Invalidates Identity-Verification Evidence Layer: Joint key ceremony (split-custody joint root) or cross-validating national roots required for cryptographic attestation (one of three evidence layers per canonical hierarchy). If either government rejects the joint-ceremony location or refuses second-country participation (estimated 5–10% probability), or if a cryptographic weakness is discovered post-deployment (estimated 5% probability per expert review), attestation evidence layer collapses. Equipment-identity confidence drops from 90%+ to 60–70% (estimate), reducing corroboration-layer options and forcing reliance on physical inspection + records alone. Redesign or national-roots pivot requires 2–4 weeks delay (absorbed in ledger envelope) but cascades with Phase One clock: if attestation failure occurs at Month 7–8 (2027-05-08 to 2027-06-08), mid-test evidence reassessment becomes necessary, triggering a Modify verdict or forensic deadlock (Tier 3, 14-day clock). Likelihood: Low. Interaction: attestation failure combined with vendor-refusal cascade (high probability) reduces fall-back examiner evidence sufficiency and accelerates unverifiable-equipment counts beyond threshold. Mitigation: By Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), submit attestation design to independent third-party cryptographic audit; by Month 2 (2026-12-08), pre-authorize a national-roots pivot contingency (two independent attestation roots cross-validating each other) and code it into the bilateral instrument as an automatic fallback if joint ceremony is rejected or key compromise occurs. Contingency: If attestation compromise is discovered during Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), invoke emergency key rotation and re-signing of all attestation records within 1 week; execute a mock re-attestation drill on calibration equipment to validate recovery procedures; pause blind exercises for 2 weeks (compress to 1 per site per month) while forensic investigation completes (no impact to 90-day window if compressed exercises complete by Month 9 = 2027-07-08).

Review 5: Critical Assumptions

  1. Both Governments Sustain Political Will and Domestic Appropriations Release Within 45-Day Window Through Month 6 (2027-04-08): The plan assumes uninterrupted political backing and fiscal discipline across 8 months of entry-condition work. If either government delays appropriation tranche release beyond 45 days (triggering a 30-day cure period; 75 days total = Stop condition per canonical facts), or if a geopolitical incident causes domestic reinterpretation of the bilateral instrument, Phase One never starts. Cost impact: USD 150–300M holding cost (estimate) if gate slip compounds to Month 9 (2027-07-08) backstop; Stop outcome terminates program entirely, rendering all prior investment sunk. Interaction: political withdrawal cascades with domestic-authority legislative delays (already 4+ weeks risk), collapsing both appropriations and vetting authority simultaneously. Recommendation: Secure high-level (presidential/cabinet-equivalent) commitment at Month 0 (2026-10-08); establish bilateral political steering committee (quarterly) to preempt reinterpretation; by Month 1 (2026-11-08), codify an 18-month appropriation hold (through Month 18 = 2028-04-08) in the bilateral instrument, decoupling fiscal availability from routine political cycles.

  2. Independent Examiners and Clean-Room Facilities Exist, Are Willing to Cooperate, and Can Achieve Stated Cost (USD 20–30k per Exam) and Capacity (5 Parallel Exams per Week per Facility): The plan assumes 3–5 examiner labs per country and 2 clean-room facilities per geography exist with equipment-identity expertise, bilateral access agreements, and cost/schedule fit. If examiners are unavailable, cost >USD 100k per exam, or capacity <5 parallel per week, contingency overrun balloons from USD 3.6–11.2M (estimate) to USD 8–15M (estimate), leaving a shortfall of about USD 8–19M (estimate) against the USD 500M reserve. Likelihood: Medium. Interaction: examiner unavailability compounds with vendor-refusal cascades (20–30% probability per site): if both Tier 1 vendors refuse AND examiners are unavailable, unverifiable equipment exceeds the <5% Go threshold within 30 days, forcing Modify (5–10%) or site failure (>10%). Recommendation: By Month 1 (2026-11-08), pre-qualify all 8–12 candidate examiner facilities via RFQ and bilateral legal review; lock cost per exam (target USD 20–30k), capacity commitment (5 parallel/week), and pre-positioned equipment via written MOUs; conduct a mock mock-examination drill at each facility by Month 3 (2027-01-08) to validate methodology and timeline. Contingency measure: if real-time examiners fall short, activate a clean-room contingency lane (2-week turnaround instead of 1-week) or pre-authorize USD 100k per exam and absorb cost via fast-lane contingency release (up to USD 50M total, 25M per side).

  3. Provisional Go/Modify/Stop Thresholds (Detection ≥90% Unreported Arrivals, ≥85% Substitutions, ≥80% Record Falsification; False Positives <5%; Unverifiable <5%) Are Realistic and Achievable Given Real Inspector Performance and Actual Equipment Mix: The plan assumes calibration exercises (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) validate thresholds; if real detection is 70% (vs. 90% target), a Modify outcome is forced not by mechanism weakness but by mis-set yardstick. Cost impact: indefinite Phase Two deferral or program redesign; USD 50–100M/year holding cost if Phase Two is postponed 12+ months pending protocol amendment. Likelihood: Medium (15–25% per expert review). Interaction: threshold miscalibration cascades with gate delays: if domestic authority slips, pre-test calibration is compressed or skipped, forcing thresholds to lock on unvalidated data, guaranteeing Modify or Stop from yardstick error rather than performance. Recommendation: Execute full calibration (50–100 events per site across 7 event types, Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) using blind methodology; by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), document detection rates and confidence intervals; if divergence >20% from provisional targets, recalibrate via bilateral agreement before formal blind challenges begin; mark all locked thresholds as 'calibrated and validated' in the ledger. Contingency measure: if calibration reveals detection is 70–85% (marginal), classify as 'Modify by default' rubric (more conservative outcome without re-tuning); alternatively, add a separate pre-clock calibration extension of 4 weeks to run additional calibration rounds and re-validate; Phase One stays 90 days and the clock starts only after thresholds are locked.

Review 6: Key Performance Indicators

  1. Blind-Challenge Detection Rate by Event Type (Target: ≥90% Unreported Arrivals, ≥85% Substitutions, ≥80% Record Falsification; Threshold: <70% Triggers Stop): This KPI directly measures the mechanism's core capability and gates the Go/Modify/Stop decision. Monthly tracking during Phase One (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) against these thresholds determines whether the verification design works in practice. Interaction: pre-test calibration (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) validates these targets; if calibration reveals detection is 70–80%, thresholds must recalibrate before formal challenges, avoiding a Modify outcome driven by yardstick error. Recommendation: operationalize independent testing unit monthly scorecards by event type with 95% confidence intervals; escalate any single-event-type detection <5% below target to bilateral technical review within 5 days; lock corrective procedures (e.g., inspector retraining, evidence-layer adjustment) by Month 8 (2027-06-08) to permit recovery before Month 10 (2027-08-08) decision.

  2. Ledger Divergence Resolution Time and Forensic-Panel Decision Latency (Target: Detection Within 2 Hours, Forensic Finding Within 48 Hours; Threshold: >7 Days Unresolved Triggers Automatic Suspension): This KPI ensures automatic-suspension triggers are substantive (real concealment) not procedural (technical sync fault). Weekly monitoring during Phase One tracks divergence incidents, investigation time, and forensic-panel consensus achievement. Interaction: divergence latency cascades with vendor-refusal escalation: if both forensic deadlock and vendor refusal overlap at a site (Tier 2 72-hour + day-10 ladder), concurrent clocks consume resolution capacity and risk overlapping suspension triggers. Recommendation: establish bilateral ledger-forensics dashboard showing divergence detection time, forensic-panel investigation start/end dates, and consensus achievement; automated alert if any divergence exceeds 2 hours detection (sync divergence >4 hours escalated) or 48-hour finding window; monthly rehearsal of mock divergence scenarios to validate shift-handover cross-signing fidelity and forensic-panel responsiveness.

  3. Contingency Budget Burn Rate and Reserve Adequacy (Target: Cumulative Spend USD 75M/Month or Reserve : This KPI tracks whether identified fallbacks (gate delay, site replacement, vendor examiners) are materializing and whether contingency is adequate. Monthly tracking of spending against envelopes by both treasuries and escalation within 5 working days of variance >5% per canonical facts. Interaction: contingency depletion cascades with concurrent fallback activation: gate slip (USD 150–300M) plus site replacement (USD 50–200M) plus examiner overrun (USD 3.6–11.2M) total about USD 515M worst-case, exceeding reserve by about USD 15M; early burn-rate escalation enables fast-lane release (up to USD 50M) or scope adjustment before Phase One begins. Recommendation: establish bilateral budget-tracking working group (biweekly meetings through Month 6 = 2027-04-08); maintain real-time contingency sub-envelope accounting (gate delay, site replacement, vendor fallbacks, surge); if cumulative burn exceeds USD 150M by Month 4 (2027-02-08), convene co-chairs for contingency reallocation or supplemental appropriation decision.

Review 7: Report Objectives

  1. Primary Objectives and Target Audience: This report comprehensively reviews a USD 5.0B bilateral US–China 90-day Phase One verification program (Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) designed to detect undeclared changes to frontier computing equipment at 4 matched declared datacenters. The intended audience is bilateral national-security leadership, appropriations authorities, participating operators, and treaty implementers. The report identifies critical risks (domestic authority delays, vendor refusal cascades, ledger divergence deadlock) and quantifies their impacts in budget (USD 150–515M exposure), timeline (4–8 week slips), and Go/Modify/Stop decision credibility.

  2. Key Decisions Informed: The report supports three categories of gating decisions: (1) entry-condition timing and backstop authority (strict simultaneous-certification gate with the Month 9 (2027-07-08) double-key extend-or-stop backstop); (2) contingency allocation and governance (whether to increase the USD 500M reserve by approximately USD 15M, pre-bind vendors, or authorize fast-lane release up to USD 50M, 25M per side); (3) threshold validation strategy (whether to conduct full pre-test calibration Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08, or compress calibration and lock thresholds on provisional data). Each decision directly determines feasibility of clock start by Month 6 (2027-04-08) and credibility of the final verdict.

  3. Version 2 Differentiation from Version 1: Version 2 should integrate bilateral expert recommendations on entry-condition decomposition, vendor pre-binding timelines, and forensic-panel pre-authorization that Version 1 left unspecified. It should lock specific completion deadlines (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23 for vendor agreements and forensic-panel charter; Month 1 = 2026-11-08 for examiner outreach and pre-qualification) and include operational procedures for shift-boundary cross-signing, divergence detection, and escalation clocks that Version 1 treated conceptually. Version 2 should also clarify the split of the USD 1.0B site-preparation envelope between physical preparation and operator compensation, and quantify monthly milestone tracking dashboards with variance thresholds and escalation triggers.

Review 8: Data Quality Concerns

  1. Vendor Pre-Binding Cost and Cooperation Timeline Lack Documented Evidence of Feasibility: The plan assumes 80% of Tier-1 vendors (8–12 per site = 32–48 vendors total across 4 sites) will give letters of intent by Month 1 (2026-11-08) and sign binding agreements by Month 4 (2027-02-08) with cost-sharing and penalty clauses (USD 500k–2M per refusal). However, the report provides no documented vendor contact lists, preliminary willingness indicators, or legal-precedent case studies showing similar vendors have agreed to comparable terms under bilateral U.S.–China programs. Consequence: if vendors refuse pre-binding or demand higher penalties/costs, contingency examiner overrun escalates from USD 3.6–11.2M (estimate) toward USD 5–15M, raising the shortfall against the USD 500M reserve to about USD 8–19M (estimate) instead of about USD 15M. Recommendation: by Month 0 (2026-10-08), conduct confidential generic (non-site-specific) bilateral outreach to at least 3–4 Tier-1 vendors per country; document preliminary willingness, cost constraints, and legal-authority concerns; validate that at least 60% of contacted vendors are receptive before drafting binding-agreement templates at Month 0.5 (2026-10-23).

  2. Domestic Legislative Authority Enactment Timelines and Critical-Path Items Not Decomposed by Country: The plan targets domestic access authority by Month 3.5 (2027-01-23) but does not name specific U.S. Congressional committees, Chinese State Council divisions, or estimated approval timelines (e.g., 'Senate Foreign Relations Committee review: 6–8 weeks; China State Council: 4–6 weeks'). Consequence: without country-specific decomposition, identifying which government's process is the critical path is impossible; a vague timeline creates indefinite delay risk and removes early-warning capacity. If either country's authority slips 4 weeks undetected, gate delay balloons from USD 50–100M/month (estimate) to an uncapped holding cost, potentially consuming the entire USD 500M contingency before Phase One starts. Recommendation: by Month 0 (2026-10-08), both co-chairs' legal teams document the specific legislative acts, approving bodies, and realistic committee-review timelines per country; map the Gantt path showing which country's approval is slowest; establish bilateral steering-committee weekly reviews with named owners and 2-week escalation triggers for any item slipping >4 weeks from baseline.

  3. Examiner Pre-Qualification Cost Estimates (USD 20–30k per Exam) Not Anchored to Market Benchmarks or Existing Supply: The plan allocates USD 0.6–1.2M per site for 30–40 equipment-identity examinations but assumes cost of USD 20–30k per exam without citing comparable bilateral inspection precedents (e.g., IAEA safeguards inspector cost per on-site visit, OPCW managed-access examiner cost). Consequence: if real market cost is USD 75–100k per exam (not verified), a cascade of 40 vendor-refusal exams per site exceeds budget by USD 2.0–3.2M per site (USD 8–12.8M total), compounding the contingency worst-case from about USD 515M to roughly USD 512–519M (estimate: 504 + revised overrun of USD 8–15M), a shortfall of about USD 8–19M (estimate). Recommendation: by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), conduct a bilateral RFQ (request for quote) to at least 3–5 candidate examiner labs in each country; collect firm pricing for equipment-identity examination (including cryptographic attestation, physical inspection, measurement, documentation); validate whether USD 20–30k is realistic or must be recalibrated upward; lock final cost estimates and adjust contingency allocation accordingly before Month 1 (2026-11-08).

Review 9: Stakeholder Feedback

  1. Bilateral Co-Chair Political Commitment and Authority Under the Strict Entry Gate: Critical stakeholder feedback needed from both national co-chairs (appointed by Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23) is whether they have authority to take the double-key extend-or-stop decision at the Month 9 (2027-07-08) backstop. Impact if unresolved: a domestic-authority enactment slip cascades to the entire Phase One clock and exhausts the USD 150–300M gate-delay contingency cost. Recommendation: both co-chairs confirm in writing by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) their authority to take the backstop decision; no per-site or conditional start is permitted.

  2. Operator Willingness to Bind Vendors via Domestic Contract Enforcement and Participate in Exercises Without Production Disruption Compensation Caps: Participating operators (2 US, 2 China) must sign binding agreements committing vendors to cooperation, equipment-identity disclosure, and evidence preservation (canonical fact: by Month 4 = 2027-02-08). Critical gap: operators have not yet confirmed their willingness to bind their supply chains contractually, nor have they negotiated compensation for production-disruption costs if exercises interfere with active computation (exercises capped at 2 per site per month per decision, but impact cost is unquantified). Unresolved: if operators demand >USD 50M per site in disruption compensation or refuse to bind strategic vendors (e.g., custom-accelerator manufacturers), the site-preparation budget (USD 250M per site allocation) or contingency (USD 500M total) will be inadequate. Impact if unresolved: operator refusal or renegotiation cascades with vendor-refusal cascades, accelerating site failure risk from 15–25% (estimate) to 30–40%, multiplying contingency exposure. Recommendation: conduct confidential bilateral operator engagement by Month 0 (2026-10-08); confirm willingness to bind Tier-1 vendors and quantify acceptable disruption-compensation caps; lock operator binding agreements with explicit vendor-binding and exercise-participation terms by Month 4 (2027-02-08).

  3. Independent Testing Unit Governance, Staffing, and Neutral-Country Acceptance by Both Governments: The plan specifies an independent testing unit staffed by neutral-country nationals (not controlled by US or China) with authority to manage sealed double-key exercise schedules and score blind-challenge detection results (decision). Critical stakeholder feedback needed: which third country, if any, will host the testing unit and its staff (Switzerland, UN facility, Sweden—all mentioned illustratively); have both national governments pre-approved the governance charter and staffing model; can neutral-country experts be recruited and security-cleared for both governments by Month 2 (2026-12-08) to allow exercise-scenario design by Month 1 (2026-11-08)? Unresolved: if a testing-unit location or neutral-country partner cannot be agreed by Month 1 (2026-11-08), exercise credibility is undermined and both governments risk contesting fairness of results. Impact if unresolved: delay of 4–8 weeks in testing-unit operationalization compresses the blind-exercise execution window (originally Months 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) and may force reduction from 2 exercises per site per month to 1, lowering statistical confidence in detection rates and increasing Modify-outcome probability by 10–15% (estimate). Recommendation: by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), both co-chairs nominate preferred neutral-country host or international organization; by Month 1 (2026-11-08), finalize bilateral acceptance of testing-unit charter, governance, and staffing; confirm neutral-country leadership appointment and security-clearance eligibility by Month 2 (2026-12-08).

Review 10: Changed Assumptions

  1. Domestic Appropriations Release Timing and Fiscal-Year Budget Cycles May Not Align with Bilateral Entry-Condition Milestones: The plan assumes appropriations tranches are released within 45 days of fiscal-year start; however, U.S. fiscal year (October 1) and China's budget cycle (January–March approval) do not synchronize with the entry-condition timeline (Month 0 = 2026-10-08 through Month 6 = 2027-04-08). If either country's fiscal-year recess, legislative schedule, or interagency review delays tranche release beyond the 45-day window (plus 30-day cure = 75-day Stop threshold per canonical facts), the phase-one clock risks deferral of 4–8 weeks, accumulating USD 50–100M holding cost (estimate). Interaction: appropriations delay cascades with domestic-authority legislative lag, doubling entry-condition bottleneck risk. Recommendation: by Month 0 (2026-10-08), both treasuries confirm their fiscal-year tranche-release schedules and identify any legislative recess or budget-cycle misalignment; establish a bilateral appropriations-acceleration working group (biweekly through Month 3.5 = 2027-01-23) with named fiscal officers to track release timelines and escalate any delays >2 weeks within 5 working days.

  2. Inspector Counterintelligence Vetting Capacity and Expedited-Review Willingness by Both Security Agencies Assumed but Not Pre-Committed: The plan targets 14–16 week inspector-clearance completion (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23 to Month 5 = 2027-03-08) for 120–150 candidates per country, but neither country's security agency has formally committed to expedited review or dedicated vetting capacity. If vetting backlogs or competing security priorities reduce clearance throughput, roster fill at Month 5 (2027-03-08) will fall below the 80% entry-condition threshold, triggering gate delay. Cost impact: delayed inspector deployment extends holding cost by USD 50–100M/month (estimate); if vetting slips 4 weeks, Phase One clock defers to Month 7 (2027-05-08), compressing blind exercises and reducing statistical power for detection-rate estimation by 20–25% (estimate), increasing Modify-outcome probability. Interaction: vetting delay cascades with pre-test calibration (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08); if rosters are not filled by Month 5 (2027-03-08), calibration personnel are insufficient and thresholds lock on simulated (not real-inspector) performance. Recommendation: by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), both counterintelligence services issue written commitment to expedited vetting timelines and assign dedicated personnel to Phase One clearance processing; establish monthly bilateral vetting-status reviews (naming individuals, clearance completion rates) from Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) through Month 5 (2027-03-08).

  3. Pre-Qualified Independent Examiner Labs and Clean-Room Facilities Assumed Available at Stated Cost (USD 20–30k per Exam) Without Market Validation or Long-Term Capacity Confirmation: The plan allocates USD 0.6–1.2M per site for 30–40 examinations but assumes examiner availability, expertise in cryptographic attestation and equipment-identity verification, and pricing of USD 20–30k per exam without obtaining firm quotes or signed capacity-commitment letters. If actual market cost is USD 75–100k per exam (not verified) or if examiners lack bilateral access credentials or equipment-specific knowledge, contingency examiner-overrun exposure balloons from USD 3.6–11.2M (estimate) to USD 8–15M (estimate), leaving a shortfall of about USD 8–19M (estimate) and triggering supplemental-appropriation request at Month 4 (2027-02-08). Interaction: examiner-cost overrun cascades with vendor-refusal cascades (20–30% probability per site per canonical facts): if both Tier-1 vendors refuse cooperation AND examiners are unaffordable, unverifiable-equipment counts exceed the <5% Go threshold (canonical), forcing Modify (5–10%) or site failure (>10%) within 30 days of Phase One start. Recommendation: by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), conduct bilateral RFQ to 5–8 candidate examiner labs and clean-room facilities; obtain firm pricing, capacity commitments (minimum 5 parallel exams/week per facility), and signed MOUs confirming bilateral access authority and security clearance readiness by Month 1 (2026-11-08); adjust contingency examiner sub-envelope or contingency-release fast-lane authority if real pricing exceeds USD 50k per exam.

Review 11: Budget Clarifications

  1. Split of USD 1.0B Site-Preparation Envelope Between Physical Infrastructure and Operator Compensation Remains Undefined: The canonical facts specify that operator and vendor compensation is administered by each national government within its USD 500M allocation (2 sites x USD 250M per site) of the USD 1.0B site-preparation envelope, but the split between physical staging, access-control systems, and redaction facilities versus direct operator payments is unspecified. Impact: if operator compensation demands (estimated USD 50–100M per site for equipment shutdown, staging access, and exercise participation) consume more than half the USD 250M per-site budget, physical site preparation (marked zones, ledger terminals, redaction workspace) becomes underfunded, delaying zone certification by 2–4 weeks and pushing Phase One clock start from Month 6 (2027-04-08) to Month 7–8 (2027-05-08 to 2027-06-08). Recommendation: by Month 1 (2026-11-08), both governments confirm operator-compensation targets and allocate the remaining balance to physical infrastructure; lock the per-site split in the bilateral instrument, with any variance >10% requiring co-chair reallocation approval.

  2. Contingency Worst-Case Exposure (USD 515M Against USD 500M Reserve) Lacks Documentation of Which Fallbacks Are Highest Priority if Budget Must Be Rationed: The contingency worst-case (gate delay USD 300M + site replacement USD 200M + examiner overrun USD 11M + incident recovery USD 4M) totals approximately USD 515M (estimate), exceeding the USD 500M reserve by approximately USD 15M. However, the plan does not specify a triage order if multiple fallbacks activate simultaneously: should gate delay be fully funded even if vendor-examiner costs exceed budget, or should examiner costs be capped and unverifiable equipment accepted as a Stop risk? Impact: if co-chairs must choose between funding a 3-month gate slip (USD 300M) versus complete vendor-refusal examiner escalation (USD 11M), the decision is undefined, risking either Phase One collapse from underfunded delay or site failure from insufficient examiner coverage. Recommendation: by Month 2 (2026-12-08), both co-chairs explicitly rank contingency priorities (e.g., gate delay >50%, site replacement >30%, examiner overrun >15%, surplus <5%); codify in the bilateral instrument which fallbacks are mandatory-fund and which trigger scope reduction if reserve is depleted.

  3. Contingency Fast-Lane Release Authority (USD 50M Total, 25M per Side, 5-Day Approval) Not Validated Against Actual Treasury Payment Processing Timelines: The canonical facts specify fast-lane contingency release up to USD 50M total (USD 25M per side) on joint co-chair signature within 5 business days. However, actual U.S. Treasury and Chinese fiscal authorities may require 10–15 business days for fund transfer, clearing, and accounting reconciliation, not 5 days. Impact: if examiner engagement or gate-delay recovery requires immediate funding (Tier 3 escalation within 14 days) but fast-lane processing takes 10–15 days, the fallback executes late, cascading into unverifiable-equipment accumulation or deferred Phase One clock start by 1–2 weeks. Recommendation: by Month 1 (2026-11-08), both treasuries confirm actual fund-release timelines under bilateral authority; if 5-day approval is infeasible, either pre-position contingency sub-allocations (up to USD 25M per side, USD 50M total, in a rapid-access escrow; any larger sum needs a recorded double-key budget change) or extend the fast-lane approval window to 10 days and adjust contingency-dependent fallback timelines accordingly.

Bilateral Entry-Conditions Steering Committee Chair and Weekly Milestone-Owner Assignment: This role must explicitly define who convenes the weekly steering committee (must be a co-chair or their named deputy with veto authority), tracks each of the 7 entry conditions against bilateral deadlines, escalates any item slipping >4 weeks within 2 working days, and owns the Month 9 (2027-07-08) backstop preparation. Unclear ownership risks that domestic-authority delays (critical path) go undetected until Month 4–5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08), consuming USD 50–100M holding cost per month before escalation occurs. Recommendation: by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), both co-chairs appoint equal named steering-committee owners with explicit authority to convene weekly, assign action items with signed sign-offs, and escalate delays to co-chairs in writing within 48 hours of detection.

  2. Joint Forensic-Identity Panel Authority and Deadlock Escalation Owner: The forensic panel (3–5 per country) must have an explicitly designated bilateral convener who activates investigations within 2 hours of divergence detection, coordinates consensus-building, and escalates to co-chairs within 24 hours if no consensus is reached by hour 48. Unclear authority creates 48-hour forensic-finding gaps; automatic suspension at 7 days then fires on procedural gridlock rather than real concealment. Impact: spurious Stop outcomes, reputational damage. Recommendation: by Month 1 (2026-11-08), appoint a named bilateral forensic-panel director (neutral or alternating co-conveners) with written charter codifying 48-hour investigation deadline and 24-hour co-chair escalation obligation; lock in the bilateral instrument.

  3. Contingency Release and Fast-Lane Fast-Drawer Authority: Fast-lane contingency release (up to USD 50M total, 25M per side, within 5 business days per canonical facts) requires a named bilateral contingency officer with pre-delegated signing authority and a clear escalation path if one co-chair disputes a USD 50M release request. Unclear ownership risks delays: if examiner engagement or gate-delay recovery requires immediate funding but ownership is contested, release is blocked and fallback execution slips 1–2 weeks, cascading into unverifiable-equipment or deferred clock start. Impact: USD 50–100M/month holding cost. Recommendation: by Month 2 (2026-12-08), both treasuries designate a named contingency officer per country with explicit pre-authority to approve release within 5 business days; codify in the bilateral instrument that release up to USD 50M total (25M per side) requires joint signature, subject to post-release audit.

Review 13: Timeline Dependencies

  1. Inspector Counterintelligence Vetting (14–16 Weeks, Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23 to Month 5 = 2027-03-08) Is Critical Path for Entry Certification; If Slipped >4 Weeks, Cascades into Compressed Calibration and Unvalidated Threshold Lock-In: Vetting must complete before all 7 entry conditions are certified at Month 6 (2027-04-08). A 4-week slip defers roster approval to Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), eliminating pre-test calibration buffer (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08); thresholds lock by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23) on provisional data, raising Modify-outcome probability from a 15–25% baseline (estimate) to 30–40% (estimate). Vendor Pre-Binding (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23 Target) Must Precede Examiner Pre-Qualification (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) to Establish Fallback Pool Feasibility; Reversed Sequencing Risks Unaffordable Examiner Costs: Binding Tier-1 vendors (8–12 per site) determines which vendors will refuse cooperation and thus how many examiners must be engaged (20–40 per site estimate). If examiner pre-qualification begins before vendor-binding outcome is known, examiners may be contracted at premium cost (USD 75–100k per exam vs. budget USD 20–30k per exam), overrunning contingency by USD 3.6–11.2M (estimate). Interaction: vendor-binding and examiner-cost sequencing cascades with the day-10 vendor-refusal ladder: if examiners are pre-committed to availability but vendors unexpectedly refuse en masse, examiner capacity may be consumed before real fallbacks are activated, leaving later refusals unmitigated. Recommendation: complete generic vendor soundings and collect letters of intent from 80% by Month 1 (2026-11-08), with countersigned binding agreements by Month 4 (2027-02-08); only then finalize examiner MOUs and cost locks by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), anchoring examiner prices to actual vendor-refusal forecast.

Ledger Forensic-Panel Authority Must Be Pre-Authorized and Operationalized (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) Before Shift-Boundary Cross-Signing Stress Testing (Month 4 = 2027-02-08); Without Pre-Authorization, Divergence Clocks Expire on Procedural Gaps: Forensic-panel charter codification, evidence-weighting hierarchy lock-in, and shift-handover procedures must precede operational testing so that mock divergence scenarios (Month 4 = 2027-02-08 stress test) validate the 2-hour detection and 48-hour resolution timeline. If forensic authority is not pre-authorized until Month 3 (2027-01-08), the stress test (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) reveals procedural gaps with insufficient time to remediate before Phase One clock start (Month 6 = 2027-04-08), leaving divergence resolution untested. Impact: automatic suspension at 7 days unresolved divergence (canon) fires on untested procedures, converting technical sync faults into spurious Stop triggers. Interaction: forensic-panel delay compounds with inspector-vetting delays—if both rosters and forensic authority are unoperationalized by Month 5 (2027-03-08), Phase One entry certification at Month 6 (2027-04-08) rests on unvalidated procedures. Recommendation: by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), recruit forensic-panel members and begin vetting; by Month 1 (2026-11-08), issue joint forensic-panel charter and lock evidence hierarchy in the bilateral instrument; conduct full operational test on non-covered equipment by Month 4 (2027-02-08), with tabletop mock divergences validating 48-hour resolution before formal clock starts.

However, if a Go decision mandates ongoing bilateral verification beyond Month 18 (2028-04-08)—e.g., continuous monitoring at 2–4 sites with standing ledger and inspection teams—sustainment costs are unbudgeted. However, contingency worst-case exposure is approximately USD 515M against USD 500M reserve (about USD 15M shortfall per canonical facts), leaving near-zero margin if spending exceeds baseline by >3%. The plan specifies escalation within 5 working days but does not define co-chair remedies if cumulative spend approaches USD 450M by Month 6 (2027-04-08): does fast-lane approval (USD 50M cap) permit supplemental contingency release, or must scope be compressed (reduce exercise frequency, defer Phase Two)? Recommendation: by Month 2 (2026-12-08), both treasuries jointly define contingency-spend-rate limits (e.g., stop-loss trigger at USD 400M cumulative); specify escalation remedies (fast-lane increase by double-key budget change, supplemental appropriation request, or automatic scope reduction) indexed to cumulative burn and months remaining until final decision.

Review 15: Motivation Factors

  1. Clear, Visible Detection of Mechanism Success in Calibration (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) and Early Phase One (Months 6–7 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-05-08) Sustains Bilateral Political and Technical Team Commitment: Motivation falters if calibration exercises fail to detect staged substitutions or unreported arrivals, signaling the mechanism may not work. If real-inspector detection of blind-challenge scenarios falls below 80% (proposed threshold) during calibration, teams face 4–6 week threshold-recalibration delay and risk of Modify verdict before Phase One formally begins, eroding confidence in Go potential. Interaction: detection failure cascades with domestic-authority delays—if entry certification already slips 4+ weeks to Month 7 (2027-05-08), low calibration results trigger further demoralization and co-chair questioning of program viability. Recommendation: by Month 3 (2027-01-08), establish a bilateral 'quick-win' dashboard tracking early Phase One detection rates (Months 6–7 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-05-08) against provisional thresholds; communicate successes (e.g., '95% substitution detection in pilot exercise') to stakeholders within 2 weeks of event completion to maintain political and operational momentum.

  2. Predictable, Transparent Escalation and Resolution of Discrepancies Within Published Tier-Clock Bounds (24–72 Hours for Tier 1–2; Day 14 for Tier 3) Prevents Perception of Arbitrary Deadlock and Bureaucratic Stalling: Motivation erodes if contested equipment-identity disputes or vendor-refusal cases drag unresolved for weeks beyond the published clocks (proposed thresholds), appearing to paralyzed by politics rather than mechanism failure. If a Tier 2 clock (72 hours) is repeatedly extended without written justification or a co-chair decision materializes on day 10 of a 14-day Tier 3 (proposed threshold), operators and inspectors perceive the process as rigged or ineffectual, reducing cooperation and increasing exit risk. Interaction: escalation-clock uncertainty cascades with contingency pressure—if a site faces 10+ unresolved discrepancies accumulating against the <10% Go threshold (proposed), teams lose faith that timely resolution is possible, spurring informal withdrawal. Recommendation: by Month 4 (2027-02-08), operationalize the bilateral adjudication unit and issue a public-facing escalation 'dashboard' showing every active discrepancy, its clock status (hours/days remaining), and assigned owner; enforce the published clock timelines rigorously with automatic escalation alerts to co-chairs 24 hours before expiry.

  3. Tangible Evidence of Bilateral Cooperation and Reciprocal Fairness in Exercise Scenarios, Inspector Access, and Evidence-Sharing by End of Month 8 (2027-06-08) Demonstrates Mutual Commitment and Prevents Perception of One-Sided Advantage or Asymmetry: Motivation collapses if inspectors from one country appear to have materially more zone access, evidence availability, or favorable exercise scenarios than the other, perceived as favoritism or bad faith. If parity metrics diverge >20% (proposed threshold) by Month 8 (2027-06-08)—e.g., US inspectors witness 60% of events, China inspectors witness 40%—teams perceive asymmetry as strategic rather than logistical, triggering accusations of rigged testing and reducing technical collaboration. Interaction: parity divergence cascades with political withdrawal—if geopolitical tension is already elevated, visible asymmetry in exercise fairness or access becomes a political weapon, collapsing reciprocal confidence and triggering consent withdrawal. Recommendation: by Month 7 (2027-05-08), both technical teams jointly publish a 'Reciprocity Report' documenting witness-participation parity, event-scheduling fairness, and evidence-sharing compliance by event type; issue monthly supplements through final decision (Month 10 = 2027-08-08), with any variance >20% escalated to co-chairs within 5 days for real-time correction.

Automated alerts route to forensic panel within 15 minutes if discrepancy exceeds tolerance. Savings: eliminates manual drift-checking workload (~4 FTE auditor-hours per month per site = ~192 FTE-hours across 4 sites annually); accelerates forensic escalation from 4–6 hours (estimate) to automated routing. Interaction: supports pre-authorized forensic-panel authority (Month 1 = 2026-11-08 deadline); if manual divergence detection remains, forensic investigations miss the 48-hour finding window and automatic suspension cascades. Recommendation: by Month 2 (2026-12-08), bilateral ledger-operations team designs and deploys the hash-comparison automation; conduct monthly validation drills on non-covered equipment.

Savings: eliminates manual clock-tracking overhead (~6 FTE adjudication-admin hours per month per site = ~288 FTE-hours annually across 4 sites); prevents missed deadlines that trigger spurious automatic suspensions. Monthly report auto-generated within 5 days of month-end; thresholds trigger escalation alerts (e.g., parity divergence >20% proposed threshold). Savings: eliminates 20–30 FTE-hours per month of bilateral data reconciliation and manual dashboard compilation (~240–360 FTE-hours annually); enables real-time parity course-correction within 5 days rather than 2–3 week delay. Interaction: supports reciprocity-maintenance motivation factor (motivation memo, third point); if parity divergence >20% is detected early, co-chairs can rebalance exercise scenarios or access within days, preventing cascading political accusations of asymmetry. Recommendation: by Month 5.5 (2027-03-23), bilateral technical teams code automated data-ingestion pipelines from both ledger copies and lock the KPI-calculation formulas; enable monthly dashboard publication within 5 days of month-end through final decision (Month 10 = 2027-08-08).

Q1: What is the core purpose of the 90-day Phase One test, and why does it require strict entry conditions certified before the clock starts rather than allowing sites to begin testing independently?

A1: Phase One verifies declared equipment changes at four matched datacenters using layered evidence and a replicated ledger, ending in a Go/Modify/Stop decision. Strict entry certification (all 7 conditions simultaneously: instrument, appropriations, authority, sites, inspectors, agreements, schedule) keeps setup failures from being logged as verification failures, protecting the integrity of detection results. However, this creates timing-veto risk: if one country's entry-condition completion lags >4 weeks, the entire 90-day clock defers, accumulating USD 150–300M holding cost and compressing pre-test calibration that validates thresholds.

Q2: Why does vendor refusal pose a material threat to Phase One success, and what fallback routes are designed to mitigate unverifiable equipment accumulation?

A2: Vendor refusal (estimated 20–30% probability per site) blocks attestation, maintenance records, or identity disclosure, leaving equipment unverifiable. The day-10 escalation ladder (vendor request → examiner notified → exam → report) depends on pre-qualified independent examiners and clean-room facilities; without pre-binding vendors and pre-qualifying examiners by Month 1 (2026-11-08), fallback routes are unavailable when refusals occur at Month 3–4 (2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08). Material equipment then exceeds the <5% unverifiable Go threshold, failing the site. Contingency worst-case exposure balloons from USD 3.6–11.2M (if examiners are pre-qualified at USD 20–50k per exam) to USD 5–15M (late-engaged at USD 75–100k per exam), exhausting the USD 500M contingency reserve entirely (about USD 15M shortfall baseline).

Q3: How does ledger divergence between the two national ledger copies escalate to automatic suspension, and what pre-authorized procedures exist to prevent technical sync faults from being misclassified as concealment?

A3: Unresolved ledger divergence >7 days (canonical threshold) triggers automatic suspension, an explicit Stop condition. However, no joint forensic-identity panel is pre-authorized before Phase One, and no evidence-weighting hierarchy is codified. Without pre-authorized forensic authority issuing findings within 48 hours, divergence clocks expire and suspension fires on procedural gridlock (sync lag, timestamp mismatch) rather than real concealment. Mitigation requires pre-recruiting and vetting a forensic panel (3–5 per country) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), codifying a dispute-resolution hierarchy in the bilateral instrument by Month 1 (2026-11-08), and operationalizing shift-boundary cross-signing (mirrored inspectors jointly signing at every 8-hour handover) so divergences are detected within 2 hours and escalated, not expired.

Q4: What is the 'strict gate' entry-condition model, and why does it create a timing veto for whichever government completes its domestic authority enactment last?

A4: The strict gate (decision, canonical) requires all 7 entry conditions—bilateral instrument, appropriations, domestic access authority, site selection, inspector approval, operator/vendor agreements, equipment schedule—to be certified simultaneously by both co-chairs before Phase One clock starts (Month 6 = 2027-04-08). If one country's domestic legislative authority lags (e.g., from Month 3.5 = 2027-01-23 to Month 5 = 2027-03-08, a 6–8 week slip), the entire test is deferred because the gate cannot be certified. The slower government gains an unilateral timing veto, violating reciprocity principles. No conditional-start fallback exists (canonical: no partial or per-site conditional start), so gate delay directly cascades into Phase One clock deferral, accumulating USD 50–100M/month holding cost (estimate) and compressing pre-test calibration that validates thresholds.

Q5: What contingency worst-case cost scenario exhausts the USD 500M reserve, and what actions can prevent cascading fallback activation from terminating Phase One prematurely?

A5: Contingency worst-case exposure is approximately USD 515M (canonical estimate): USD 300M gate-delay holding cost (if Phase One clock slips 3 months to Month 9 = 2027-07-08 backstop) + USD 200M site-replacement cost (4–8 week activation if operator withdraws) + approximately USD 11M vendor-examiner overrun (if independent examiners cost USD 75–100k per exam instead of budgeted USD 20–50k) + USD 4M exercise-incident recovery, totaling approximately USD 515M, exceeding the USD 500M contingency by approximately USD 15M (canonical). Simultaneous gate slip and vendor refusal cascade depletes contingency by Month 4 (2027-02-08), leaving no surge margin. Mitigation: pre-bind 80% of Tier-1 vendors by Month 1 (2026-11-08) to reduce examiner overrun; authorize contingency fast-lane release up to USD 100M (vs. USD 50M current cap) on joint signature within 5 business days; or pre-allocate contingency sub-envelopes (e.g., USD 200M gate delay, USD 150M site replacement, USD 100M examiner fallbacks) to prevent one category from consuming the entire reserve.

Q6: What are the core ethical tensions between bilateral verification transparency and the protection of intellectual property, and how does the plan balance these conflicting obligations?

A6: The plan explicitly prioritizes IP protection: narrow marked zones (staging, spare, maintenance only), operator-run evidence redaction audited by inspectors, and filtered metadata (equipment identifiers and seals only, not workload or model weights). However, this creates an ethical tension: inspectors cannot verify absence of concealment in unmapped areas, leaving 'blind spots' where substitution or unreported arrival could hide. The plan acknowledges this trade-off (Decision 3) but does not resolve the ethical question of whether reciprocal access with knowable gaps constitutes honest verification or mutual consent to incomplete coverage. The three-tier zone-infraction protocol (Tier 3 = immediate removal for boundary violation) enforces compliance but may also chill legitimate investigation if inspectors fear accusation of boundary-testing.

Q7: What is the Stop-condition trigger for 'funding withheld,' and why does allowing a 75-day cure period create asymmetric incentive structures between the two governments?

A7: Funding withheld (canonical: 45-day disbursement window plus 30-day cure = 75 days total, then Stop) is an explicit Stop condition, applying symmetrically to both countries. However, the asymmetry lies in incentive timing: the government with slower domestic fiscal processes (or one facing competing budget priorities) can deliberately delay its tranche up to 44 days without legal Stop trigger, while the other government's contingency holding costs accumulate at USD 50–100M/month (estimate). The delayed-payer government can extract negotiating leverage (e.g., demand protocol amendments or site substitution) knowing that stopping Phase One costs both sides political credibility but imposes disproportionate cost on the faster-moving party. The 75-day threshold was designed to prevent indefinite stalling, but does not prevent 2–3 month delays that exhaust contingency and compress calibration.

Q8: How does the plan's assumption that 'no single evidence source is decisive' interact with the controversial doctrine that cryptographic attestation, physical inspection, and maintenance records can collectively confirm equipment identity without vendor cooperation, and what happens if that assumption fails?

A8: The evidence-corroboration rule (canonical: identity confirmed when at least 2 independent layers agree, including physical inspection plus identifier match and—where available—validated attestation) assumes that if a vendor refuses attestation keys, physical inspection plus maintenance records are sufficient corroboration. However, this assumption is unvalidated: a sophisticated attacker (either operator or third-party manufacturer) could physically modify equipment while maintaining serial numbers and maintenance-record authenticity, defeating the two-layer corroboration. The plan acknowledges vendor refusal as a 20–30% probability (estimate) per site, yet does not document whether the pre-qualified independent examiners have demonstrated capability to detect internal modification without attestation hooks. If the two-layer fallback fails in blind-challenge exercises (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08 calibration), detection rates for substitutions could fall from the 85% (proposed threshold) target to 60–70%, forcing a Modify or Stop outcome that reflects the evidence-rule assumption failure, not mechanism weakness.

Q9: What is the controversial distinction between a 'Stop' decision triggered by mechanism failure (detection <70%, unverifiable equipment >10%) versus 'Stop' triggered by procedural breakdown (ledger divergence unresolved >7 days, automatic suspension), and how does the plan prevent conflating the two?

A9: The plan defines Stop as either mechanism failure (detection rates miss targets, unverifiable equipment exceeds threshold, asymmetric access unresolved) or procedural breakdown (automatic suspension at 7-day ledger divergence expiry, funding withheld at day 75). However, the plan does not distinguish these categories in the final Go/Modify/Stop decision document. If a site is automatically suspended because the forensic panel did not issue a finding within 48 hours (procedural gap), it is recorded identically to a site that failed because substitution-detection rate was 60% (mechanism failure). This conflation is controversial because: (1) a procedural-shutdown Stop does not reflect on the mechanism's real capability and may damage bilateral confidence unfairly; (2) the other side can credibly blame the mechanism's design when the real cause was vetting, staffing or decision-authority gaps; (3) Phase Two expansion decisions rest on the narrative of why Phase One ended, and a procedurally-shutdown Stop may be more easily remedied (add forensic-panel capacity, shorten divergence clocks) than a mechanism-failure Stop (redesign evidence layers, retrain inspectors). The plan does not require documenting the Stop rationale category (procedural vs. substantive).

Q10: Does the plan's scope exclusion ('no total-capacity estimates, no workload or weight inspection, no hidden-facility claims') limit its strategic value for deterring frontier AI development that occurs outside declared datacenters, and what is the implicit political acceptance of this limitation?

A10: The plan verifies changes at 4 declared sites only (user constraint); it explicitly excludes capacity estimation, workload inference, hidden-facility detection, and comprehensive AI governance (user constraint). This is a deliberate scope boundary, not a technical limitation. The strategic implication is that a Go decision certifies only that declared equipment changes at known sites can be verified—it does not validate that all frontier AI work is at declared sites, nor does it detect undeclared facilities or classify unmonitored training runs. If either government operates frontier AI work at sites not in the 4 declared locations, Phase One verification is silent and provides no deterrent. The plan assumes both governments accept this limitation as a fair trade-off: verification of transparency at observable locations in exchange for acceptance that clandestine work outside declared sites cannot be detected. However, this assumption is politically fragile: if a Go decision is seen as a clean bill of health for all frontier AI, a later discovery of hidden work at an undeclared site would catastrophically damage bilateral trust and be portrayed as verification failure, even though the mechanism functioned as designed.

A premortem assumes the project has failed and works backward to identify the most likely causes.

Assumptions to Kill

These foundational assumptions represent the project's key uncertainties. If proven false, they could lead to failure. Validate them immediately using the specified methods.

ID Assumption Validation Method Failure Trigger
A1 Both governments will complete domestic access authority, appropriations and inspector vetting within roughly 4 weeks of each other, so the strict gate certifies at Month 6 (2027-04-08) without a timing veto. By Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), obtain written decompositions of required domestic acts, approving bodies and realistic timelines from both governments, plus vetting-agency capacity commitments. Either country's critical-path act or vetting is projected more than 4 weeks behind the Month 3.5 (2027-01-23) or Month 5 (2027-03-08) milestones, or no written commitment is obtained.
A2 Critical vendors will sign binding cooperation agreements, and independent examiners and clean-room facilities exist at the assumed cost (USD 20-30k per exam budgeted, estimate) and capacity (5 parallel exams per week, estimate). Fewer than 60% of contacted vendors are receptive, or firm quotes exceed USD 75k per exam, or capacity is below 5 exams per week.
A3 Both governments will accept the evidence rules, locked thresholds and independent testing unit as principled, so a Go, Modify or Stop verdict is not contested as tuned or biased. Run a tabletop with both red teams and technical leads, scoring five paired scenarios for difficulty parity and testing calibration results against provisional thresholds. Paired scenario difficulty scores diverge by more than 20%, or calibration results diverge more than 20% from provisional thresholds, or either co-chair rejects the fairness rubric.
A4 Narrow marked zones with operator-run redaction will give inspectors enough evidence to meet identity-confidence targets without leaking IP, so neither government withdraws consent. Run a walkthrough at one candidate site with security teams from both sides, mapping evidence available per zone against the 2-layer corroboration rule and logging every redaction removal. More than 20% (proposed threshold) of sampled intake events cannot reach 2 independent layers inside the zones, or either security team identifies an IP exposure path it will not accept.
A5 Operators will accept binding agreements, exercise participation and the USD 250M per-site planning allocation (decision) without demanding compensation or protections that exceed the site-preparation envelope. Hold confidential talks with candidate operators in both countries to obtain written compensation expectations, disruption-liability terms and willingness to bind vendors. Any operator demands compensation that pushes its site above USD 250M, or refuses vendor binding or the exercise cap in writing.
A6 Staffing of about 434 FTE (estimate) at USD 0.5-0.625M loaded cost (estimate) can be recruited, cleared, retained and rotated across 4 sites with 24/7 coverage and no single-person critical functions. Survey both governments' personnel and security agencies for candidate pool size, bilingual availability, loaded-cost benchmarks and rotation constraints for 144 inspectors per country. Qualified candidates are fewer than 120 per country, or loaded cost exceeds USD 0.625M per FTE, or 24/7 coverage cannot be rostered within the 750M envelope.
A7 Both governments will keep political will and fund each tranche within 45 days of fiscal-year start (proposed threshold) despite geopolitical shocks, so no tranche counts as withheld funding. Obtain written confirmation from both treasuries of tranche-release schedules, fiscal-year alignment and recess calendars, plus a leadership-level commitment letter from each government. Either treasury cannot confirm release within 45 days, or schedules show a legislative recess or budget-cycle gap longer than 30 days before Month 6 (2027-04-08).
A8 Cryptographic attestation and the split-custody key ceremony will work as one trusted evidence layer, with both governments accepting a shared facility and no key compromise. Commission an independent cryptographic design review and a tabletop of the joint key ceremony with security teams from both countries, including the national-roots fallback. Either security team rejects the joint facility, the review finds a critical weakness, or the national-roots fallback takes more than 4 weeks (estimate) to stand up.
A9 Mirrored inspectors and operators will cooperate in good faith, and neither government will shield an operator or use infractions and vetoes as political weapons during Phase One. Run a tabletop with conduct-committee members from both countries on five contested infraction and veto cases, scoring whether outcomes are accepted by both sides. Either side rejects more than 1 of 5 tabletop outcomes as politically motivated, or an operator refuses a protocol element in writing.
